q: Ransomware encrypts every file on a file server. The attacker never views or copies the data, but staff cannot open any of their documents. Which leg of the CIA triad is MOST directly harmed?
options: Availability, because legitimate users can no longer access or use their data
Confidentiality, because the attacker has taken control of the contents of the files
Integrity, because the encrypted files no longer match their original readable form
Non-repudiation, because the attacker cannot be identified from the encrypted data
explain: Ransomware harms availability: the data still exists and was never read, but authorized users cannot use it. Confidentiality would require disclosure to an unauthorized party, and integrity concerns unauthorized alteration of content, not loss of access.

q: An accountant discovers that a supplier's bank details on an invoice were quietly changed, so a payment went to a fraudster's account. Which leg of the CIA triad failed?
options: Availability, because the funds are no longer available to the business
Integrity, because the invoice data was altered without authorization
Authentication, because the invoice arrived without proof of its sender
Confidentiality, because the payment details were exposed to an outsider
explain: The data was changed by an unauthorized party, which is an integrity failure: data must be what it claims to be. Nothing in the scenario shows the data was disclosed (confidentiality) or that a system became unavailable.

q: A database containing customer records is copied and posted publicly by an intruder, but the original database is untouched and the service keeps running. Which leg of the CIA triad was violated?
options: Accounting, because the intruder's actions were not recorded in any log
Integrity, because a copy of the database now exists outside the company
Confidentiality, because sensitive data was disclosed to unauthorized people
Availability, because customers may lose trust and stop using the service
explain: Copying and publishing data is a disclosure to unauthorized parties, which is the definition of a confidentiality breach. The original data was not altered, so integrity held, and the service stayed up, so availability held.

q: A hospital adds a second, independent power feed and a generator so its records system keeps running through a utility outage. Which leg of the CIA triad does this control primarily support?
options: Confidentiality, because patient records are hidden from unauthorized viewers
Integrity, because redundant power prevents records from being altered
Authentication, because staff must prove identity before the system starts
Availability, because the system remains usable when legitimate users need it
explain: Redundant power keeps systems running and accessible during an outage, which is availability. It does nothing to hide data (confidentiality) or prevent alteration (integrity).

q: Before a downloaded software update is installed, the administrator compares its published SHA-256 hash with the hash computed from the downloaded file. What is this check designed to protect?
options: Integrity, because matching hashes show the file was not altered in transit
Availability, because the check confirms the update server is reachable
Non-repudiation, because the hash proves who originally wrote the update
Confidentiality, because hashing hides the contents of the update file
explain: Hash comparison detects any change to the file, which is integrity. Hashing does not hide content the way encryption does, and a hash alone does not prove who created the file.

q: An employee signs in with a password and a fingerprint scan. In AAA terms, what has just occurred?
options: Confidentiality, because the credentials were kept secret during sign-in
Authentication, because the user proved their identity with two factors
Authorization, because the user has been granted a set of permissions
Accounting, because a record of the sign-in has been written to a log
explain: Presenting credentials to prove identity is authentication. Authorization happens after, when the system decides what that proven identity may access, and accounting is the record kept of the activity.

q: After signing in, a nurse can open patient charts for her ward but is denied access to payroll records. Which element of AAA is being enforced at the moment of denial?
options: Authentication, because the system is checking who the nurse really is
Accounting, because the denied attempt will be recorded in the audit log for later review
Authorization, because the system is applying what her identity is allowed to do
Availability, because the payroll system remains online for other staff
explain: Once identity is proven, the decision about what that identity may touch is authorization. Authentication already happened at sign-in, and accounting is the logging of events, not the permission decision itself.

q: Three months after an incident, investigators reconstruct exactly which accounts opened a sensitive file and when, using retained sign-in and access records. Which element of AAA made this possible?
options: Authentication, because each user originally proved who they were
Confidentiality, because the records were stored away from other users
Authorization, because permissions on the file were reviewed and tightened
Accounting, because records of user activity were kept and can be reviewed
explain: Accounting is the record of what was done, which is what lets investigators reconstruct events later. Authentication and authorization controlled the access at the time, but the historical trail is accounting.

q: A company abandons the model of trusting every device inside the office network. Now every request, from any location, is verified before access is granted. Which model has it adopted?
options: Zero Trust, built on the principle of never trust, always verify
Implicit trust, built on verifying identity once at the network edge
Defense in depth, built on layering several different kinds of controls
Perimeter security, built on a hardened boundary around the network
explain: Zero Trust removes trust based on network location and verifies every request on its own merits. Defense in depth is about layering controls, which can complement Zero Trust but is not the model described.

q: Under a Zero Trust design, a user working from the office requests access to one application. What should happen before access is granted?
options: The request is allowed automatically because it originates from inside the office network, where the device was already admitted earlier that day
The request is authenticated and authorized on its own merits, with least privilege for that request
The request is approved once for the whole day based on the user's morning sign-in
The request is checked only against the firewall rules at the network perimeter
explain: Zero Trust verifies every request regardless of where it comes from and grants only the least privilege needed for that request. Location inside the office earns no automatic trust.

q: A firm layers a firewall, endpoint protection, multi-factor authentication, and user training so that no single failure exposes its data. Which concept does this BEST illustrate?
options: Least privilege, limiting each user to the minimum access needed
Security through obscurity, hiding systems and hoping attackers never find them
Defense in depth, using several different controls layered together
Zero Trust, removing all trust from devices inside the network
explain: Layering multiple different controls so one failure is not a breach is defense in depth. Least privilege is about limiting a user's access rights, not about stacking independent safeguards.

q: Which of the following is a technical (logical) control?
options: A guard who patrols the building on a set schedule
A written policy requiring annual security awareness training
A locked door controlling entry to the server room
Firewall rules that filter traffic between network segments
explain: Firewall rules are enforced by technology, making them technical/logical controls. Policies are managerial, locks are physical, and guard patrols are operational because people perform them.

q: A company's information security policy, approved by senior leadership, sets out the rules every department must follow. Which control category is this?
options: Managerial (administrative), because it is enforced through decisions and documents
Technical (logical), because it will eventually be enforced by security software
Physical (environmental), because printed copies are kept in the office
Operational, because department managers carry it out during daily work
explain: Policies are managerial/administrative controls: they are enforced through decisions and documents rather than technology, physical barriers, or defined hands-on work by people.

q: Cameras, fences, and a fire suppression system protect a data center. Which control category do these belong to?
options: Managerial (administrative), because a facilities team manages them
Physical (environmental), because they are enforced by the physical world
Operational, because staff monitor the camera feeds around the clock
Technical (logical), because the cameras record to a digital system
explain: Locks, cameras, fences, and fire suppression act on the physical environment, so they are physical/environmental controls, regardless of who manages or monitors them.

q: Security guards patrol a warehouse on a defined route, and analysts review access logs every morning as part of their assigned duties. Which control category covers this work?
options: Physical (environmental), because the patrols take place in the building
Managerial (administrative), because supervisors assign the patrol routes
Operational, because people perform defined tasks as part of the control
Technical (logical), because the log review uses monitoring software
explain: Operational controls are enforced by people doing defined work, such as guard patrols and scheduled log reviews. The category follows who or what performs the control, not the tools they happen to use.

q: An intrusion prevention system automatically drops malicious traffic before it reaches a web server. What type of control is the IPS?
options: Detective, because it identifies malicious traffic patterns
Deterrent, because attackers may avoid a protected server
Corrective, because it removes attacks after they occur
Preventive, because it stops the event from succeeding
explain: A control that blocks the event is preventive. An IPS inspects traffic, but its defining action here is dropping the attack before it lands; a detective control would only report it.

q: An intrusion detection system sends an alert to the security team when it sees suspicious traffic, but it takes no action to stop the traffic itself. What type of control is it?
options: Detective, because it finds and reports the event without blocking it
Corrective, because the team can fix the problem after the alert
Compensating, because it substitutes for a missing blocking control
Preventive, because its alerts let the team respond more quickly
explain: If a control only tells you about an event, it is detective. The IDS reports; it does not block, so it is not preventive, and it repairs nothing itself, so it is not corrective.

q: A login screen displays a banner stating that activity is monitored and unauthorized use will be prosecuted. The banner's PRIMARY purpose is which control type?
options: Preventive, because it stops unauthorized users from signing in
Deterrent, because it discourages attempts before they happen
Detective, because it warns that activity will be recorded
Directive, because it tells users the rules they must follow
explain: Warning banners and visible cameras are classic deterrent controls: they work by discouraging the attempt. The banner does not itself block access (preventive) or detect an event (detective).

q: After ransomware damages a file server, the team restores the data from clean backups and returns the service to normal operation. The restore is which type of control?
options: Preventive, because it stops the ransomware from spreading further
Detective, because it reveals which files the ransomware encrypted
Corrective, because it repairs the damage after the event has occurred
Compensating, because backups substitute for the failed server hardware
explain: Restoring from backup repairs the effects of an incident after it happened, which is corrective. Backups do not stop the attack (preventive) or uncover it (detective); the restore action itself is the repair.

q: A legacy application cannot support multi-factor authentication. Until it is replaced, the company places it behind extra monitoring and restricts it to a small, isolated network segment. These added measures are which control type?
options: Directive, because they instruct staff how the application may be used
Deterrent, because they make the application a less attractive target
Corrective, because they fix the application's authentication weakness
Compensating, because they substitute for the control that cannot be used
explain: Compensating controls substitute when the real control cannot be implemented. The MFA gap is not fixed, so the measures are not corrective; they stand in for the missing control instead.

q: A company issues a standard requiring passwords of at least fourteen characters and runs annual training so staff understand it. The standard and training are which control type?
options: Directive, because they direct how people are expected to behave
Technical, because password length is enforced by the sign-in system
Preventive, because they stop users from choosing weak passwords
Detective, because they reveal accounts with noncompliant passwords
explain: Policies, standards, and awareness training direct behavior, making them directive controls. Even though a system may later enforce the length, the documents and training themselves guide people rather than block or detect.

q: Highly visible security cameras are installed at every entrance of a building, and signs state that recording is in progress. Which control type is PRIMARILY at work?
options: Detective, because the recordings can be reviewed after an incident
Deterrent, because visible cameras discourage people from attempting wrongdoing
Preventive, because the cameras stop intruders from entering the building
Physical, because cameras are part of the building's installed equipment
explain: The question asks for the control type, and the primary purpose of highly visible cameras with warning signs is to discourage attempts, which is deterrent. Recordings can serve a detective role, but visibility is aimed at discouragement, and 'physical' is a category, not a type.

q: A quarterly audit compares user access rights against job roles and reports several accounts with permissions they no longer need. The audit itself is which type of control?
options: Preventive, because the audit stops staff from requesting extra access
Managerial, because senior leaders commissioned the audit report
Detective, because it finds and reports problems that already exist
Corrective, because the excess permissions will be removed afterward
explain: An audit discovers and reports existing issues, which is detective. Removing the permissions afterward would be corrective, but that is a separate action from the audit itself, and 'managerial' names a category, not a type.

q: Which pairing of control and type is correct?
options: A warning banner at sign-in — corrective
An IDS raising an alert on traffic — preventive
Restoring a server from backup — detective
An IPS dropping an attack in progress — preventive
explain: An IPS blocks attacks, so it is preventive. An IDS only alerts, making it detective; restoring from backup is corrective; and a warning banner is a deterrent, not corrective.

q: A new hire in accounts payable is given access only to the payment system her job requires, and nothing else. Which principle is being applied?
options: Least privilege, granting only the access a role actually needs
Defense in depth, layering controls so one failure is not a breach
Separation of duties, splitting one task between two people
Zero Trust, verifying every request regardless of its source
explain: Least privilege limits each user to the minimum access their job requires. Nothing here splits a task between people (separation of duties) or layers multiple controls (defense in depth).

q: Which of the following is a managerial control?
options: A badge reader controlling entry to an office suite
A documented risk assessment reviewed and approved by leadership
A scheduled review of firewall logs carried out by an analyst every morning
Encryption applied to data stored on a file server
explain: Risk assessments and policies are managerial/administrative controls because they are enforced through decisions and documents. Encryption is technical, a badge reader is physical, and a scheduled log review is operational.

q: Data at a research firm is labeled so that only named project members can open the most sensitive files. The labeling and restricted access work together to protect which leg of the CIA triad?
options: Accounting, because the labels record who accessed each file
Integrity, because the labels prevent anyone from changing the files
Confidentiality, because only the right people can see the data
Availability, because project members can always reach their files
explain: Classification and access control limit who can see data, which protects confidentiality. Labels do not stop an authorized editor from changing content, and they record nothing by themselves.

q: A web application checks each signed-in user's role before displaying the administration menu. Users without the role never see the option. Which AAA element is this?
options: Authentication, because the application confirms each user's identity
Accounting, because the application records each menu request made
Confidentiality, because the menu contents are hidden from most users
Authorization, because the application applies what each identity may do
explain: Showing or hiding features based on a proven identity's permissions is authorization. Identity was already proven at sign-in (authentication), and no record-keeping is described (accounting).

q: A company requires a badge tap plus a PIN to enter its network operations center. The badge and PIN together are an example of which AAA element in action?
options: Authentication, because the person must prove who they are to enter
Accounting, because the reader logs every entry and exit time
Availability, because authorized staff can reach the room when needed
Authorization, because entry rights were assigned when the badge was issued
explain: Presenting a badge (something you have) and a PIN (something you know) proves identity, which is authentication. The reader may also log entries, but the act described is proving who the person is.

q: An attacker changes the amount stored in a payment database from 100 to 10,000. No data is copied and the system stays online. Which leg of the CIA triad is violated?
options: Authentication, because the attacker bypassed the sign-in controls
Integrity, because stored data was altered without authorization
Confidentiality, because the attacker gained access to the database
Availability, because the business can no longer trust its reports
explain: Unauthorized alteration of data is an integrity violation, even if nothing was copied and the system kept running. Access alone is not the harm described; the change to the data is.

q: A distributed denial-of-service attack floods a retailer's website on its busiest sales day, and customers cannot check out. Which leg of the CIA triad is the attack targeting?
options: Confidentiality, because customer payment data is at risk of exposure
Integrity, because the flood corrupts the retailer's sales records
Availability, because the service is unusable by legitimate customers
Non-repudiation, because the attackers cannot be traced afterward
explain: A DDoS attack overwhelms a service so legitimate users cannot use it, which is an availability attack. No disclosure or alteration of data is described.

q: Which control is technical in category AND preventive in type?
options: A camera system that records the data center entrance
A procedure for restoring services after an incident
A policy that requires staff to report suspicious messages
A firewall rule that blocks inbound traffic to a closed port
explain: Firewall rules are enforced by technology (technical) and stop traffic from passing (preventive). The policy is managerial and directive, the camera is physical and detective or deterrent, and the restore procedure is corrective.

q: A user reports that a shared spreadsheet's figures no longer match the source system, although nobody on the team edited it. The security team suspects tampering. Which triad leg should guide their investigation?
options: Integrity, because the data may have been changed without authorization
Authentication, because the editors' identities were never verified
Availability, because the team cannot rely on the spreadsheet being current
Confidentiality, because the figures may have been viewed by an outsider
explain: Data that no longer matches what it should be, with suspected unauthorized change, is an integrity concern. The investigation centers on whether the data was altered, not on disclosure or uptime.

q: In a Zero Trust architecture, what replaces network location as the basis for access decisions?
options: A one-time verification performed when a device first joins the internal network, after which the device is trusted for all later requests
Verification of each request, using identity and context, with least privilege granted per request
The strength of the perimeter firewall standing between the user and the resource
Membership in a trusted department whose devices are pre-approved for access
explain: Zero Trust decides every request on its own merits, verifying identity and granting only the least privilege needed. A single check at join time, a strong perimeter, or department membership all reintroduce location- or group-based trust.

q: A security team wants a control that will notice unauthorized changes to critical system files and alert administrators, without stopping the changes itself. Which type of control should they choose?
options: Corrective, because it returns the files to their original state
Directive, because it instructs administrators on file handling
Detective, because it finds and reports the event as it happens
Preventive, because it acts on the files before damage spreads
explain: A control that notices and reports without intervening is detective. Preventive would block the change, corrective would undo it, and directive controls guide behavior rather than monitor files.

q: Patch management software automatically installs a fix for a vulnerability that was exploited last week, closing the hole the attackers used. The patching action is which control type?
options: Compensating, because it stands in for a control that failed
Detective, because it identifies systems missing the fix
Deterrent, because it discourages attackers from returning
Corrective, because it repairs the weakness after the event
explain: Applying a patch to fix the exploited flaw repairs the problem after the event, which is corrective. Scanning for missing patches would be detective, but the patching itself is the repair.

q: Which of the following BEST describes the accounting element of AAA?
options: Keeping a record of what each authenticated user did, so events can be reconstructed later
Deciding which resources a signed-in user is permitted to open or change
Checking a password, fingerprint, or passkey to confirm a user's identity before any access is granted
Encrypting stored records so that only authorized staff can read them
explain: Accounting is the record of activity that supports later review and investigation. Deciding permissions is authorization, checking identity is authentication, and encrypting records is a confidentiality control, not part of AAA.

q: A policy states that all staff must lock their screens when leaving their desks, and posters in the office repeat the message. Which control type are the policy and posters?
options: Technical, because screen locking is performed by the computer
Directive, because they direct the behavior expected of staff
Detective, because they help identify staff who leave screens open
Preventive, because they stop others from using unattended screens
explain: Policies and awareness posters tell people how to behave, which is directive. The automatic lock timer a system applies would be a separate technical control; the documents and posters themselves only direct.

q: A small business cannot afford an IPS. Instead, it keeps its IDS, shortens log review intervals, and documents the accepted risk until budget allows the upgrade. The shortened reviews and documented acceptance together act as which control type for the missing prevention?
options: Directive, because the documentation instructs staff on the risk
Corrective, because they repair the security gap left by the missing appliance permanently
Compensating, because they substitute for the preventive control that cannot be used yet
Deterrent, because faster reviews discourage attackers from probing
explain: When the preferred control cannot be implemented, substitute measures that address the same risk are compensating controls. The gap is not repaired, so they are not corrective; they stand in for the missing IPS.

q: Which set contains ONLY the three elements of AAA, in the order they occur?
options: Access control, authorization, auditing
Authentication, availability, accounting
Authorization, authentication, accounting
Authentication, authorization, accounting
explain: AAA is authentication (prove who you are), then authorization (what you may do), then accounting (the record of what you did). Availability belongs to the CIA triad, and the order in the last option is reversed.

q: A cloud storage bucket is misconfigured so anyone with the link can read the files inside. Which leg of the CIA triad has failed?
options: Confidentiality, because data is exposed to people who should not see it
Availability, because the files can now be reached from anywhere
Accounting, because reads through the link are not tied to a user
Integrity, because the bucket settings were changed from their defaults
explain: Public exposure of data to unauthorized readers is a confidentiality failure. The data itself was not altered, and being reachable from anywhere is not the availability the triad means, which is access for legitimate users.

q: An organization encrypts laptop drives so that a stolen laptop's contents cannot be read. Which leg of the CIA triad does drive encryption primarily protect?
options: Authentication, because the key proves the laptop owner's identity
Confidentiality, because the data stays hidden from anyone without the key
Integrity, because encryption prevents the data from being changed by anyone who finds it
Availability, because the owner can still recover the data later
explain: Encryption protects confidentiality by making data unreadable without the key. It does not by itself detect changes (integrity) or guarantee the data remains accessible (availability).

q: Two controls guard a vault: a steel door that physically blocks entry, and a sign warning that the area is under surveillance and trespassers will be prosecuted. Which pairing is correct?
options: The door is deterrent and physical; the sign is preventive
The door is preventive and technical; the sign is detective
The door is preventive and physical; the sign is deterrent
The door is detective and physical; the sign is compensating
explain: A door that blocks entry prevents the event and is physical. A warning sign discourages the attempt, which is deterrent. Neither control merely reports events, so detective does not apply.

q: A help desk resets a user's password only after verifying the caller's employee number and a one-time code sent to their phone. Which AAA element is the help desk performing?
options: Accounting, because it is creating a record of the password reset
Confidentiality, because it is protecting the account from disclosure
Authorization, because it is deciding which systems the caller may use
Authentication, because it is confirming the caller is who they claim to be
explain: Verifying identity before a reset is authentication: proving who the caller is. The reset may be logged (accounting), but the verification step itself establishes identity.

q: Which scenario describes a detective control paired with a corrective control?
options: Log monitoring flags a malware infection, and the team then rebuilds the infected workstation
A fence surrounds the site, and a sign warns visitors that the site is monitored
A firewall blocks a port scan, and the blocked addresses are added to a deny list for all future connection attempts
A training video explains phishing, and staff sign a form accepting the policy
explain: Log monitoring detects the infection (detective), and rebuilding the workstation repairs the damage (corrective). The firewall is preventive, the training is directive, and the fence and sign are preventive and deterrent.

q: A company keeps three independent backup copies of its data, one of them offline, and tests restores every quarter. The PRIMARY triad leg these backups defend is:
options: Integrity, because three copies make unauthorized changes impossible
Availability, because data can be recovered and used after a loss
Confidentiality, because an offline copy cannot be read by attackers
Non-repudiation, because the copies prove who created the data
explain: Backups defend availability: when primary data is lost or damaged, a working copy keeps the business running. Multiple copies do not prevent changes to the live data, and an offline copy's protection is a side benefit, not the primary purpose.

q: Which statement about control categories is correct?
options: Category and type are two names for the same classification and can be used interchangeably when documenting controls
A control's category is fixed by its vendor, while its type is chosen by the security team
The category describes how a control is implemented, while the type describes what the control does
The category describes what a control does, while the type describes how it is implemented
explain: Every control has a category (how it is implemented: technical, managerial, physical, operational) and a type (what it does: preventive, detective, and so on). The two dimensions are independent, not interchangeable.

q: An analyst notices that a single firewall rule change would be the only barrier between the internet and a payment database, and recommends adding application-level checks and monitoring as well. Which concept drives the recommendation?
options: Security by design, so that the application is rebuilt from scratch
Least privilege, so that the database accepts fewer user requests
Fail-safe defaults, so that the firewall denies traffic when it errors
Defense in depth, so that one failed control does not become a breach
explain: Adding independent layers so a single failure is not a breach is defense in depth. The recommendation is about stacking different controls, not about limiting user rights or rebuilding the application.

q: A biometric reader at a data center door records the identity and time of every entry, and security reviews the records weekly. The RECORDS primarily support which AAA element?
options: Accounting, because they form a record of who did what and when
Authentication, because the reader verified each person's identity
Authorization, because the reader decided who was allowed to enter
Availability, because the records show the door system was working
explain: The question asks about the records, and retained records of activity are accounting. The reader also authenticates and the door enforces authorization, but the log itself is the accounting element.

q: Which of the following is an operational control?
options: Software that automatically flags unusual sign-in locations
Analysts performing a scheduled review of access logs each morning
A turnstile that admits one badge holder at a time
A written standard defining how access reviews must be performed
explain: Scheduled log reviews performed by people are operational controls. The written standard is managerial, the flagging software is technical, and the turnstile is physical.

q: A retailer classifies data into public, internal, and restricted tiers, and requires encryption for anything marked restricted. Classification primarily supports which triad leg?
options: Accounting, because each tier generates its own access records
Integrity, because classified data cannot be modified by project staff or by outside contractors at any time
Confidentiality, because it ensures sensitive data gets the protection its sensitivity requires
Availability, because staff can quickly find the data tier they need
explain: Classification exists so that data is protected according to its sensitivity, keeping restricted data from unauthorized eyes, which is confidentiality. It does not prevent authorized edits or create logs by itself.

q: A web server is protected by a web application firewall that inspects requests and blocks exploit attempts before they reach the application. Which pairing of category and type is correct for the WAF?
options: Technical and detective, because software inspects each request it sees
Operational and preventive, because administrators maintain its rule set and update it as new threats appear
Managerial and preventive, because its rules reflect security policy
Technical and preventive, because software blocks the attack before it succeeds
explain: A WAF is enforced by technology (technical) and its defining action is blocking exploit attempts (preventive). Inspection alone would be detective, but the scenario states the WAF blocks the attempts.

q: Which of the following actions would be classified as a deterrent control?
options: Posting notices that a parking area is patrolled and violators will be towed
Reviewing camera footage after a vehicle is reported stolen from the area
Replacing a stolen vehicle permit with a new one after the theft is reported
Installing a barrier arm that physically prevents entry to the parking area
explain: Notices about patrols and towing discourage violations before they happen, which is deterrent. The barrier prevents, the footage review detects, and the replacement permit is corrective.

q: An organization decides that even administrators must request temporary elevation for each privileged task, with each request verified and approved individually. Which TWO principles does this combine? (Choose the option that lists the complete correct pair.)
options: Confidentiality and integrity: privileged data is hidden, and changes to it are prevented
Zero Trust and least privilege: every request is verified, and only the minimum access is granted for that task
Defense in depth and deterrence: layered controls discourage administrators from misusing access
Accounting and availability: every request is logged, and access is available whenever it is needed, day or night
explain: Verifying every request individually is Zero Trust, and granting only the minimum access needed for the task is least privilege. Logging (accounting) may also occur, but it is not one of the two principles the scenario describes.

q: A new security manager sorts the company's controls into a matrix. Where does 'security awareness training for all staff' belong?
options: Technical in category and preventive in type, because training stops incidents from occurring
Operational in category and detective in type, because trainers observe staff behavior
Managerial in origin and directive in type, because it is a program decision that directs behavior
Physical in category and deterrent in type, because posters are displayed in the office
explain: Awareness training is run as a management program (managerial) and works by directing how people behave (directive). It does not technically block incidents, and observing behavior is not its mechanism.

q: A database administrator's account can read every table in the production database, including salary data her job never touches. Which principle has been violated, and what is the fix?
options: Zero Trust; move the database inside the trusted network zone
Separation of duties; require a second administrator for queries
Defense in depth; add a second database in case the first fails
Least privilege; remove the access her role does not require
explain: Access beyond what a job requires violates least privilege, and the fix is to trim the permissions to the role. Nothing in the scenario concerns redundancy, network zones, or splitting a task between two people.

q: Which control type is a backup schedule policy, by itself, BEFORE any restore is ever performed?
options: Directive, because the policy directs that backups be taken on a schedule
Detective, because the schedule reveals when a backup was missed
Corrective, because the backups will repair damage when a loss occurs
Preventive, because scheduled backups stop data loss from happening
explain: A policy document directs behavior, so the schedule policy itself is directive. The restore performed later is the corrective act; the policy alone neither repairs, prevents, nor detects anything.

q: A company replaces its 'trusted internal network' design so that applications check the identity and authorization of every connecting user and device, even for connections from the same building. This change is driven by which model?
options: Defense in depth, because more layers are added around each application
Zero Trust, because trust is no longer granted based on network location
Perimeter defense, because the building's network is treated as a safe zone
Air gap, because applications are isolated from one another physically
explain: Checking every connection regardless of source location is the core of Zero Trust. The building network is explicitly no longer a safe zone, which rules out perimeter defense, and no physical isolation is described.

q: After a phishing incident, a firm requires all staff to complete refresher training and adds a banner to external emails warning recipients to verify requests. The training is directive; the email banner is primarily:
options: Corrective, because it repairs the weakness the phishing exploited
Preventive, because it blocks fraudulent messages from being delivered to staff inboxes
Deterrent, because it discourages recipients from acting on fraudulent requests
Detective, because it identifies which incoming messages are external
explain: The banner warns and discourages action on fraudulent requests, which is deterrent. It does not block delivery (preventive), and although the mail system may tag external mail, the banner's stated purpose is the warning.

q: Which combination of controls provides BOTH a detective and a preventive layer for the same risk of unauthorized network access? (Choose the option that lists the complete correct pair.)
options: Security training for users and a written policy prohibiting unauthorized access
Two IDS sensors placed on different segments, both alerting on intrusion attempts in real time
A firewall blocking connections and a second firewall configured the same way
An IDS alerting on intrusion attempts and a firewall blocking unauthorized connections
explain: The IDS detects and the firewall prevents, giving one layer of each type against the same risk. Two IDS sensors are both detective, two identical firewalls are both preventive, and training plus policy are both directive.

q: A network engineer plans to upgrade the firmware on the company's VPN gateway, which serves all remote staff. Before anything is scheduled, what should the engineer produce FIRST?
options: A documented change request describing what will change, why, and which systems it touches
A maintenance window booked for the coming Saturday night with the service desk and announced to all departments
A snapshot of the gateway configuration stored on a local file share
An email to all remote staff announcing that VPN access may be interrupted
explain: The process starts with a documented request: what, why, and what it touches. Scheduling, snapshots, and announcements all come later, after the request exists and impact has been assessed.

q: A change request proposes replacing the core switch in a hospital. Which question is the impact assessment PRIMARILY meant to answer?
options: Which maintenance window has the fewest staff scheduled to work in the building?
What could this change break, and which people and systems depend on the equipment it touches?
How quickly can the old switch be returned to the vendor after the replacement?
Who will sign the approval form once the change has been fully documented, tested, and scheduled?
explain: Impact assessment asks what the change could break and who depends on the affected systems. Approval, scheduling, and logistics are separate steps that rely on the assessment's findings.

q: An administrator applies a 'quick fix' to a production firewall during lunch without telling anyone. That evening, a business application fails and nobody can reconstruct what changed. Which step of the change process would have prevented this situation?
options: Closure, requiring the change record to be updated once the work was finished
Sandbox testing, requiring the fix to be tried on an isolated copy of the environment first before it is approved
Documentation and approval, requiring the change to be written down and approved before implementation
Scheduling, requiring the fix to be applied during an agreed maintenance window
explain: An undocumented, unapproved change is exactly what the request-and-approval steps exist to prevent: no approval, no change, and the written record is what lets others reconstruct events. Testing and scheduling matter, but the failure here is that the change bypassed the process entirely.

q: A change advisory board reviews a proposal to migrate the email system. The board finds the backout plan missing and sends the proposal back. What is the board's role in the process?
options: To implement approved changes during the scheduled maintenance window on behalf of the requesters
To test proposed changes in a sandbox before they reach production
To document what happened after a change has been completed
To review and approve changes before implementation, refusing those that are not ready
explain: The CAB reviews and approves (or refuses) changes before anyone implements them. Implementation, sandbox testing, and closure documentation belong to other roles and steps.

q: Before a database upgrade goes live, the team runs the upgrade against an isolated copy of the production environment and signs in with test accounts. What is this step called, and what is its purpose?
options: Testing in a sandbox, so surprises surface where they are cheap instead of in production
A backout rehearsal, so the team can practice returning to the previous version
Scheduling, so the upgrade lands during a low-impact maintenance window
Impact assessment, so the team can list every system that depends on the database and every user group that relies on it
explain: Trying the change in an isolated copy of the environment is sandbox testing, done so problems appear where they are cheap. Impact assessment lists dependencies, and a backout plan reverses a failed change; neither is the trial run itself.

q: A patch to the VPN gateway is approved for Saturday night. The plan states: snapshot the current configuration, keep the old firmware staged, and roll back if tunnels fail for more than ten minutes. What has the team documented?
options: A closure report, recording what actually happened during the maintenance window
A backout plan, defining exactly how to reverse the change and the trigger for doing so
An impact assessment, listing the systems and users the gateway change could affect
A test plan, describing the accounts and checks used in the sandbox environment
explain: Instructions for reversing a change, with a defined trigger, are a backout plan. The impact assessment and test plan are written earlier in the process, and the closure report can only be written after the change happens.

q: Midway through a maintenance window, a software upgrade fails its verification checks. The documented plan says the previous version cannot be restored because the data format has already been converted, so the team fixes the new version in place and moves ahead. Which strategy is the team executing?
options: Backout, restoring the previous configuration from the staged snapshot
Rollback testing, confirming the old version still works in the sandbox
Fail forward, repairing the new version instead of returning to the old state
Change closure, recording the failure and ending the maintenance window
explain: Fail forward means fixing the new version and moving ahead when returning to the old state is not the planned response. A backout would restore the previous state, which the plan explicitly rules out.

q: A development team argues that because fail forward worked once, they can skip writing backout plans for future releases. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Backout plans are only needed when a change advisory board has formally rejected the original change request at review
Fail forward removes the need for testing, so the team should drop sandbox testing rather than the backout documentation
Fail forward is only permitted for hardware changes, while backout plans are required for every software release regardless of its design
Fail forward is a decision made in advance in the plan for a specific change, not a substitute for planning how to respond when a change fails
explain: Fail forward is chosen ahead of time, in the plan, for a change whose design makes it the right response; it is not a blanket excuse to stop planning failure responses. Each change still needs a documented response, whether that is backout, fail forward, or another defined path.

q: A company schedules its riskiest infrastructure changes for 2 a.m. on Sundays, a time agreed with business units as the lowest-impact period. What is this agreed period called?
options: A maintenance window, a low-impact time agreed with the business for changes
A sandbox period, the time set aside for testing changes before approval
A backout window, the period during which a failed change can be reversed
A freeze period, a span of time during which no changes are permitted at all
explain: A maintenance window is the agreed low-impact time when changes land. A freeze period is the opposite idea (no changes), and the sandbox is an environment, not a time slot.

q: During the busiest retail week of the year, a company prohibits all non-emergency changes to its point-of-sale systems. Which practice is this?
options: A maintenance window, concentrating changes into the busiest trading period of the entire year
A change freeze, suspending changes during a period when the cost of failure is highest
Fail forward, accepting that any failure will be repaired in place quickly
Standard change scheduling, routing routine changes through pre-approval
explain: Prohibiting changes during a critical period is a change freeze. A maintenance window is when changes are allowed to land, and fail forward describes a failure response, not a scheduling restriction.

q: A change to a payroll system is requested, assessed, approved, tested, and implemented successfully. Two weeks later a new team member asks how the system reached its current configuration, and there is no record of the work. Which step failed?
options: Approval, because the change advisory board never reviewed the payroll change request
Scheduling, because the change was not placed inside an agreed maintenance window
Documentation and closure, because what actually happened was never recorded at the end of the process
Impact assessment, because the dependencies of the payroll system were never properly mapped before the change was approved
explain: The process ran, but the final step — recording what actually happened and closing the change — was skipped, leaving no history for the next team. Every earlier step is described as completed in the scenario.

q: A firewall rule change is small, routine, and performed the same way every week with a well-documented procedure and a history of success. Which handling is MOST appropriate?
options: Classify it as an emergency change so it can bypass the normal approval process each week
Require a full change advisory board hearing for every weekly repetition of the rule change, with no exceptions allowed
Skip documentation entirely because the change is familiar to the engineer performing it
Treat it as a standard change, pre-approved for low-risk, repeatable work performed to a known procedure
explain: Low-risk, repeatable changes with a proven procedure are standard changes, pre-approved so they do not need a full board review each time. They are still documented, and familiarity alone never justifies skipping the record or misusing the emergency path.

q: At 3 p.m., an actively exploited vulnerability is found in the company's internet-facing servers. Waiting for next week's board meeting would leave the company exposed. Which path should the patch take?
options: The emergency change path, with expedited approval and the full documentation completed as the process requires
The standard change path, because patching servers is a routine and repeatable activity that the team performs on a regular schedule
No process at all, because any delay for paperwork increases the company's exposure
The normal change path, waiting for the scheduled board meeting the following week
explain: Urgent, high-risk fixes use the emergency change path: approval is expedited, not skipped, and documentation still happens. Waiting a week leaves the exposure open, and bypassing the process entirely repeats the 'quick fix' failure mode.

q: A proposed change will replace the authentication system used by every application in the company. The request lists only the authentication servers as affected. What is the impact assessment MOST likely missing?
options: The maintenance window, which has not yet been agreed with the business units
The downstream dependencies: every application and user population that relies on authentication
The backout trigger, which defines when the team would abandon the change
The approval signature, which must be collected before the assessment can be written by the board chair
explain: An authentication change touches everything that signs users in, so an assessment listing only the servers misses the dependent applications and users. Signatures, windows, and triggers belong to other steps and do not fix an understated impact.

q: After a change, users report that a reporting tool can no longer reach the database, although the database itself is healthy. The change record shows the team tested only the database upgrade. Which step most directly failed to catch this?
options: Scheduling, because the change should have waited for a longer maintenance window
Closure documentation, because the outcome of the change was recorded too late to help the investigation
Impact assessment, because the reporting tool's dependency on the database was never identified
Approval, because the board should have tested the reporting tool during its review
explain: Testing covered only what the team knew was affected; the missed dependency is an impact assessment failure. The board reviews rather than tests, and neither the window length nor the closure record would have revealed the dependency.

q: A team implements a change exactly as approved, but during the work they discover they must also restart a service that was never mentioned in the request. What should they do?
options: Proceed with the restart, because it is a small step needed to finish the approved change successfully and the window is already open
Restart the service and add a note about it to the closure record when the window ends
Cancel the entire change and restore the previous state using the backout plan immediately
Stop and return to the process: document the expanded scope and obtain approval for the additional impact before proceeding
explain: Scope discovered mid-change must be documented and approved before it is implemented; approval covers what was assessed, not whatever the team later finds convenient. Noting it afterward repeats the undocumented-change problem, and an immediate backout is not required when a pause and re-approval are possible.

q: Which sequence shows the change process in the correct order?
options: Request and documentation, impact assessment, approval, testing, scheduling, implementation with a backout plan, closure
Testing, impact assessment, request and documentation, implementation, approval, closure, scheduling
Request and documentation, implementation, impact assessment, approval, testing, closure, scheduling
Approval, request and documentation, testing, impact assessment, implementation, scheduling, closure, and post-implementation review
explain: The process runs: document the request, assess impact, obtain approval, test in a sandbox, schedule the window, implement with a backout plan ready, then document and close. Every other sequence implements before approval or assesses impact after the fact.

q: A change request is approved by the CAB but the sandbox test then reveals the patch breaks a legacy integration. What should happen next?
options: The engineer quietly drops the legacy integration from the scope and proceeds with the rest
The change returns for reassessment and re-approval with the new information before any production implementation
The change proceeds as approved, because the board's decision cannot be revisited once it is given by anyone on the team
The team implements the patch and monitors the legacy integration closely during the window
explain: Failed testing changes what the board approved, so the change goes back through assessment and approval with the new facts. Proceeding on a stale approval, or silently shrinking the scope, both bypass the process.

q: Why does the change process require the backout plan to be written BEFORE implementation begins?
options: Because the backout plan doubles as the impact assessment the board uses to approve the change in the first place, so a separate assessment is unnecessary
Because regulations require backout plans to be filed with the change board at least thirty days in advance
Because once a change is failing, there is no time to design a reversal under pressure, and an improvised response makes the outage worse
Because the sandbox environment cannot be built until the backout plan has been fully documented
explain: A backout plan written in advance lets a team execute a rehearsed reversal the moment the trigger is met, instead of improvising at the worst possible time. It is a separate document from the impact assessment, and no thirty-day filing rule is part of the process.

q: A stakeholder in the finance department objects that a proposed system change lands on the last day of the quarter, when her team closes the books. Which step of the process is designed to surface and resolve exactly this conflict?
options: Approval, in which the change board reviews the technical merits of the proposed change
Closure, in which the results of the change are recorded for the teams that follow
Testing, in which the change is tried against an isolated copy of the production environment
Scheduling, in which the maintenance window is agreed with the business units the change affects
explain: Scheduling exists to land changes at a low-impact time agreed with the business, which is exactly where a quarter-end conflict gets resolved. Testing checks the change works; it does not negotiate timing with affected departments.

q: An engineer wants to test a configuration change but production data cannot be copied to the test system for privacy reasons. Which approach keeps the test meaningful within the change process?
options: Test in a sandbox built as an isolated copy of the environment, using representative test data instead of live records
Ask the change board to waive the testing step because the engineer is experienced with the system and has done this change many times before
Skip testing for this change and rely on the backout plan if the configuration causes problems
Apply the change to production during the maintenance window and watch the monitoring closely
explain: A sandbox is an isolated copy of the environment; using representative test data preserves both the test and the privacy constraint. Skipping testing, testing in production, or waiving the step for experience all remove the step that catches surprises cheaply.

q: A change was approved, tested, and implemented, and verification shows the service working. What remains to complete the process?
options: Re-run the sandbox tests to confirm the production result matches the test result
Document what actually happened during the change and close the change record
Submit a new change request so the board can approve the completed work
Extend the maintenance window until every user has confirmed the service works
explain: Closure — recording what actually happened and closing the record — is the final step. The work is already verified; a new request or an open-ended window adds process without adding the missing record.

q: Which of the following changes carries the HIGHEST inherent risk and therefore needs the most rigorous assessment, even though the technical edit itself is small?
options: A label correction on an internal documentation page read by one support team
A screensaver timeout adjustment on kiosk displays in the company lobby
A single firewall rule change on the gateway that carries all remote access for the company
A desktop wallpaper update pushed to the workstations in one small branch office during the lunch hour
explain: Risk follows impact, not edit size: a small change to the single gateway all remote staff depend on can cause a company-wide outage. The other changes are small in both edit and blast radius.

q: A vendor releases a security patch. The change record includes the request, impact assessment, approval, and successful sandbox results, but no backout plan. The board should:
options: Reject the change permanently, because a missing backout plan means the patch can never be applied safely
Approve the implementation, because successful sandbox testing makes a backout plan unnecessary for this patch in the board's judgment
Approve the implementation and ask the engineer to write the backout plan during the maintenance window
Refuse or defer approval to implement until a backout plan is documented, because reversal must be planned before the change starts
explain: A backout plan must exist before implementation begins; good test results reduce risk but do not remove the need for a planned reversal. Deferring until the plan exists is the process working as designed — not a permanent rejection.

q: Two departments both submit changes for the same Sunday window, and the changes touch the same database. What should the change process do about this?
options: Identify the conflict during assessment and scheduling, and sequence or separate the changes so they do not collide
Allow both changes, because each one was individually approved by the change board earlier in the week after full review
Cancel both changes automatically, because changes sharing a window are never permitted to proceed
Let the two teams negotiate informally on Sunday and record the outcome in the closure notes
explain: Assessment and scheduling exist partly to catch collisions between changes sharing systems or windows, and to sequence them safely. Individual approval does not account for the interaction between the two changes.

q: A change implements successfully, but the closure record is filled in from memory three weeks later and omits a configuration value that was adjusted. Months later, a troubleshooting team is misled by the record. Which lesson does this illustrate?
options: Backout plans must be retained indefinitely, because any change might need to be reversed months after it was implemented
Closure documentation must record what actually happened, promptly and accurately, because later teams depend on it to understand the current state
Sandbox testing must include troubleshooting scenarios, because test environments reveal documentation errors before production systems ever do
Impact assessments must be repeated after every change, because the environment will have changed in ways nobody predicted
explain: The record is the next team's map of the environment; writing it late and from memory made it wrong. The failure is in the closure step itself, not in assessment, backout retention, or testing.

q: A SaaS provider plans to release a new version whose database migration cannot be undone once customer data is converted. The release plan states that if the new version misbehaves, engineers will fix it in place rather than restore the old version. This is an example of:
options: An emergency change, because the release must proceed without the normal approval sequence
Backout, because the engineers will return customers to the previous working version of the service
Fail forward, chosen in advance because the old state cannot simply be restored after the migration
A change freeze, because the provider is restricting which changes may occur during the release
explain: When a migration makes the old state unreachable, the planned response to trouble is to repair the new version and move ahead — fail forward, decided in the plan rather than improvised. Nothing here restores an old version, freezes changes, or skips approval.

q: Which item belongs in an impact assessment for a proposed upgrade to the company's single sign-on system? (Choose the option that lists the complete correct set.)
options: The names of the engineers scheduled for the maintenance window and the order in which they will work throughout the night of the upgrade
The exact commands used to perform the upgrade and the screenshots taken during sandbox testing
The approval signatures collected from the change board and the date of the next scheduled review
The applications that depend on single sign-on, the user groups affected, and what happens to access if the upgrade fails
explain: An impact assessment covers what the change touches and what could break: dependent applications, affected users, and the consequences of failure. Staffing order, test screenshots, and signatures belong to scheduling, testing, and approval respectively.

q: A change board member asks why a routine patch needs any assessment at all. Which answer BEST reflects the purpose of impact assessment?
options: Because even a small change can break the systems that depend on the patched component, and the assessment finds those dependencies before the business does
Because the assessment replaces sandbox testing for changes the team has performed successfully many times before
Because the assessment transfers responsibility for any failure from the engineering team to the change board
Because the assessment generates the paperwork the auditors require, and its content is secondary to having the form completed and signed by the requesting team's manager
explain: Impact assessment exists to find what a change could break — including the dependents nobody remembered — before implementation. It is not paperwork for its own sake, it does not replace testing, and it does not transfer blame.

q: During implementation, verification shows the change has broken a critical service, and the failure matches the trigger written in the plan. What should the team do?
options: Document the failure in the closure record and schedule a repair for the next window
Execute the backout plan to restore the previous state, as the plan directs when the trigger is met
Continue troubleshooting the new configuration until the maintenance window expires
Wait for the change board to reconvene and vote on whether a reversal is appropriate before anyone touches the system
explain: The backout plan exists for exactly this moment: the trigger is met, so the team executes the rehearsed reversal without waiting for a meeting. Troubleshooting past the trigger and deferring repair both extend an outage the plan was written to end.

q: A change is proposed to upgrade the operating system on a server that hosts a legacy application no other team admits to owning. The request is approved quickly because 'nothing depends on that server.' After the upgrade, the legacy application fails and a business unit reports an outage. Which step failed FIRST?
options: Testing, because the sandbox copy of the server should have included the legacy application automatically as part of its standard build
Approval, because the board should have refused the change until the server's owner came forward
Impact assessment, because the dependency between the server and the business unit's application was never identified
Closure, because the outage was not recorded in the change record until the business unit complained
explain: The root failure is the assessment that declared nothing depended on the server. Testing can only cover dependencies the assessment identifies, and the board approved based on the assessment it was given.

q: An organization tracks every change in a ticketing system where each change has an owner, a status, and a linked record of approvals and test results. What is the PRIMARY security benefit of this discipline?
options: The ticketing system automatically tests each change, removing the need for a separate sandbox environment
Auditors no longer need to review the environment, because the tickets prove every system is configured correctly
Engineers can implement changes faster, because tickets remove the need for any approval before work begins on a system, which is the main reason teams adopt ticketing in the first place
Every change is attributable and reconstructable, so unauthorized or undocumented changes stand out and incidents can be traced to the change that caused them
explain: A complete change record makes work attributable and lets investigators trace an incident back to the change that caused it; undocumented changes become visible by their absence. Tickets do not remove approval or testing, and records alone do not prove correct configuration.

q: A change request describes upgrading 'the file servers' but does not say which servers, which shares, or which departments use them. The board returns the request. What information is the request missing that the board needs?
options: A precise scope: exactly what will change and what the change touches, so impact can be assessed
A commitment from the engineering team that the change will definitely succeed
The names of the users who will be logged in during the maintenance window on Sunday
The vendor's marketing summary explaining the benefits of the new file server version and its new features
explain: Impact cannot be assessed until the request states precisely what changes and what it touches. The board does not need a login roster or marketing material, and no team can guarantee success — which is why backout plans exist.

q: After several incidents traced to rushed Friday-afternoon changes, a company moves all standard production changes to a single approved window each week and requires board review for anything outside it. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this policy?
options: To reduce the total number of changes the company makes, regardless of whether each change is needed
To ensure changes land at predictable, low-impact times with oversight, instead of whenever an individual engineer decides
To guarantee that no change will ever fail, because weekly windows are inherently safer than other times of the week or month
To allow engineers to skip impact assessments for changes that fall inside the approved weekly window
explain: A fixed, agreed window with oversight outside it makes change timing predictable and low-impact. The window does not reduce the need for assessment, does not guarantee success, and is not mainly about doing fewer changes.

q: A patch is tested successfully in the sandbox, approved, and scheduled. During implementation the engineer notices the production system is running a different version than the sandbox copy. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Update the sandbox copy to match production and proceed with the change in the same window
Apply the patch to half the production system and compare behavior before finishing the rest
Pause the change and reassess, because the test results were produced against a different version than the one being changed
Proceed with the patch, because sandbox testing is only an approximation and small version differences are expected in real environments
explain: Test evidence only supports the change if the test environment matches what will actually be changed. A version mismatch invalidates the sandbox results, so the change pauses for reassessment rather than proceeding on evidence that no longer applies.

q: Which of the following is the BEST example of a change whose backout plan is straightforward and reliable?
options: A one-way encryption of archived records where the original plaintext copies are destroyed as part of the change
A database migration that converts all records to a new format and deletes the conversion tooling once the migration completes and reports success
A cloud service upgrade performed entirely by the vendor, where the customer has no access to the previous version
A configuration change on a gateway where the previous configuration is snapshotted and the old firmware remains staged for immediate reload
explain: A snapshot plus staged old firmware makes reversal a defined, executable step. The other options each destroy or surrender the old state — converted data, vendor-held versions, destroyed originals — which is exactly what makes backout hard or impossible.

q: A change board approves a network segmentation project in phases: the first phase affects one department, results are reviewed, and only then is the next phase scheduled. Which risk-reduction principle is the board applying?
options: Limiting the impact of each change by implementing in stages and reassessing between them
Fail forward, because each phase commits the company further to the new network design
Standard change handling, because segmentation is a routine and repeatable weekly task
Change freezing, because the board is preventing other departments from changing anything
explain: Phased implementation with review between phases limits the blast radius of any single step and feeds real results into the next assessment. Nothing here repairs a new version in place, routinizes the work, or freezes other changes.

q: A technician proposes skipping the change process for a 'two-minute' edit to a DNS record, arguing the process takes longer than the change. Which response BEST reflects sound change management?
options: The process can be skipped this once, provided the technician writes up the change record by the end of the week
The process still applies, because risk is set by what the change touches — a DNS edit can take every service offline — not by how long the edit takes
The edit should be reclassified as an emergency change so it can proceed immediately without the normal steps
The technician is right, because changes completed in under five minutes are exempt from documentation and approval requirements under the company's informal practice
explain: Change risk follows impact, not duration: a two-minute DNS edit can break every dependent service, which is why the process scales with what a change touches. There is no under-five-minutes exemption, and retroactive paperwork is the undocumented-change failure with extra steps.

q: A completed change record shows the request, approval, test results, implementation notes, and the verified outcome, all linked and searchable a year later. Which later activity does this record MOST directly support?
options: Extending the maintenance window retroactively to cover the time the change actually took
Approving the next change to the same system without any further impact assessment or testing
Investigating a future incident by tracing the environment's current state back to the changes that produced it
Replacing the sandbox environment, because the record describes the environment in sufficient detail to rebuild it exactly
explain: A complete, retrievable record lets future investigators reconstruct how the environment reached its state. It never substitutes for assessing the next change, rebuilding a sandbox, or rewriting history.

q: Which set lists ONLY elements that belong in a complete change record for a server patch? (Choose the option that lists the complete correct set.)
options: The request and its reason, the engineer's personal notes, the vendor's advertising claims, and a verbal assurance that testing went well from the team lead
The approval, the maintenance window booking, the team's lunch schedule, and the previous year's patching statistics
The impact assessment, the backout plan, a copy of the old server, and a promise to document the outcome at year end
The request and its reason, the impact assessment, the approval, the test results, the backout plan, and the closure notes recording the outcome
explain: A complete record documents why the change was requested, what it could affect, who approved it, how it was tested, how it could be reversed, and what actually happened. Personal notes, advertising, and verbal assurances are not process evidence.

q: A company needs to encrypt a 500 GB archive for storage. Speed matters, and the same team holds the key at both ends. Which type of encryption is the right tool?
options: Symmetric encryption such as AES, which uses one shared key and is fast enough for bulk data
Hashing such as SHA-256, which converts the archive into a fixed-size fingerprint
A digital signature, which proves the archive came from the team that created it
Asymmetric encryption such as RSA, which uses a key pair and is designed for bulk data
explain: Bulk data is encrypted symmetrically: AES with one shared key is fast, and key delivery is manageable when the same team holds both ends. RSA is far too slow for bulk data, and hashing and signatures do not encrypt anything.

q: Two companies that have never worked together need to exchange an encrypted file. They have no secure channel for sharing a secret key. What does asymmetric encryption give them that symmetric encryption cannot?
options: A guarantee that the file cannot be decrypted by anyone, including the intended recipient, once it is sent
Each side can publish a public key for the other to encrypt with, while the matching private key stays secret and is never transmitted
A single shared key that both sides can derive from the file's contents without exchanging any information at all before the exchange takes place
Encryption that never requires keys, because the public key both encrypts and decrypts the data on its own
explain: Asymmetric encryption solves key delivery between strangers: encrypt with the recipient's public key, and only their private key decrypts it. Symmetric encryption still needs the shared secret delivered somehow, which is the problem in this scenario.

q: In an asymmetric key pair, which key must the owner protect and never share?
options: The public key, because it can be used to derive the matching private key
Both keys equally, because the pair stops working if either one is revealed
The private key, because anyone holding it can decrypt messages and sign as the owner
Neither key, because asymmetric systems remain secure even when both are public
explain: The private key is the secret half of the pair: it decrypts and signs, so it never leaves the owner. The public key is designed to be shared with the world and cannot be used to derive the private key.

q: A user encrypts a message with the recipient's public key. Who can decrypt it?
options: Only the sender, using the public key they applied when encrypting
Both the sender and the recipient, using either key of the pair
Anyone, because the public key used for encryption is publicly known
Only the recipient, using the matching private key that only they hold
explain: What the public key encrypts, only the matching private key decrypts. The sender cannot undo it, and public knowledge of the public key does not help an eavesdropper decrypt.

q: Why do real-world systems such as TLS use asymmetric encryption only briefly, then switch to symmetric encryption for the actual data?
options: Asymmetric math is slow, so it is used to agree on a fresh symmetric session key, and fast symmetric encryption then carries the data
Symmetric encryption is stronger per bit, so asymmetric encryption is kept only as a backup in case the session key fails
Symmetric keys expire after a few seconds, so asymmetric encryption must be restarted repeatedly to keep the session alive for its whole duration
Asymmetric encryption cannot encrypt data at all, so it can only be used to transmit the names of symmetric algorithms
explain: The hybrid design divides the labor: slow asymmetric crypto handles the introduction and key agreement, and fast symmetric crypto moves the bulk data. Asymmetric encryption can encrypt data — it is simply too slow to do so at volume.

q: Diffie-Hellman is BEST described as a method for:
options: Encrypting bulk data quickly using a single key that both parties already share securely from an earlier exchange
Two parties agreeing on a shared secret key over an unsafe channel, without transmitting the key itself
Producing a fixed-size fingerprint of data so that any later change can be detected
Signing a message with a private key so that recipients can verify who sent it
explain: Diffie-Hellman belongs to the asymmetric family as a key-agreement method: both sides derive the same secret over an open channel without sending it. It does not itself encrypt bulk data, hash, or sign.

q: Which algorithm is an asymmetric encryption algorithm?
options: SHA-256, which produces a one-way fixed-size fingerprint of its input
3DES, which applies a symmetric block cipher three times in sequence
RSA, which encrypts and decrypts with a matched public and private key pair
AES, which encrypts and decrypts with a single shared secret key
explain: RSA is asymmetric, built on a key pair. AES and 3DES are symmetric ciphers using one shared key, and SHA-256 is a hash function, not an encryption algorithm at all.

q: A key grows from 128 bits to 129 bits. What happens to the number of possible keys an attacker would have to search?
options: It squares, because each bit interacts with every bit already present
It grows by 128, because each bit adds that many new possible keys
It stays the same, because key length affects speed rather than keyspace
