It doubles, because every additional bit multiplies the keyspace by two
explain: Keyspace is 2 raised to the key length, so each extra bit doubles the possibilities: a 128-bit key has about 3.4 x 10^38 possibilities, and 129 bits doubles that. The growth is exponential, not additive.

q: A 10-bit key has 1,024 possible values. Approximately how many possible values does a 128-bit key have, and what does this mean for brute-force attacks?
options: About 3.4 x 10^38 possibilities, making exhaustive guessing computationally infeasible
About 131,072 possibilities, making a patient brute-force attack practical overnight
About 1,280 possibilities, because each bit contributes ten possible values to the total
About 16,384 possibilities, because the keyspace grows by squaring the 10-bit result
explain: Each bit doubles the keyspace: 2^10 is 1,024, and continuing to 2^128 gives roughly 3.4 x 10^38 — far beyond any feasible guessing effort. The other figures come from adding or multiplying instead of doubling.

q: A system stores user passwords. Instead of storing the passwords themselves, it stores a one-way fingerprint of each password that cannot be reversed into the original. Which technique is this?
options: Tokenization, because each password is replaced by a random value stored in a vault
Hashing, because a hash is one-way math whose output cannot be turned back into the input
Encoding, because the password is converted into a different readable representation
Symmetric encryption, because the stored value can be decrypted when the user signs in
explain: Hashing is one-way: the fingerprint cannot be reversed, so verification works by hashing the attempt and comparing. Encryption would be reversible with a key, which is exactly what password storage must avoid.

q: A user hashes a one-word file and a 4 GB database backup with SHA-256. How do the two outputs compare?
options: Both outputs are 256 bytes, because SHA-256 pads every result to a fixed storage block
The backup's output is much longer, because hash output grows in proportion to the size of the input data being hashed at the time
Both outputs are exactly 256 bits, because a hash function always produces a fixed-size result regardless of input size
The word's output is 256 bits, while the backup's output is capped at the size of the original file
explain: SHA-256 always outputs exactly 256 bits, whether the input is a word or a warehouse of data. Fixed output size is a defining property of hashing, and the unit is bits, not bytes.

q: Two files differ by exactly one character. Their SHA-256 hashes are compared. What should the analyst expect?
options: Nearly identical hashes, because a one-character change alters only a small part of the result
Identical hashes, because files of the same length always produce the same fingerprint
Hashes that differ only in the final digit, marking the position of the changed character
Completely different hashes, because changing even one input bit changes the output entirely
explain: Hash functions avalanche: a single changed bit produces an output that looks unrelated to the original. Similar inputs do not produce similar hashes, and same-length files do not share fingerprints.

q: An attacker steals a password database in which every password was hashed with a unique random value mixed in before hashing. Precomputed rainbow tables prove useless against it. What is the random value called, and why does it work?
options: A salt; the attacker's tables were built for unsalted hashes, so the salted hashes match nothing in them
An initialization vector; it hides the password pattern so identical passwords produce identical hashes
A nonce; it is transmitted with each login so the server can reverse the hash and compare passwords
A key; the attacker cannot decrypt the hashes without the matching private key held by the server
explain: Salting mixes a unique random value into each password before hashing, so precomputed tables built for unsalted hashes match nothing, and identical passwords produce different hashes. Hashes are not decrypted, and the salt's job is uniqueness per password, not transmission at login.

q: Two users of the same service choose the identical password, 'Sunshine42'. In a properly salted password store, what will their stored entries look like?
options: Identical hashes, because salting changes the login process rather than the stored value
Different hashes, because each password was mixed with its own unique salt before hashing
Identical hashes, because the same password always produces the same hash output
Different hashes, because the service encrypts each password with the user's private key
explain: A unique salt per password means identical passwords hash to different stored values, which also stops an attacker from spotting shared passwords. Without a salt the hashes would match — that is the weakness salting removes.

q: A sender wants recipients to be able to prove a message came from her and that she cannot later deny sending it. Which mechanism provides this?
options: A hash of the message, published alongside it so recipients can recompute it themselves at any time
Symmetric encryption of the message with a key shared by all the recipients
A digital signature, created by encrypting a hash of the message with her private key
A copy of her public key, attached to the message as proof of her identity
explain: Signing a message hash with the private key gives authenticity and non-repudiation: only the private key's owner could have produced it, and anyone can verify with her public key. A bare hash proves nothing about who sent the message, since anyone can compute one.

q: A recipient verifies a digital signature on a document. The verification succeeds. What has the recipient established?
options: The signer is a trustworthy person, because the signature confirms their good intentions
The document was written recently, because signatures include the current date by default
The document's contents are secret, because signature verification decrypts the document body for the verifying recipient
The document is unchanged since signing, and only the holder of the matching private key could have signed it
explain: A valid signature proves integrity (the content matches what was signed) and authenticity (only the private key holder could sign). It does not encrypt the content, vouch for intentions, or by itself establish when the document was written.

q: In the digital signature process, what exactly does the sender encrypt with their private key?
options: A hash of the message, which recipients decrypt with the sender's public key and compare against a freshly computed hash
Their public key, which recipients compare against the copy held by the certificate authority in its public directory of issued keys
The entire message, which recipients then decrypt in full using the sender's public key
A symmetric session key, which recipients use to decrypt the message body that follows
explain: Signing encrypts the message's hash, not the whole message; verifiers decrypt the hash with the public key and compare it to a hash they compute themselves. Encrypting a session key describes key exchange, a different use of asymmetric crypto.

q: During a TLS connection, in which beat does the browser check that the server's certificate has not expired?
options: After the symmetric session key is established, as part of the first encrypted data exchange between the two sides of the connection that follows
When the server presents its certificate and the browser validates it against its trusted authorities, before any session key is agreed
Before the browser sends its first hello message, by consulting a downloaded list of expired certificates
Only when the user clicks the padlock icon, because expiry is not part of the automatic handshake checks
explain: Certificate validation — name, CA signature, and validity dates — happens when the server presents its certificate, early in the handshake and before key agreement. An expired certificate stops the connection at that point.

q: A browser refuses to open a banking site because its certificate expired yesterday, even though the site's encryption itself still works mathematically. Why does the browser stop?
options: Because the certificate authority automatically revokes the site's private key on the expiry date
Because the site's public key stops functioning as a mathematical object once the certificate expires
Because trust has a validity window: an expired certificate fails validation, so the browser cannot confirm the key still belongs to the site
Because expired certificates cause the symmetric session key to be computed incorrectly by the browser whenever a user visits a site whose certificate has lapsed
explain: Certificates bind a key to an identity for a defined period; outside that window the binding is no longer vouched for, so validation fails. The keys still work mathematically, the CA does not seize the private key, and the failure is about trust, not computation.

q: What does a digital certificate actually bind together?
options: Two public keys, so that either one can be used to decrypt the same data
A private key and a password, with the pair stored on the owner's server
A symmetric key and a session, with the key destroyed when the session ends
A public key and an identity, with the binding signed by a certificate authority
explain: A certificate ties a public key to an identity, and a CA's signature vouches for the tie. Private keys are never placed in certificates, and session keys are separate, short-lived symmetric keys.

q: A user's browser trusts a website's certificate because it follows a chain of signatures from the site's certificate up to a root authority the browser already trusts. This system as a whole is called:
options: Public key infrastructure (PKI), the system of authorities, certificates, and trust chains that lets strangers trust a public key
A web of trust, in which individual users personally vouch for each other's keys without any central authority involved in issuing or revoking them
Symmetric key management, in which a single shared key is distributed to every participant in advance
Certificate pinning, in which one application hard-codes a single expected certificate for one server
explain: PKI is the infrastructure of CAs, certificates, and chains up to trusted roots that lets a browser trust a stranger's key. A web of trust replaces authorities with personal vouching, and pinning is a single-application technique, not the whole system.

q: An attacker intercepts traffic between a user and a shopping site but cannot read the order details, because the session is encrypted with a fresh key agreed during the handshake. Which property of the design defeated the eavesdropper?
options: The user's browser signed the order with its private key, hiding the contents from anyone without the public key
The two sides agreed a symmetric session key using asymmetric math, so the key itself was never sent in readable form
The certificate hid the traffic, because certificates encrypt all data that passes through a TLS connection
The shopping site hashed the order details, converting them into a fingerprint the attacker cannot interpret
explain: Key agreement over an open channel is the asymmetric step of the handshake: the session key is derived, never transmitted readably, and the eavesdropper cannot derive it. Hashing and signatures do not hide content, and certificates authenticate rather than encrypt traffic.

q: Which question does ENCRYPTION answer, in contrast to hashing and signatures?
options: 'Can this be recovered?' — encryption guarantees the content survives a loss of the device
'Has this been changed?' — encryption detects any alteration to the content
'Can anyone else read this?' — encryption protects the confidentiality of the content
'Who sent this?' — encryption proves the identity of the content's author
explain: Encryption answers the confidentiality question: only key holders can read the content. Detecting change is hashing's job, proving the sender is the signature's job, and recovery is a backup concern, not a cryptographic one here.

q: A forensic analyst needs to confirm that a disk image has not changed since it was collected. Which technique is correct?
options: Decrypt the image with the public key recorded at collection and read the contents to check for differences against the original notes
Re-encrypt the image with a fresh symmetric key and compare the ciphertext with the original stored copy
Ask the certificate authority to re-issue the image's certificate with a new validity period
Compare a hash of the image taken now against the hash recorded at collection; matching hashes show the image is unchanged
explain: Integrity is verified by hashing: recompute the fingerprint and compare it with the recorded one. Decryption and re-encryption do not prove sameness, and certificates bind keys to identities, not to evidence files.

q: Which statement about ECC compared with RSA is correct?
options: ECC is an asymmetric algorithm that reaches comparable strength to RSA with shorter keys
ECC is a hashing algorithm that produces fixed-size fingerprints of arbitrary data
ECC is a key-agreement protocol that replaces the need for any public or private keys
ECC is a symmetric cipher that encrypts bulk data faster than AES on the same hardware
explain: ECC and RSA are both named asymmetric algorithms; ECC achieves comparable security with shorter keys. AES is the symmetric workhorse, SHA-256 is the hash, and Diffie-Hellman is the key-agreement method.

q: A developer proposes storing passwords by encrypting them with AES so the support team can decrypt and read them out to users who call in. What is the core problem with this design?
options: Support teams are prohibited from reading passwords aloud under the TLS standard that governs sign-in pages
Passwords should be hashed, not encrypted: hashing is one-way, so a stolen store reveals no recoverable passwords, while an encryption key compromise exposes every password at once
AES is too slow for password storage, so sign-in checks would take several seconds for every user on the system, making the design impractical for any service with more than a handful of accounts
Encrypted passwords cannot be compared at sign-in, because the ciphertext changes every time it is produced
explain: Password storage must be one-way: salted hashes let the system verify an attempt without being able to recover the original. Reversible encryption means anyone who obtains the key — or the database plus key — recovers every password, which is the failure the design must avoid.

q: In the TLS handshake, what does the server present to prove its identity to the browser?
options: Its private key, which the browser compares against a stored copy for that site
A symmetric session key, which the browser checks against the key used last time the user visited
Its certificate, which the browser validates against its trusted certificate authorities
A signed hash of its home page, which the browser recomputes and compares
explain: The server presents its certificate; the browser checks the name, the CA signature, and the dates. A private key is never sent, the session key is agreed afterward, and page hashes play no role in the handshake.

q: Which of the following provides non-repudiation?
options: Symmetric encryption, because only the two key holders could have produced the ciphertext
A certificate, because the authority records every message the key owner sends
A hash, because the fingerprint is unique to the message and cannot be produced by anyone else who does not already know the message contents
A digital signature, because only the private key holder could have produced it, so the signer cannot credibly deny signing
explain: Non-repudiation comes from the signature: anyone can compute a hash, both symmetric key holders can produce the same ciphertext, and CAs vouch for keys rather than log messages — but only one private key holder could have signed.

q: A company must send a large database extract to a partner nightly. The partner publishes a public key. Which design fits the hybrid model used by real systems?
options: Encrypt a fresh symmetric key with the partner's public key, send it, and encrypt the extract itself with that symmetric key
Sign the extract with the company's public key so the partner can decrypt it with the company's private key
Encrypt the entire extract directly with the partner's public key, accepting the slower processing for stronger security
Hash the extract with SHA-256 and send the hash, which the partner reverses to recover the original extract
explain: The hybrid pattern uses asymmetric crypto only to deliver a fresh symmetric key, then fast symmetric crypto for the bulk data. Hashes cannot be reversed into data, and signing uses the signer's private key, not their public key.

q: What is the role of the certificate authority in PKI?
options: To generate and store the private keys of every organization that requests a certificate from the authority
To sign certificates, vouching that a public key belongs to the identity named in the certificate
To encrypt the traffic that passes between browsers and the websites they visit
To decide which cipher suites a browser and server will use during a handshake
explain: A CA's signature is the vouch that binds a key to an identity. Private keys stay with their owners, traffic encryption is done by the endpoints with session keys, and cipher suite selection happens between browser and server.

q: A website's certificate is valid, correctly signed, and unexpired — but it was issued for 'shop-example.com' while the user is visiting 'shop-examplle.com'. What should the browser do?
options: Connect, but switch the session to hashing instead of encryption until the name is corrected
Ask the certificate authority to rename the certificate to match the site the user typed
Refuse or warn, because the name on the certificate does not match the site being visited, so the identity check fails
Connect normally, because a valid CA signature matters more than the name printed on the certificate for the site being visited
explain: Validation checks that the certificate's name matches the site, the CA signature is valid, and the dates are in window; a name mismatch fails the identity check even when everything else is in order. Certificates are not renamed on request, and hashing is not a fallback transport mode.

q: Which pairing of tool and question is correct?
options: Hashing answers 'Who sent this, and can they deny it?'
Encryption answers 'Has this been changed?'
Digital signatures answer 'Can anyone else read this?'
Hashing answers 'Has this been changed?'
explain: Hashing detects change, encryption protects readability (confidentiality), and signatures answer who sent it and provide non-repudiation. The three tools answer three different questions, and the exam's favorite trick is offering the right tool for the wrong question.

q: An eavesdropper records an entire TLS session, including the handshake. Why can they not simply decrypt the recorded data afterward using the handshake messages?
options: Because the session key was agreed through asymmetric math that an observer cannot reverse from the exchanged messages, and the key itself was never transmitted
Because the data was hashed before sending, so the recording contains only fingerprints rather than readable content
Because the server's certificate encrypted the session, and certificates can only be decrypted by certificate authorities, who hold the master keys for every site they certify
Because each message used a different public key, and the corresponding private keys were destroyed after each use
explain: The handshake's key agreement lets both endpoints derive the same session key while an observer of the same messages cannot. The data is encrypted, not hashed; certificates authenticate rather than encrypt; and keys are not rotated per message.

q: A security team compares two candidate systems. System A uses a 128-bit symmetric key; System B uses a 64-bit symmetric key. How much larger is System A's keyspace?
options: 64 times larger, because each additional bit contributes one more multiple of the original keyspace
2^64 times larger — each of the 64 additional bits doubles the keyspace, compounding to an astronomically larger search
About 4,096 times larger, because keyspace grows with the square of the number of bits in the key
Twice as large, because 128 is twice 64 and the keyspace grows in direct proportion to the key length used by the cipher in question
explain: Keyspace doubles per bit, so 64 extra bits multiply the keyspace by 2^64. Linear and squared guesses both wildly understate exponential growth, which is the entire argument for modern key lengths.

q: Which statement about symmetric encryption's key distribution problem is correct?
options: Symmetric keys never need distribution, because the algorithm itself contains the key used by all participants
Each side generates its own unrelated key, and the two keys are mathematically linked so either can decrypt
Both sides need the same secret key, and delivering that key safely to both sides is the hard part
The key can safely be sent in plaintext alongside the first encrypted message, because attackers rarely record handshakes
explain: Symmetric encryption's weakness is delivery: one shared secret must reach both sides without exposure, which is why hybrid systems use asymmetric crypto for that step. Sending the key in plaintext with the data would hand it to any observer.

q: A sender signs an email and also needs its contents hidden from intermediaries. Signing alone does not hide the contents. Which statement explains why?
options: A digital signature encrypts the whole message by default, so the contents are hidden from everyone including the recipient until it is opened
A digital signature replaces the message with its hash, so the recipient receives only a fingerprint and no content
A digital signature requires the recipient's private key to open the message, which intermediaries could also obtain
A digital signature provides authenticity and integrity, not confidentiality; the message body remains readable unless it is also encrypted
explain: Signatures prove who sent a message and that it is unchanged; they do not conceal it. Confidentiality requires encryption as a separate step — the two are commonly combined, but they are different tools answering different questions.

q: Which algorithm would a system use to encrypt data at rest on a high-volume storage array?
options: AES, a fast symmetric cipher designed for bulk data
SHA-256, a hash function that encrypts with a 256-bit key
Diffie-Hellman, a protocol that encrypts stored data at rest
RSA, an asymmetric algorithm designed for bulk data
explain: Bulk data at rest is encrypted symmetrically, and AES is the workhorse. RSA is asymmetric and slow, SHA-256 hashes rather than encrypts, and Diffie-Hellman agrees keys rather than encrypting data.

q: A browser and server complete a TLS handshake. Which description of the resulting session is correct?
options: Both sides hash each message instead of encrypting it, relying on the fingerprint to keep the contents private
Both sides now encrypt traffic with the same fresh symmetric session key, which is discarded when the session ends
Both sides encrypt traffic with the server's public key, and the server decrypts everything with its private key
The browser encrypts with its private key and the server decrypts with the browser's public key for the whole session
explain: After the asymmetric introduction, the conversation runs on one shared symmetric session key. Public-key encryption of the whole session would be far too slow, and hashing provides no confidentiality at all.

q: An organization issues smart cards whose certificates let staff sign documents. An employee leaves, and the organization must ensure her signatures are no longer trusted for new documents. Which PKI mechanism addresses this?
options: Deleting her public key from every document she previously signed for the company
Rotating the root authority's certificate so that all employee certificates change
Revoking her certificate, so validation checks no longer accept it as a trusted binding
Hashing her certificate so that its contents can no longer be read by verifiers
explain: Revocation marks a certificate as no longer trustworthy before its expiry, and verifiers check for it during validation. Past documents keep their keys, the root is untouched by one departure, and hashing a certificate does not change its trust status.

q: Which of the following is TRUE of a hash function?
options: Its output length grows steadily as the input grows, keeping the fingerprint proportional to the data that produced it in the first place
Its output is identical for any two inputs that share the same first character or opening bytes
Its output can be decrypted with the matching private key whenever the original data is needed again
Its output cannot be used to recover the original input, no matter how much computing power is applied to the fingerprint alone
explain: Hashing is one-way by design: the fingerprint does not contain the input in recoverable form. There is no decryption key for a hash, the output size is fixed, and even near-identical inputs produce unrelated outputs.

q: A software vendor publishes the SHA-256 hash of its installer on its website. A user downloads the installer from a mirror and computes a different hash. What is the correct conclusion?
options: The downloaded file is not identical to the vendor's file — it was altered or corrupted — and it should not be trusted or installed
The file is safe, because a hash mismatch only matters when the file sizes are also different from each other
The mirror's file is a newer version, because a different hash always indicates the file was legitimately updated by the vendor's release team
The user's hashing tool is incompatible, because hashes of the same file differ between computers by design
explain: A hash mismatch means the file differs from the one the vendor hashed — any single changed bit produces a completely different output — so the file cannot be trusted. Hashes are deterministic across computers, and a mismatch is never explained away by file size.

q: Two parties use Diffie-Hellman to agree a session key over a public network, then encrypt their traffic with that key. An attacker who recorded the entire exchange still cannot read the traffic. Which statement explains the division of labor?
options: Diffie-Hellman encrypted the traffic directly; the session key was used only to sign each message sent during the exchange
Diffie-Hellman (asymmetric family) handled key agreement; symmetric encryption with the agreed key handled the data
The session key was hashed before use, and the hash is what the attacker would need to steal
The parties' certificates encrypted the traffic, while Diffie-Hellman verified their identities
explain: Diffie-Hellman's job is agreeing a shared secret over an unsafe channel; the symmetric cipher then does the fast work of encrypting data with that secret. Certificates authenticate identity but encrypt nothing, and signing is not part of this exchange.

q: Which scenario calls for a digital signature rather than encryption?
options: A database administrator must protect stored customer records so a stolen disk reveals nothing readable
Two servers must exchange a large nightly data feed quickly, with the same key held securely at both ends
A regulator must be able to prove that a report was submitted by the bank's compliance officer and was not altered afterward
A team must send next quarter's pricing to a partner so that no competitor who intercepts it can read the figures in the document
explain: Proving who sent something, that it is unchanged, and that the sender cannot deny it is the signature's job. The other scenarios ask for confidentiality — of a message, of stored records, and of a bulk feed — which is encryption's job.

q: A private key used for signing is stolen. What is the MOST serious consequence?
options: The certificate authority's root key is exposed, compromising every certificate it has issued
Anyone holding it can recompute the hashes of the owner's previously signed documents
The matching public key immediately stops working, so past signatures can no longer be verified by any recipient of those documents
Anyone holding it can sign as the owner, producing signatures that verify as genuine and destroying non-repudiation
explain: The private key is the signing identity: whoever holds it can impersonate the owner in signatures, and the owner can no longer credibly deny signatures. Hashes are public computations, the public key keeps verifying, and one leaf key does not expose the root.

q: Which set contains ONLY asymmetric-family techniques? (Choose the option that lists the complete correct set.)
options: RSA, ECC, and Diffie-Hellman
AES, RSA, and SHA-256
ECC, 3DES, and Diffie-Hellman
RSA, AES, and ECC
explain: RSA and ECC are asymmetric algorithms, and Diffie-Hellman belongs to the asymmetric family as a key-agreement method. AES and 3DES are symmetric ciphers, and SHA-256 is a hash function, so every other set is contaminated.

q: A password store uses a strong hash but NO salt. An attacker with a rainbow table attacks it. What happens?
options: Only the administrator's password is recovered, because rainbow tables target the first entry in the store before moving to the others
Passwords that appear in the precomputed table are recovered, because unsalted hashes match the table's entries exactly
The attack fails, because a strong hash algorithm alone makes precomputed tables useless against any store
Nothing, because rainbow tables only work against encrypted passwords rather than hashed ones
explain: Rainbow tables are precomputed hash chains built for unsalted passwords; without a salt, stored hashes match the table and common passwords fall. Salting — not the hash's strength alone — is what makes the table useless.

q: During the TLS handshake, the browser lists the cipher suites it supports and the server selects one. In which later beat is the session key established?
options: At the end of the session, when both sides exchange keys to protect the next connection between them
Before the browser's first hello, when it downloads the server's session key from the certificate authority that issued its certificate
After the server presents its certificate, the two sides use asymmetric math to agree on a fresh symmetric session key
During the first data transfer, when the server derives the key from the contents of the browser's request
explain: The order is: hello and suite list, server's choice and certificate, then asymmetric key agreement, then symmetric data transfer. The CA never supplies session keys, and the key protects this session, established before data flows.

q: Which statement BEST describes why a longer symmetric key is stronger?
options: Each added bit adds a fixed number of new keys, so strength grows steadily and predictably with length of the key being used
Longer keys make the cipher run more slowly, and the delay is what discourages attackers from trying
Longer keys allow the same key to be shared with more parties without weakening the encryption
Each added bit doubles the number of possible keys, so the search an attacker must perform grows exponentially
explain: Strength comes from keyspace size, and keyspace doubles with every bit — that exponential growth is what puts brute force out of reach. Length is not about cipher speed or about how many parties can share the key.

q: A company wants customers to verify that invoices genuinely come from the company and were not altered in transit, while the invoices themselves do not need to be secret. Which combination achieves this?
options: Sign each invoice: hash it and encrypt the hash with the company's private key, so customers can verify with the company's public key
Hash each invoice and keep the hash on the company's internal server, telling customers the invoices were checked before they were sent out
Send each invoice through a certificate authority, which re-issues it under the authority's own name
Encrypt each invoice with a symmetric key printed on the invoice, so customers can decrypt and read the contents
explain: Signing — private-key encryption of the invoice's hash — gives customers authenticity and integrity they can verify with the public key. A hash kept privately proves nothing to the customer, and encryption answers a confidentiality question the scenario does not ask.

q: An intermediate certificate authority's certificate expires. What is the effect on the chain of trust for certificates below it?
options: The root authority automatically re-signs every certificate below it with fresh validity dates
Certificates chained through it can no longer be validated up to a trusted root, so browsers will reject or warn on them until the chain is restored
Nothing changes, because only the end-entity certificate's dates are ever checked during validation
The private keys of every certificate below it stop working, so those sites lose encryption entirely, and their servers can no longer decrypt any traffic at all
explain: Validation walks the whole chain to a trusted root and checks each link, including dates; a broken middle link breaks validation for everything below it. The keys still function mathematically — it is trust that fails, and nothing re-signs automatically.

q: Which property distinguishes a digital signature from a plain hash of the same message?
options: The signature produces a longer output, and the extra length is what makes forgery mathematically impossible for anyone who does not hold the corresponding private key
The signature encrypts the message contents, while the hash leaves the contents readable to anyone
The signature involves the signer's private key, so it binds the message to an identity; a plain hash binds it to nothing and can be produced by anyone
The signature changes every time it is computed, while the hash of an unchanged message stays constant
explain: A hash is a public computation anyone can perform, so it cannot prove origin. Signing the hash with a private key ties it to the one key holder, providing authenticity and non-repudiation — without encrypting the message body.

q: A messaging app generates a fresh key pair for a user. The user asks which key to post on their profile so others can send them encrypted messages. The correct answer is:
options: Both keys — the pair only works when contacts hold a complete copy of both halves
Neither key — contacts should encrypt with their own private keys and send those instead
The private key — others need it to encrypt messages in a way that proves they came from senders
The public key — others encrypt with it, and only the user's private key can decrypt what they send
explain: Encryption to a recipient uses the recipient's public key, which is safe to publish precisely because it cannot decrypt. The private key never leaves the owner; publishing it would let anyone read the user's messages.

q: A system must verify file integrity across thousands of servers every night, comparing each file against a known-good reference. Why is hashing the practical tool for this?
options: A hash gives a short, fixed-size fingerprint for any file, so comparisons are cheap and any single changed bit produces a completely different result
A hash signs each file with the server's private key, so the reference proves which server created the file
A hash encrypts each file with the reference key, so unauthorized versions cannot be opened by the servers at all, including the servers that legitimately host the production copies
A hash stores a compressed copy of each file, so the original can be restored whenever a difference is found
explain: Fixed-size fingerprints make mass comparison trivial, and the avalanche effect means any change shows up. Hashes neither encrypt, compress for restore, nor sign — those are different tools with different jobs.

q: Which of the following is the correct order of the beats in a TLS handshake?
options: Server presents its certificate; browser lists its cipher suites; data flows under symmetric encryption; the sides agree a session key at the end
Browser hello with its cipher suites; server chooses a suite and presents its certificate; the sides agree a symmetric session key asymmetrically; data flows under symmetric encryption
The sides agree a symmetric session key; browser hello with its cipher suites; server presents its certificate; data flows under the server's public key
Browser downloads the session key from the authority; server presents its certificate; browser lists its cipher suites; data flows under symmetric encryption for the rest of the session between them
explain: The handshake runs hello and suites, server selection and certificate validation, asymmetric agreement on a fresh symmetric key, then fast symmetric data transfer. Keys are agreed before data flows and are never downloaded from an authority.

q: A developer asks why the application should not simply use RSA to encrypt its database backups directly. The BEST answer is:
options: RSA keys are too short to be secure, so regulators require AES for any data stored longer than a day
RSA encryption is reversible only by certificate authorities, who will not decrypt commercial backups
RSA is asymmetric and slow, so real systems encrypt bulk data symmetrically and use asymmetric crypto only to protect or exchange the symmetric key
RSA cannot encrypt data larger than a single block, and no padding scheme exists to work around that limit in any implementation of the algorithm available today
explain: The objection is speed and design fit: asymmetric math handles keys and introductions, symmetric math handles volume — the hybrid pattern. RSA keys are not inherently insecure, and CAs play no role in decrypting anyone's backups.

q: Which combination of mechanisms does a signed AND encrypted email use, in the correct roles? (Choose the option that lists the complete correct set.)
options: The certificate authority signs the message for authenticity; the root key encrypts it for confidentiality
The sender's public key signs the message for authenticity; the recipient's private key encrypts it for confidentiality throughout the exchange
A shared password hashes the message for authenticity; the certificate encrypts it for confidentiality
The sender's private key signs a hash for authenticity; encryption with a symmetric key (protected asymmetrically) provides confidentiality
explain: Signing always uses the signer's private key, and confidentiality comes from encryption — in practice a symmetric key wrapped with asymmetric crypto. Public keys verify rather than sign, and authorities neither sign user mail nor encrypt it with root keys.

q: An attacker obtains a database of SHA-256 hashes of passwords, all unsalted, along with the usernames. Users who chose common passwords are at greatest risk PRIMARILY because:
options: Identical passwords produce identical hashes, and precomputed tables map common passwords' hashes straight back to the passwords
SHA-256 outputs can be decrypted with the usernames, which act as the matching keys for each stored hash
Unsalted hashes expire after a fixed period, after which the original passwords are transmitted in plaintext to the server at sign-in
The attacker can change one bit in each hash to produce the password that the user originally chose
explain: Without salt, the same password always yields the same hash, so tables of precomputed hashes for common passwords reverse them instantly. Hashes cannot be decrypted, do not expire into plaintext, and cannot be edited into passwords.

q: Which statement about public keys is correct?
options: A public key is used by its owner to decrypt messages that others encrypted with the owner's private key
A public key can be shared openly, because knowing it lets others encrypt to the owner or verify the owner's signatures, but not decrypt or sign as the owner
A public key expires whenever the matching certificate is viewed by an untrusted party on the network
A public key must be guarded as carefully as the private key, because it can be used to reconstruct the private key through a short calculation that any attacker can perform
explain: Public keys are designed for open distribution: they enable encryption to the owner and verification of the owner's signatures, while the powers that matter — decrypting and signing — stay with the private key. Others encrypt with the public key, not with the owner's private key.

q: A team must choose how to protect a one-time exchange of a small contract file with a new partner, and ongoing nightly transfers of multi-gigabyte data files afterward. Which plan applies each tool correctly?
options: Sign the nightly files with the partner's private key, which the partner should send over so the team can apply it
Use the partner's public key to encrypt everything including the nightly transfers, because asymmetric encryption is the stronger choice at any size of data being protected
Use the partner's public key to protect the small exchange and to wrap symmetric keys; use fast symmetric encryption with those keys for the nightly bulk transfers
Hash both the contract and the nightly files, because a fingerprint protects content as effectively as encryption while using less space
explain: This is the hybrid model: asymmetric crypto handles introductions and key protection, symmetric crypto handles volume. Hashing gives integrity only, and a partner's private key must never be sent to anyone.

q: Which of the following BEST explains what a salt does NOT do?
options: It does not need to be unique per password; a single shared salt for all users defeats rainbow tables just as completely
It does not change the stored hash; the salt is applied only during the sign-in attempt and never during storage
It does not protect against guessing; a salted password of '123456' remains exactly as strong as an unsalted one against all attacks, including dictionary attacks run entirely offline
It does not encrypt the password or make the hash reversible only to the server; the stored value remains a one-way fingerprint that cannot be turned back into the password
explain: A salt is mixed in before hashing and stored with the hash; it keeps hashing one-way while making each stored value unique. It must be unique per password to fully defeat precomputed tables, and it does not stop an attacker from guessing weak passwords directly — it only defeats the precomputation shortcut.

q: A security analyst wants a single reference that lets her scanner, a vendor advisory, and a news report all point to exactly the same disclosed flaw. What does the CVE system provide for that flaw?
options: A unique identifier and a standard description assigned when the vulnerability is publicly disclosed
A numerical severity score from 0.0 to 10.0 calculated from a vector of base metrics
A live feed of indicators that updates automatically as attackers change their tooling
A prioritized patching order that ranks the flaw against every other finding in the queue for the team each week
explain: CVE gives each publicly disclosed vulnerability one unique identifier and a standard description, so every tool and report means the same flaw. The 0.0 to 10.0 score describes CVSS, and a feed or a patching order is a separate process built on top of the identifier.

q: A vulnerability carries the CVSS vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N. Working the base metrics through gives an impact sub-score of about 3.60 and an exploitability sub-score of about 3.89. What is the correct base score and severity?
options: 9.8, rated Critical, because network exploitation with no privileges always scores near the top of the scale
7.5, rated High, because the two sub-scores add to 7.49 and CVSS always rounds the result up
5.3, rated Medium, because only one of the three impact measures is affected by this flaw
7.4, rated High, because the two sub-scores add to 7.49 and CVSS rounds to the nearest value
explain: Impact of 3.60 plus exploitability of 3.89 totals 7.49, and CVSS rounds up, giving 7.5, which sits in the 7.0 to 8.9 High band. A 9.8 needs high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability together; this flaw affects confidentiality only, and rounding down or to nearest is not how CVSS works.

q: A small company subscribes to vendor advisories, a government alert service, and an industry sharing group, and routes all three into its ticketing system. What are these sources collectively providing?
options: A vulnerability scan schedule that tests each asset in turn and records which ports respond
A set of compensating controls that reduce the impact of flaws the company cannot patch yet
Threat intelligence from threat feeds and intelligence sources about attackers and their tools
A risk register that records the owner, due date, and residual risk for each accepted finding for the coming year
explain: Vendor feeds, government advisories, and industry sharing groups are classic threat intelligence sources, supplying information about attackers and their tools. They do not themselves scan assets, act as compensating controls, or maintain the company's risk register.

q: A patch queue holds two findings. Finding A scores 9.8 and sits in a test application on an isolated lab network, with no exploitation reported anywhere. Finding B scores 6.5 on the internet-facing VPN gateway, and two threat feeds report it under active exploitation this week. Which action best applies sound prioritization?
options: Patch Finding A first in an emergency window because the higher CVSS score always takes precedence over context
Patch both findings in the same regular cycle because a difference of one severity band rarely justifies urgency
Defer Finding B because a 6.5 is only Medium severity and Medium findings never warrant an emergency change
Patch Finding B first in an emergency window because reachability and active exploitation make it the worse risk
explain: The 9.8 is the worse flaw, but the 6.5 is the worse risk: it sits on the front door, is reachable by everyone, and is being used right now, so it gets the emergency window while the isolated lab flaw waits for the regular cycle. Score alone never sets the order; exposure, asset value, and exploitation status complete the judgment.

q: For a CVSS vector with scope unchanged and high impact on confidentiality only, with integrity and availability unaffected, what is the impact sub-score (ISS) before it is weighted?
options: 0.56, because ISS equals 1 minus (0.44 times 1 times 1) when only confidentiality is high
0.915, because ISS combines all three impact values as though each one were rated high in the stated vector
0.44, because ISS is simply the numeric value assigned to a single high impact rating
0.00, because ISS only counts a flaw when at least two impact measures are affected
explain: High converts to 0.56 and none to 0, so ISS = 1 - [(1-0.56) x (1-0) x (1-0)] = 1 - 0.44 = 0.56. The 0.915 figure is the ISS when confidentiality, integrity, and availability are all high, which is not this vector.

q: During a risk discussion, a manager asks how probable it is that a particular attack succeeds against the company this quarter, given current exposure and attacker interest. Which half of the risk judgment is she asking about?
options: Impact, because she is asking about a specific attack against a specific asset in a set period
Likelihood, because she is asking how probable the event is for this organization right now
Severity, because she is asking for the rating the vulnerability scanner assigned to the flaw
Exposure, because she is asking which systems an attacker can reach from outside the network
explain: Likelihood asks how probable an event is, for us, now, which is exactly her question. Impact is the other half and asks how badly it hurts if it happens; a scanner severity rating and a reachability check inform the judgment but are not the judgment itself.

q: A hospital estimates that a ransomware outage in its imaging department would cancel procedures for two days and trigger regulatory reporting, even though such an attack is considered unlikely this year. Which concept does the two-day outage and reporting burden describe?
options: Likelihood, because any consequence described in days can be converted into a probability estimate
Exploitability, because the estimate assumes the attacker can reach the imaging systems at will
Impact, because it describes how badly the organization is hurt if the event actually happens
Residual risk, because the estimate already accounts for the controls the hospital has in place
explain: Impact asks: if it happens, how badly does it hurt? Cancelled procedures and regulatory reporting are harm, so they describe impact, regardless of how unlikely the event is. Likelihood is the probability half, and nothing in the estimate says controls were already factored in, so residual risk is not established.

q: A threat is spotted in the wild, analysts study how it works, the team builds indicators and detections from that study, and those detections are pushed into the firewall and endpoint tools. Which process has the team just walked through?
options: The vulnerability disclosure process, where a researcher reports a flaw and the vendor prepares a fix
The incident response cycle, where a confirmed compromise is contained, eradicated, and recovered from step by step
The change management process, where a proposed control change is reviewed, approved, and documented
The threat life cycle, where intelligence is observed, analyzed, turned into detection, and fed into defenses
explain: That path — observed, analyzed, converted into indicators and detection, then fed back into defenses — is the threat life cycle. No flaw was disclosed to a vendor, no confirmed compromise was handled, and no control change was approved, so the other cycles do not fit.

q: A scanner reports a vulnerability with a CVSS base score of 8.5. How should the analyst classify its severity when writing up the finding?
options: High, because scores from 7.0 through 8.9 fall in the High severity band
Critical, because any score above 8.0 is treated as Critical severity
Medium, because scores stay Medium until they reach at least 9.0
Low, because a single decimal score cannot be classified without the vector
explain: The CVSS bands place 7.0 to 8.9 at High; Critical starts at 9.0, Medium ends at 6.9, and Low ends at 3.9. The score alone is enough to name the band, even though the vector explains how the score was reached.

q: An analyst notices that famous vulnerabilities scoring 9.8 almost always share a pattern in their vectors. What pattern produces a score that high?
options: A changed scope combined with a low attack complexity and a requirement for user interaction
High impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability together, with easy network exploitation
A high confidentiality impact paired with a physical attack vector and administrator privileges
Low impact on all three measures offset by a very high exploitability sub-score from the network in the vector
explain: With C, I, and A all high, the impact sub-score rises to about 0.915 and impact to about 5.87; added to strong network exploitability of about 3.89, the total rounds up to 9.8. One high impact alone caps a flaw in the 7s, and physical vectors or required privileges pull scores down, not up.

q: A manufacturing firm learns about a new attack technique against plant controllers first from peer companies in its sector, weeks before any vendor publishes guidance. Which intelligence source served the firm here?
options: A commercial scanner feed that pushed a new detection plugin to the firm's vulnerability tool
An open-source news article that summarized the technique after it was already widely reported
An industry sharing group where organizations in the same sector exchange threat information
A government advisory that assigned the technique an identifier and a standard description
explain: Peer companies in the same sector exchanging what they are seeing is an industry sharing group, one of the named intelligence sources. The information arrived before vendor guidance and wider reporting, which rules out the scanner feed and the news summary, and no identifier assignment is described.

q: A security team pays for a premium threat feed, but nobody reviews it, no detections are built from it, and no decision has ever changed because of it. How should this feed be assessed?
options: As high-value intelligence, because premium feeds are curated and therefore reliable by default
As a compensating control, because subscribing to it reduces the likelihood of a successful attack
As partial compliance evidence, because holding the subscription satisfies intelligence requirements
As trivia, because intelligence is only useful when it changes a decision or a defense
explain: Intelligence earns its value by changing a decision; a feed nobody acts on is trivia, whatever it costs. It blocks nothing, so it is not a control, and merely holding a subscription demonstrates no actual intelligence practice.

q: In a CVSS vector, what does the metric pair AV:N and AC:L together tell an analyst about a vulnerability?
options: It can be exploited over the network and the attack requires no special conditions beyond the attacker's control
It can only be exploited by an adjacent network attacker and the attack needs precise timing to succeed reliably
It requires the attacker to log in first and the exploit works only under rare, target-specific circumstances
It can be exploited over the network only when a victim user performs an action such as opening a file
explain: AV:N means the flaw is exploitable over the network, and AC:L means low complexity — no special conditions beyond the attacker's control must line up. Login requirements are captured by PR, and victim action by UI, so those readings belong to different metrics.

q: Two flaws both score 7.5. One requires administrator privileges before it can be exploited; the other needs no privileges at all. In the CVSS vector, which metric captures that difference?
options: User interaction, because needing an account is treated as a form of interaction with the system
Privileges required, because it records the level of access an attacker must already hold to exploit
Attack complexity, because holding privileges makes the attack steps themselves harder to carry out in practice
Scope, because exploiting with privileges lets the flaw affect components beyond its own authority
explain: PR — privileges required — records the access an attacker must already hold, and none (0.85) versus high privileges changes the exploitability math. UI covers a separate victim's action, AC covers conditions beyond the attacker's control, and scope covers crossing an authority boundary, not the starting privilege level.

q: A flaw lets an attacker escape a sandboxed application and alter the hypervisor running other virtual machines. When scoring it, which CVSS metric reflects that the affected component sits outside the vulnerable component's authority?
options: Confidentiality impact, because data belonging to the other virtual machines can be read by the attacker
Integrity impact, because the hypervisor's code and configuration can be changed by the escaped attacker
Scope, because the vulnerability in one component impacts resources managed by a different authority
Availability impact, because the other virtual machines may be stopped or starved by the escaped attacker
explain: Scope is the metric for crossing an authority boundary: S:C means the vulnerable component and the impacted component sit under different authorities. The C, I, and A metrics then measure how much harm follows inside that new scope; they do not themselves record the boundary crossing.

q: A database flaw can be triggered only when a logged-in clerk clicks a crafted link the attacker sends. The rest of the vector is network-based, low complexity, and needs no attacker privileges. Which metric value must the vector carry for the clerk's click?
options: PR:L, because the clerk holds a low-privilege account on the database application being attacked
AC:H, because depending on a person to click makes the attack conditions unusually difficult
AV:A, because the attack travels through an adjacent user rather than directly over the network
UI:R, because exploitation requires a user other than the attacker to perform an action
explain: UI:R — user interaction required — is exactly the metric for a flaw that needs a victim to click or open something. PR describes the attacker's own privileges, AC describes conditions beyond the attacker's control, and AV still stays network because the link is delivered and triggered over the network.

q: An analyst is handed a CVE identifier in an advisory, formatted like CVE-2026-12345. What can she reliably conclude from the identifier alone?
options: It names one specific publicly disclosed vulnerability that every scanner and vendor will reference the same way
It tells her the vulnerability scores in the High band and should be patched inside the current change window this quarter
It guarantees that a working exploit for the vulnerability is already circulating among attacker groups
It confirms that the vendor has released a patch and that applying it will fully remove the vulnerability
explain: A CVE identifier is a naming guarantee, not a severity, exploitation, or patch guarantee: it pins one disclosed flaw so everyone references the same thing. Severity comes from CVSS, exploitation status from threat intelligence, and patch availability from the vendor.

q: A flaw scores 0.0 on the CVSS scale even though a CVE identifier exists for it. What does a 0.0 base score mean?
options: The flaw has been fully patched everywhere, so scoring systems retire it at the lowest possible value
The flaw's impact measures are all none, so it carries None severity despite being publicly disclosed
The flaw is being exploited so quietly that scoring systems cannot measure any of its impact values
The flaw affects only test systems, and scoring systems automatically zero out non-production findings
explain: On the severity table, 0.0 is None: the vector's impact measures come out to none, yet the flaw can still be disclosed and carry a CVE. Patching status, exploitation, and whether a system is a test box are context a base score does not encode.

q: A retailer must choose which of two equally scored flaws to patch during a short freeze exception. One flaw affects the payment platform that processes every transaction; the other affects an internal wiki used by one small team. Which prioritization factor most clearly separates the two?
options: The age of each flaw, because the older disclosed flaw is always the one attackers prefer to use
The length of each advisory, because a longer vendor write-up signals a more serious underlying flaw
The value and exposure of the affected asset, because the payment platform carries far more business weight
The scanner that found each flaw, because findings from a newer scanner are treated as more trustworthy on the team
explain: Prioritization weighs score alongside context, and asset value is the separating context here: the payment platform's compromise hurts far more than the small team's wiki. Disclosure age, advisory length, and scanner brand do not rank risk.

q: Threat intelligence reports that a flaw in a common library has just moved from theoretical discussion to working exploits shared in attacker forums, though no score change has been published. How should a defender treat the flaw's priority?
options: Lower it, because forum discussion without a score change means vendors consider the flaw unimportant
Leave it unchanged, because priority may only move when the official base score is formally revised
Raise it only after the first confirmed victim, because forum exploit code is routinely non-functional in most reported cases
Raise it now, because intelligence that exploitation is becoming practical changes the risk even at the same score
explain: Prioritization ranks by score and context, and credible intelligence of working exploitation is decisive context — the risk rose even though the number did not. Waiting for a revised score or a first victim surrenders exactly the lead time intelligence exists to provide.

q: A CVSS vector reads AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. Compared with the same vector at AV:N, how does the adjacent attack vector affect the assessment?
options: It lowers exploitability, because the attacker must sit on a logically adjacent network rather than reach the target from anywhere
It raises exploitability, because adjacent networks are trusted and therefore skip most perimeter filtering controls on the target's segment
It changes only the impact sub-score, because the attack vector describes how much data the attacker can reach
It removes the flaw from scoring entirely, because adjacent-network flaws are tracked by a separate scoring system
explain: AV:A is worth less than AV:N in the exploitability math because the attacker must be on a logically adjacent network, a real constraint on who can reach the flaw. The impact metrics are untouched by the vector choice, and adjacent flaws are scored by the same CVSS system.

q: A security lead tells her board that a moderate flaw under active attack worries her more than a severe flaw nobody can currently exploit. Which principle is she applying?
options: Severity and risk are identical, so the moderate flaw must secretly carry a higher unpublished score
Likelihood and impact combine into risk, so an exploited moderate flaw can outrank an unexploited severe one
Scanner severity bands are unreliable, so any ranking built on them should be discarded entirely
Active attacks are always brief, so the moderate flaw will resolve itself before it causes real harm for the organization
explain: Risk is judged on likelihood and impact together: the actively exploited moderate flaw is far more likely to hurt the organization now than the severe flaw nobody can use. That does not make the scores identical or the bands useless — it means context completes the judgment the score starts.

q: An analyst scores a flaw that discloses full database contents to an unauthenticated network attacker but cannot be used to alter or delete any data, and the service keeps running. Which impact profile fits the vector?
options: C:N/I:H/A:H, because reading the database implies the attacker can also change and stop it
C:H/I:H/A:N, because full disclosure of contents is treated as both a confidentiality and integrity loss
C:H/I:N/A:N, because the harm is disclosure only, with no modification and no loss of availability
C:N/I:N/A:H, because any database flaw is scored primarily as an availability problem for the service
explain: The described harm is pure disclosure: confidentiality high, integrity none, availability none. Reading data does not by itself grant modification, and CVSS scores the impact that is demonstrated, not impacts an analyst assumes might follow.

q: A government advisory warns that a flaw in a widely used edge appliance is being exploited by attackers this week and urges immediate patching. A company running that appliance reads the advisory during its morning review. Which two 2.1 concepts has the advisory just combined for the company?
options: A CVE-style identifier for the flaw and a calculation of the company's internal audit findings for the quarter under review
A severity band for the flaw and a schedule for the company's next penetration test against the appliance
A statement of business impact and a record of which employee is accountable for the appliance's patching
Threat intelligence about current exploitation and the affected flaw, which together drive patch prioritization
explain: The advisory is threat intelligence — current, external information about attacker behavior — and pairing it with the specific flaw is what lets the company prioritize. No identifier mechanics, audit record, test schedule, or accountability assignment is doing the work in this scenario.

q: A flaw requires the attacker to win a race condition that succeeds roughly one attempt in a thousand, with no way to improve the odds. Which CVSS metric records this difficulty, and at what value?
options: Attack complexity at high, because conditions beyond the attacker's control must align for exploitation to succeed
Privileges required at high, because repeated attempts are treated as equivalent to holding elevated access
User interaction at required, because each failed attempt needs a fresh action from a legitimate system user when it triggers
Attack vector at adjacent, because unreliable exploits are scored as though reach were also restricted
explain: AC:H covers exactly this: success depends on conditions beyond the attacker's control, such as winning an unlikely race. PR measures access held beforehand, UI measures a victim's action, and AV measures where the attack can be launched from — none of them describe reliability.

q: A company's scanner lists 4,000 findings. The security lead refuses to hand the raw list to the patching teams and instead produces a ranked short list. What is the lead practicing?
options: Threat modeling, because ranking findings requires drawing the data flows of every affected application first
Prioritization, because findings are ordered by score together with exposure, asset value, and exploitation context
Risk acceptance, because shortening the list means the remaining findings are formally accepted as tolerable
Compensating control design, because a ranked list substitutes for patching the findings it leaves at the bottom it produces
explain: Turning a raw findings list into a ranked order using score plus exposure, asset value, and active exploitation is prioritization. Nothing was formally accepted as risk, no control substitutes for the patches, and no data-flow modeling is described.

q: A newly published flaw scores 4.5. A junior analyst tells the team it can be ignored because it is 'only Medium.' What is the best correction?
options: Medium findings are actually scored 7.0 to 8.9, so the analyst has read the wrong severity band entirely
A 4.5 is really a Low finding, and Low findings are the ones that may safely be ignored indefinitely
The band is a starting point only; a Medium flaw on a critical, exposed, actively exploited asset can still go first
Any flaw with a published score must be patched before all unscored flaws, whatever the band or the context or the asset involved
explain: Medium is correctly 4.0 to 6.9, but the score is the start of the conversation, never the whole of it — exposure, asset value, and active exploitation can push a Medium finding to the front. Bands do not license ignoring a finding, and unscored does not automatically mean lower priority either.

q: During tabletop planning, a team lists the raw materials it will monitor continuously: vendor feeds, sharing-group posts, government advisories, and open-source reporting on attacker tooling. What single term covers all of these inputs?
options: Indicators of compromise gathered from the company's own firewall and endpoint logs after incidents
Vulnerability scan results collected from the company's authenticated scans of its internal address ranges
Penetration test reports commissioned from an external firm that simulates attacks against the company
Threat intelligence sources that report on attackers, their tools, and their current campaigns
explain: Feeds, sharing groups, advisories, and open-source reporting are the named sources of threat intelligence — information about attackers and their tools. The other choices are internally generated artifacts: the company's own logs, its own scans, and a test it commissioned.

q: A flaw's exploitability sub-score comes out higher than a colleague expected. The vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N. Why is the exploitability value so strong?
options: Every factor is at its most favorable value for the attacker: network reach, low complexity, no privileges, no interaction
Exploitability ignores the attack vector entirely, so only the impact metrics can move the final base score
Exploitability is fixed at the same value for all flaws and only changes when the scope metric is set to changed
The value is strong because confidentiality is high, and impact values feed directly into the exploitability sub-score in this case
explain: Exploitability multiplies 8.22 by AV, AC, PR, and UI; with all four at their attacker-friendliest values (0.85, 0.77, 0.85, 0.85) it reaches about 3.89. Impact values feed the separate impact sub-score, and exploitability is anything but fixed across vectors.

q: A team debates whether a flaw in a public demo kiosk matters. The flaw is trivially exploitable, but the kiosk holds no accounts, no payment data, and no path into the internal network. Which judgment best fits the 2.1 framework?
options: High likelihood and high impact, because trivial exploitation automatically makes any flaw a serious risk
High likelihood and low impact, because exploitation is easy but the harm if it happens is small
Low likelihood and high impact, because kiosks are rarely targeted but hold a privileged network position
Low likelihood and low impact, because a system with no data can never be used in any further attack
explain: The two halves separate cleanly here: exploitation is easy, so likelihood is high; the kiosk holds nothing of value and leads nowhere, so impact is low. Ease of exploitation alone does not manufacture impact, and claiming a compromised device could never be misused at all overstates the low-impact case.

q: An analyst must explain to a new hire why the same CVE appears in the scanner report, the vendor bulletin, and a podcast's show notes with identical meaning. What property of the CVE system makes that possible?
options: Each identifier embeds the flaw's severity band, so every audience reads the same risk level from the number
Each identifier is assigned by the scanner vendor, so tools from that vendor stay consistent with each other over time
Each publicly disclosed vulnerability receives one unique identifier and a standard description everyone references
Each identifier expires after a set period, so older references are retired before meanings can drift apart
explain: One flaw, one identifier, one standard description — that shared naming is what lets a scanner, a bulletin, and a podcast all mean the same vulnerability. Identifiers do not embed severity, are not vendor-assigned, and do not expire on a schedule.

q: A flaw in a building controller can only be triggered by someone physically present at the device's local console, using a debug cable. Which attack vector value belongs in its CVSS vector?
options: AV:N, because the controller is connected to the building network even though the flaw needs local access
AV:L, because local console access sits one step above physical contact in the vector value ordering
AV:A, because the attacker must be adjacent to the device on the same building management segment
AV:P, because exploitation requires physical access to the target system or a component of it
explain: AV:P — physical — is the value when exploitation requires physical access to the device, which a debug cable at the console plainly is. Network connectivity elsewhere in the product does not change how this particular flaw is reached.

q: A security team wants its intelligence program judged at the end of the year. Which measure best shows whether the program is working as 2.1 intends?
options: Decisions and detections that changed because of intelligence, such as priorities reordered and rules built from feeds
The total number of feed subscriptions held, counted across every vendor and sharing group the team belongs to this year
The total volume of advisories stored, measured by the size of the archive the team has accumulated this year
The number of analysts with intelligence in their job title, compared against the team's overall headcount
explain: Intelligence is only useful if it changes a decision, so changed priorities and detections built from it are the honest measure. Subscription counts, archive size, and job titles measure accumulation, not effect — a large archive nobody acts on is trivia at scale.

q: A flaw scores 6.5 on an internet-facing gateway. A month later, with the score unchanged, the team escalates it to the emergency patch window. What most plausibly justifies the escalation?
options: The flaw's identifier was republished in a second advisory, which automatically doubles its effective severity
Threat feeds began reporting the flaw under active exploitation, changing its risk without changing its score
The gateway's vendor extended its support contract, which raises the priority of all flaws on supported systems
A second scanner confirmed the finding, and scanner agreement is the formal trigger for emergency patching
explain: Active exploitation reported by threat feeds is the classic context change that moves a mid-scored, internet-facing flaw into the emergency window while its CVSS number stays put. Republication, support contracts, and scanner agreement do not reorder risk.

q: When an analyst reads the vector string AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N aloud for a report, which expansion of the impact letters is correct?
options: Confidentiality none, integrity high, availability none, because the letters are read in reverse vector order
Confidentiality high, integrity high, availability none, because a disclosure flaw is presumed to allow changes
Confidentiality high, integrity none, availability none, because only the C metric is set to high in this vector
Confidentiality none, integrity none, availability high, because the final letter position carries the real impact
explain: The vector states C:H/I:N/A:N directly: confidentiality high, integrity none, availability none. Nothing in CVSS reverses the order or presumes extra impacts, which is why this vector lands at 7.5 rather than 9.8.

q: An attacker group backed by a foreign government maintains quiet access to a power utility's network for over a year, copying operational documents and never disrupting anything. Which actor type and primary motivation best fit this behavior?
options: Organized crime motivated by extortion, because long dwell time is used to maximize pressure before a demand
A hacktivist group motivated by a cause, because utilities are symbolic targets chosen for public embarrassment publicly
A competitor motivated by advantage, because operational documents reveal pricing the rival can undercut
A state-sponsored actor motivated by espionage, because a government's resources fund patient, hidden collection
explain: Very high resources, long-term hidden access, and document collection without disruption are the signature of a state-sponsored espionage operation. Extortion crews want to be noticed when they strike, hacktivists seek publicity for a cause, and a competitor's prize is commercial advantage rather than a utility's operations.

q: A criminal enterprise runs ransomware as a business, with affiliates, a payment portal, negotiators, and a leak site where stolen data is posted when victims refuse to pay. Which actor type best describes this enterprise?
options: Organized crime, because the operation is structured and resourced around sustained financial gain
A script kiddie, because the affiliates use tools built by others rather than writing their own malware
A hacktivist collective, because publishing victim data is a form of protest against the target companies
An insider threat, because the operation depends on employees inside victim firms opening the first email
explain: Affiliates, negotiators, and leak sites describe a business: organized crime, with high resources and money as the goal. Using others' tools does not make an operation a script kiddie, the leak site is payment leverage rather than protest, and no insider participation is described.

q: A recently fired systems administrator uses still-active credentials to delete backups and corrupt a database on his last weekend, telling a coworker the company 'would finally feel it.' Which actor type and motivation pair fits best?
options: A terrorist actor motivated by fear, because the deletion was meant to frighten the remaining workforce
An insider motivated by revenge, because he used access his job granted to strike back at the company
A state-sponsored actor motivated by disruption, because the attack targeted the company's core data stores
A shadow IT actor motivated by carelessness, because the damage followed from ordinary administrative habits
explain: The access came from his job and the stated purpose was payback, which is the insider driven by revenge. Nothing suggests political terror aims, a foreign sponsor, or accident — the deletion and the parting comment were deliberate.

q: A teenager downloads a free stresser tool and knocks a school gaming server offline for an evening, then posts screenshots in a chat to show off. Which actor type and motivation best describe this?
options: A hacktivist motivated by influence, because the outage was meant to change the school's gaming policy
Organized crime motivated by extortion, because the screenshots were a demand for payment in disguise
A script kiddie motivated by notoriety, because low-skill tool use was aimed at bragging rights among peers
A competitor motivated by advantage, because taking a rival server offline improves the attacker's ranking at school
explain: Downloaded tooling, low resources, and showing off for peers are the script kiddie pattern, with notoriety as the motivation. There is no cause being protested, no payment demanded, and no commercial rival gaining an advantage.

q: A company's design files for an unreleased product appear in a rival manufacturer's hands two months before launch, and investigators find the rival quietly funded the intrusion. Which actor type and motivation pair fits best?
options: A state-sponsored actor motivated by espionage, because unreleased designs are strategic national information
A hacktivist motivated by a cause, because leaking designs embarrasses a large manufacturer publicly
An insider motivated by curiosity, because an employee browsing design files needs no external sponsor at all
A competitor motivated by advantage, seeking intellectual property such as designs, plans, and pricing
explain: A rival funding an intrusion to obtain unreleased designs is the competitor actor, and the motivation is advantage through stolen intellectual property. No government sponsor, protest cause, or merely curious employee accounts for the rival ending up with the files.

q: After a controversial court ruling, a loosely organized group defaces a government agency's public website and floods it with traffic, posting manifestos explaining the protest. Which actor type best fits?
options: Hacktivists, because the group acts for a cause and seeks embarrassment and protest visibility
