options: Publishing the model's full decision rules so attackers no longer need to probe the system to learn how it behaves
Removing all input validation so the model sees raw submissions exactly as the attackers choose to format them
Rate-limiting and monitoring queries, and requiring human review for high-value decisions instead of trusting the model alone
Training the model once and never evaluating it again, so its decision boundary stays fixed and predictable forever according to the evidence described in the case
explain: Query limits and monitoring make boundary-mapping expensive, and human review protects high-stakes outcomes. Publishing the rules hands attackers the map, removing validation helps crafted inputs, and a frozen, unevaluated model stays predictably exploitable.

q: A small patterned sticker on a stop sign causes a vehicle vision model to read it as a speed-limit sign, while human drivers still see a stop sign. Which AI threat is this?
options: Poisoning, because the sticker changes the examples the model will learn from when it is next retrained on road data
A hallucination, because the model generated a confident description of a sign that was not actually present there
Jailbreaking, because the sticker defeats the safety restrictions the model's provider placed on its generated outputs given the facts presented in the scenario here
Evasion, because a crafted real-world input exploits the model's decision boundary without touching the model or its training
explain: Stickers that fool a deployed model are the classic evasion example: input as weapon, model untouched. Poisoning requires training influence, hallucination is false generation, and jailbreaking targets output restrictions.

q: A spammer rewords a message with invisible characters so an AI content filter classifies it as benign, though readers see the same pitch. Which threat and lesson are correct?
options: Evasion — a model's decision boundary is itself an attack surface, so high-stakes filtering decisions need layered checks beyond the model
Poisoning — the message will enter the training set and teach future models that this spam category is acceptable content
Hallucination — the filter invented a category for the message that does not exist in the provider's policy taxonomy
Bias — the filter treated the message differently because its training data underrepresented the sender's demographic group
explain: Invisible-character tricks that flip a classification are evasion, and the lesson is that model decisions alone are fragile for high-stakes calls. No training, invented category, or group disparity is described.

q: Which control BEST reduces the impact of evasion attacks against an AI document-screening system?
options: Allowing submitters to see the model's confidence score and the exact features it used, so they can adjust documents until they pass the screen
Adding independent verification for consequential decisions, such as human review or a second check, rather than relying on the model's classification alone
Training the model exclusively on documents submitted by the public, so it learns the current appearance of evasion attempts automatically
Disabling the screening system whenever an evasion attempt is detected, so no document can be misclassified during the outage period
explain: Evasion is blunted when the model's word is not final for consequential decisions. Showing scores and features teaches attackers the boundary, public-only training invites poisoning, and disabling screening removes the control entirely.

q: A model writes a compliance summary citing three court cases, complete with docket numbers, none of which exist. No attacker is involved. Which AI risk is this?
options: A jailbreak, where the user defeated the model's restrictions to make it produce material it should have refused to give in the situation the scenario describes in full
An evasion, where a crafted input caused the model to misclassify the cases it was asked to summarize for the report
A hallucination, where the model generates fluent, confident content that is simply false and must be verified before use
Data poisoning, where false cases were planted in the training data specifically so the model would cite them later
explain: Invented citations are the textbook hallucination — a failure mode, not an attack. Nothing was refused, misclassified, or planted; the model generated falsehoods on its own.

q: Which practice BEST manages hallucination risk when staff use AI to draft security reports?
options: Require the model to state its confidence in percentages, and accept any statement it rates above ninety percent as verified
Ask the model to repeat the same question three times and treat any answer that appears twice as confirmed factual content
Route all drafts through a second model from the same provider and accept the output when both models agree on the wording
Verify AI-generated facts, citations, and code against authoritative sources before the output is relied on or distributed
explain: Hallucinations are managed by checking output against authoritative sources. Self-reported confidence, repetition, and same-family agreement do not verify facts — models can be consistently, confidently wrong.

q: A model generates a script calling a software function that does not exist in the library, and the script fails in testing. Which statement about this event is MOST accurate?
options: It is a hallucination with operational cost, illustrating why AI-generated code must be reviewed and tested like any untrusted contribution
It is a code execution attack, because the model ran the script itself inside the production environment without approval from staff in line with the observations recorded in the case
It is prompt injection, because the library documentation the model read contained an instruction to invent the function name used
It is bias, because the model favored functions from popular libraries over the less common library the team actually uses today
explain: Invented API calls are hallucinations; the failure surfaced safely because the code was tested. The model did not execute anything in production, no planted instruction is described, and preferring familiar libraries is not the fairness issue bias names.

q: A hiring-screening model trained on a decade of company data consistently advances candidates from a few schools and rejects equally qualified candidates from others. Which AI risk is PRIMARY here?
options: A hallucination, because the model is generating candidate summaries that contain facts the applicants never provided at all
Bias, because the model learned unfair patterns in historical data and now repeats them at machine speed in its screening decisions
Evasion, because candidates are formatting their resumes specifically to exploit the screening model's known decision boundary according to the details supplied in the question
Explainability, because the central problem is that the vendor cannot describe the model's internal weighting in plain terms
explain: Skewed outcomes across groups learned from history are bias, creating legal and ethical exposure. The scenario describes real disparate outcomes, not invented facts, applicant gaming, or an inability to explain the model.

q: Which action BEST addresses AI bias before and after deployment?
options: Asking the model to explain each decision in a paragraph, because a fluent explanation proves the decision was made fairly
Removing group data from the evaluation process entirely, so disparities can never be measured or attributed to the model
Testing outcomes across demographic groups on a continuing basis and treating skewed results as defects to be corrected
Accepting historical hiring data as ground truth, because past human decisions are the most reliable standard available
explain: Bias is found by measuring outcomes across groups and fixed by treating disparities as defects. Fluent explanations can rationalize unfair results, refusing to measure hides them, and historical data is exactly where the bias lives.

q: A lending model denies applicants from certain neighborhoods at far higher rates, though individual credit factors are similar. Regulators ask the bank to respond. The bank's FIRST step should be which of the following?
options: Announce that the model is objective because it never receives the neighborhood as an explicit input field at all
Replace the model with the previous year's version and assure regulators the older system could not have the same issue
Stop collecting outcome data by neighborhood so future reports cannot show a disparity in the approval statistics
Investigate the disparity as a bias defect — audit outcomes by group and the data and features driving the difference
explain: A measured disparity is treated as a defect and investigated, including proxy features. A model can discriminate through correlated inputs, an older version may share the flaw, and destroying measurement data worsens the compliance position.

q: A model denies a loan and the bank can only tell the applicant 'the system decided.' Under V8's framing, why is this a security and compliance problem?
options: An unexplainable decision cannot be audited or defended, so explainability failures become compliance and incident-response problems
An unexplainable decision means the model was certainly poisoned, because honest models can always describe their reasoning
An unexplainable decision is only a customer-service issue, because regulators accept model outputs without any supporting records based on the information provided in the stem
An unexplainable decision proves the applicant was discriminated against, so no further investigation of the outcome is required
explain: 'The model said so' is not an audit trail; regulated decisions must be reconstructable and defensible. Opacity does not prove poisoning or discrimination, and regulators do not accept unexplained automated decisions on faith.

q: Which practice BEST improves the defensibility of consequential AI decisions?
options: Deleting input logs after each decision so reviewers cannot second-guess the factors the model used in reaching its outcome
Logging model inputs and outputs, preferring interpretable models where decisions must be defended, and keeping a human able to override
Requiring the model to generate a confident narrative for each decision and filing that narrative as the official audit record
Restricting all knowledge of the model's decisions to the vendor, so internal staff cannot be questioned about them later
explain: Defensibility comes from records, interpretable models for high-stakes calls, and human override. A generated narrative is not evidence, deleting logs destroys the trail, and vendor secrecy defeats accountability.

q: During an incident review, a fraud model cleared a transaction that lost the company money, and no one can reconstruct what the model saw or why it cleared it. Which AI concern does this MOST directly illustrate?
options: Hallucination, because the model must have invented transaction details that were never present in the payment record itself based on the details given in this scenario
Poisoning, because an unexplained clearance always means the training data was tampered with before the model shipped
Explainability, because without logged inputs, outputs, and reasoning the team cannot investigate or defend the model's decision
Privacy, because reconstructing the decision would require the team to look at the customer's personal data unlawfully
explain: The inability to reconstruct a decision is the explainability problem applied to incident response. Nothing shows invented details, training tampering, or unlawful data use — the gap is the missing audit trail.

q: An employee pastes a confidential merger draft into a free public chatbot to polish the wording. Which AI risk has MOST directly occurred?
options: Prompt injection, because the merger draft contains sentences the chatbot might interpret as instructions to follow next
Bias, because the chatbot's polished wording may favor the writing style of one party to the merger over the other
Session hijacking, because the chatbot now holds a token that grants it access to the company's document system directly
Data loss and exposure, because control of sensitive material ends when it is pasted into a service that may log, retain, or train on it
explain: Pasting sensitive content into a public AI service is the guide's canonical data loss example — the AI version of shadow IT. The draft carries no attack instructions, the risk is exposure rather than style, and no session token changed hands.

q: Which control set BEST prevents AI-related data loss by employees?
options: A clear AI-use policy, approved enterprise AI tools with contractual data protections, and data-loss monitoring on the channels staff actually use
A ban on all AI tools with no approved alternative, relying on employees to comply even when deadlines make the tools tempting to use
A reminder in the employee handbook that public chatbots are convenient, paired with no monitoring of what is pasted into them at work
Moving all sensitive documents into a single shared folder, so any paste into a chatbot can be traced to that one location afterward
explain: Policy plus a sanctioned, contractually protected tool plus monitoring is the guide's defense trio. A bare ban without alternatives drives shadow use, reminders without monitoring do not control anything, and centralizing documents does not prevent pasting.

q: A developer pastes proprietary source code into a public AI service to debug it, and the code later surfaces in the service's suggestions to another user. Which two failures combined here?
options: Jailbreaking by the other user, who defeated the service's restrictions to extract the code, and evasion by the developer who uploaded it originally in the situation the scenario describes in full
Data loss through employee use of an unapproved AI service, and a retention failure by a service that reused submitted content beyond the developer's control
Hallucination by the service, which invented code that happened to match the developer's, and bias in how the suggestions were distributed to users
Prompt injection by the code itself, which instructed the service to repeat it, and session hijacking of the developer's account by the other user
explain: Submitting proprietary code to a public service surrenders control of it; its reappearance is retention and reuse outside the owner's control. No guardrail bypass, invented coincidence, embedded instruction, or stolen session is needed to explain it.

q: A customer asks a company's chatbot about another customer and the model recites that person's real phone number, which appeared in its training data. Which AI risk is demonstrated?
options: A hallucination, because the phone number was generated randomly and only coincidentally matched a real customer's number
An evasion, because the customer phrased the question carefully so the model would classify it as an allowed request type
A privacy failure, because the model memorized personal information from training data and regurgitated it to an unauthorized person
Data loss by an employee, because a staff member must have pasted the phone number into the chatbot during this conversation based on the information provided in the stem
explain: Models can memorize and disclose personal data from training — a privacy risk governed by minimize, consent, and retention duties. The number was real, no classification trick is described, and no employee paste occurred in this interaction.

q: Which practice BEST applies privacy duties to an AI system that handles customer prompts?
options: Retaining every prompt indefinitely, because complete records make it easier to answer any future question a customer might ask
Sending full customer records with each prompt so the model has maximum context, trusting the vendor to sort out what it needs
Publishing the retention policy only after an incident, so competitors cannot learn the company's data handling approach in advance in the situation the scenario describes in full
Minimizing the personal data sent to the model, obtaining appropriate consent, and controlling how long prompts and outputs are retained
explain: Privacy for AI is the familiar duties — minimize, consent, control retention — applied to a system that remembers in bulk. Indefinite retention and maximal data sharing increase exposure, and policies must exist before incidents, not after.

q: An AI note-taking tool records meetings and stores transcripts containing personal health details mentioned by participants who never agreed to recording. Which concern is PRIMARY?
options: Privacy and consent, because personal information is being collected and retained without the knowledge or agreement of the people it describes
Explainability, because participants cannot see a plain-language description of how the transcription model makes its decisions
Hallucination, because the transcripts may contain statements that the participants did not actually make during the meeting
Code execution, because the tool can act on the transcripts by creating tasks in the company's project management system
explain: Recording and retaining personal details without consent is a privacy failure first. Transcription accuracy and task creation are secondary, and decision explainability is not what unconsented collection violates.

q: A company plans to use AI to screen benefits claims and asks what its guiding accountability principle should be. Which answer reflects the exam's ethical framing?
options: The vendor is accountable for every outcome, because the organization purchased the model rather than building it in-house itself
A named human and the organization remain accountable for the model's decisions, and the use must be one the organization can defend publicly
No one is accountable for individual errors, because a statistical system cannot be expected to be correct in every single case
Accountability matters only after a regulator opens an inquiry, so the company can assign responsibility when a problem is raised
explain: Ethical considerations resolve to human accountability, consent, and defensible use. Buying a model does not outsource responsibility, statistical error does not erase it, and accountability must be assigned before harm, not after an inquiry.

q: An AI dataset was scraped from people's posts without their permission, and leadership asks whether the resulting model can be used for a public product launch. Which consideration should dominate the decision?
options: Model accuracy — whether the scraped data produces benchmark scores high enough to justify the launch on quality grounds alone based on everything the case record shows here
Explainability tooling — whether a dashboard exists that can display feature weights for the model's individual decisions
Consent and defensibility — whether the data was collected with permission and whether the organization can publicly defend the use
Session security — whether user tokens for the product are stored using current encryption standards by the platform team
explain: The guide frames ethics as consent, accountability, and appropriate use. Accuracy, dashboards, and token storage are real concerns but none answers whether the data should have been used at all.

q: A manager proposes quietly using an AI tool to score employees' messages for 'attitude' and feed the scores into promotion decisions without telling staff. Which response BEST reflects sound AI ethics judgment?
options: Approve it, because keeping the scoring secret prevents employees from changing their behavior to game the model's inputs unfairly
Approve it if the model's accuracy is high, because accurate covert monitoring is ethically equivalent to disclosed monitoring
Postpone it until the model can also write explanations, because explainability alone makes any covert use acceptable to staff
Reject or redesign the use: covert scoring of people for consequential decisions fails consent, transparency, and defensibility expectations
explain: Secret, consequential scoring of people is indefensible use — the professional answer keeps a human accountable and the use defensible. Accuracy and explanations do not cure covert collection, and secrecy to prevent gaming compounds the problem.

q: An AI agent works inside a ticketing system under an authenticated session. An attacker steals the agent's session token from a log file. What does the attacker gain?
options: The agent's authenticated access and trust within the ticketing system, letting them act as the agent until the session is invalidated
The model's training data, because session tokens are the keys used to decrypt the stored weights and datasets at rest
The ability to retrain the model, because an authenticated session includes permission to replace the model's learned parameters in the situation the scenario describes in full
Nothing of value, because agent sessions carry no permissions beyond displaying the agent's own conversation history text
explain: Session hijacking inherits whatever the session could do — here, the agent's access and trust in the ticketing system. Tokens do not decrypt training data or grant retraining rights, and agent sessions act, not merely display.

q: Which defense set BEST protects AI agent sessions?
options: Storing tokens in application logs for convenience, so administrators can replay any agent session when troubleshooting a fault based on everything the case record shows here
Protecting tokens from exposure, keeping sessions short-lived, and requiring re-authentication before sensitive actions are performed
Granting agent sessions permanent validity, because frequent re-authentication interrupts long-running automated workflows
Letting the agent share one session across all users, so individual user sessions never need to be created or managed at all
explain: Agent sessions get the classic defenses: guard the token, shorten its life, and step up authentication for sensitive actions. Logged, permanent, or shared sessions each destroy one of those protections.

q: A browser extension flaw leaks the session cookie of a user chatting with an AI assistant that can also query the user's cloud console. Which risk statement is MOST accurate?
options: The stolen session is harmless because chat sessions contain only text and cannot be connected to any other system access at all
The stolen session only matters if the attacker also knows the user's password, because cookies are never accepted on their own by servers
The stolen session can be replayed to inherit both the chat context and the assistant's connected console access, extending the hijack beyond conversation
The stolen session lets the attacker poison the model, because any authenticated chat can alter the model's permanent training data directly
explain: Agent sessions bind conversation to connected tools, so a replayed session inherits that reach. Cookies are bearer tokens accepted on their own, and chatting does not retrain the model.

q: An AI agent with shell access reads a planted instruction in a document and runs a command that changes a firewall rule. Which AI risk turned a content problem into a system compromise?
options: Hallucination, because the agent generated a command that did not exist and the firewall accepted it without validation checks based on the details given in this scenario
Bias, because the agent's training made it more likely to obey documents from certain sources than instructions from its owner
Privacy, because the document the agent read contained personal information about the network administrator on duty that day
Code execution, because the agent's ability to act on systems converted a successful prompt injection into real configuration change
explain: The guide's agent problem: talk-only models leak words, but agents that run commands turn injection into compromise. The command was real and executed, no group disparity is involved, and the document's content was an instruction, not personal data.

q: Which control set BEST limits code execution risk for an AI agent that manages cloud resources?
options: Least-privilege tool scoping, sandboxing of agent actions, and human approval for destructive or irreversible changes before they run
Full administrative tools with broad logging, because detailed records make it possible to reverse any change the agent makes later as described by the team reviewing this incident
Unrestricted API access during business pilots, because limiting tools early prevents the team from learning the agent's full value
A single shared agent identity for all tasks, because accountability is simpler when every action appears under one account name
explain: Agent power is bounded by scoped tools, a sandbox, and human approval for irreversible steps. Logging does not undo destructive changes, pilots are when limits matter most, and a shared identity destroys accountability.

q: A chatbot that can only answer questions is upgraded into an agent that can reset passwords, unlock accounts, and modify group memberships. Which statement BEST captures the security change?
options: The security posture improves, because an agent that acts quickly leaves less time for an attacker to interfere with its work in progress
The blast radius of any successful manipulation grows from leaking words to changing identity state, so controls must grow with the new tool access
Nothing changes, because the model itself is the same and only the surrounding interface gained additional menu options for users
The risk moves entirely to the vendor, because tool integrations are implemented and secured by the model provider's platform team
explain: Granting action tools converts model failures into identity changes; that is why least privilege and approval gates join the control set. The model being unchanged does not keep risk unchanged, and the deployer owns the integration risk.

q: A firm rents virtual servers in the cloud and installs its own operating systems on them. Who is responsible for patching those guest operating systems?
options: Nobody, because virtual servers in the cloud are patched automatically by the hypervisor, applied consistently across the environment in question
The provider, because the provider owns the physical hosts the servers run on
The customer, because infrastructure as a service leaves the guest OS under customer control
The provider, because every cloud service model includes operating system patching
explain: With IaaS the provider secures the physical plant and hypervisor while the customer patches the guest OS and everything above it. SaaS and platform models shift patching to the provider, but owning the physical host does not transfer the guest OS in IaaS.

q: A development team deploys code to a platform service and never manages servers or operating systems. Which responsibility statement is MOST accurate for this platform as a service model?
options: The provider patches the platform and runtime, while the team remains responsible for its code, configuration, and data
The provider becomes responsible for the security of the application code the team writes
The team has no remaining security responsibilities once the platform is adopted
The team remains responsible for patching the underlying operating system and database engine, subject to periodic review by the responsible team
explain: PaaS moves patching of the platform, runtime, and OS to the provider. It does not move responsibility for the customer's own code, insecure configuration, or data, and it does not leave OS patching with the customer.

q: A company runs event-driven functions that execute only when triggered, with no servers for staff to administer. In this serverless model, which duties remain with the company?
options: Patching the operating systems of the servers that execute the functions
Securing its function code, its configuration and permissions, and the data the functions process
Maintaining the physical data centers where the functions are hosted
Approving every runtime patch the provider applies to the shared platform, in line with the organization's documented standards for comparable systems
explain: In serverless the provider patches everything below the code, so no server OS duties remain with the customer. The customer's duties shrink to code, configuration, permissions, and data.

q: Employees use a cloud email suite that the vendor hosts, patches, and upgrades. Which task still belongs to the customer organization?
options: Patching the mail application servers whenever the vendor releases an update, following the same approval process used elsewhere in the organization
Configuring user access, multifactor authentication, and data handling settings for its own tenant
Writing the next version of the email application for the vendor
Replacing failed disks in the vendor's data centers on a scheduled basis
explain: With SaaS the vendor runs and patches the application itself. The customer still owns tenant configuration, identity and access choices, and how its data is handled, rather than hardware or application maintenance.

q: A retailer rents computing capacity that is shared with many unrelated organizations and billed by usage. Which cloud deployment model is this?
options: Hybrid cloud, because the retailer also owns a point-of-sale server
Public cloud, because the infrastructure is shared among many tenants and rented on demand
Private cloud, because the retailer is a single company using the service, with ownership assigned and the arrangement reviewed on a regular schedule
Community cloud, because retailers share an interest in selling products
explain: A public cloud is shared, multi-tenant infrastructure rented by the slice. Private means one organization only, community means several organizations with shared concerns operating a common environment, and hybrid is a deliberate mix of models.

q: A bank runs its core systems on cloud infrastructure dedicated exclusively to the bank, with no other tenants. Which deployment model BEST fits?
options: Public cloud, because the systems are reachable over a network connection, as part of the standard operating procedure for systems of this kind
Multicloud, because the bank operates more than one core system
Private cloud, because the environment serves a single organization exclusively
Community cloud, because other banks exist in the same industry sector
explain: Exclusivity to one organization defines a private cloud, regardless of where it sits. Industry membership alone does not make a community cloud, and running several systems is not the same as using several providers.

q: A manufacturer keeps sensitive design systems in its own data center but runs its public website and seasonal workloads in a rented cloud, deliberately linking the two. Which model is this?
options: Private cloud, because the sensitive systems never leave the company building, under the same governance applied to similar decisions across the business
Hybrid cloud, because on-premises and cloud environments are deliberately combined
Community cloud, because two different locations are involved in the design
Multicloud, because the manufacturer uses more than one type of computer
explain: A deliberate mix of private or on-premises infrastructure with public cloud is a hybrid cloud. Multicloud specifically means spreading workloads across multiple cloud providers, not mixing locations.

q: Several hospitals subject to the same health-data rules jointly operate a shared cloud environment built for their common compliance needs. Which deployment model is this?
options: Private cloud, because health data must always be kept completely isolated
Hybrid cloud, because the hospitals each keep separate administrative staff, documented in the runbook and checked again at the next scheduled review
Community cloud, because organizations with shared concerns operate a common environment
Public cloud, because the environment is used by more than one organization
explain: A community cloud serves several organizations with shared concerns, such as hospitals under the same health-data rules. Mere multi-tenancy describes the public cloud, but the defining feature here is the shared concern and jointly operated environment.

q: An enterprise deliberately runs comparable workloads with two different cloud providers so that one vendor's outage, price increase, or product decision cannot halt the business. What is this strategy called, and what is its main cost?
options: Hybrid cloud; its cost is the link between the data center and the cloud
Serverless adoption; its cost is losing visibility into function execution time, consistent with how the organization already handles comparable cases today
Multicloud; its cost is managing different provider systems that are never identical
Monolithic design; its cost is that one failure can bring down everything
explain: Spreading workloads across providers is multicloud, adopted to avoid vendor lock-in and single-provider failure. Its accepted trade-off is operational complexity, because each provider's tooling and controls differ.

q: A legacy application is deployed as one single unit: the interface, business logic, and reporting all ship and run together, and a fault in reporting takes the whole application down. Which architecture is this, and what is its key weakness?
options: A monolith; one compromise or failure can affect the entire application at once
Serverless; the functions share one runtime and therefore fail together always
Open source; the single codebase means anyone can modify the production system
Microservices; services are so isolated that failures spread between them easily
explain: One deployable whole is a monolith — simple to build and run, but with a total blast radius. Microservices are the opposite design, splitting the application so a failure can stop at a service boundary.

q: An online store is split into small independent services for checkout, inventory, and payments that communicate through controlled interfaces. Attackers compromise the inventory service. Why is the damage expected to stay limited?
options: Splitting an application removes the need for authentication between services
The payment service automatically encrypts itself whenever another service fails, applied the same way in every department that operates this kind of system
Microservice boundaries contain the blast radius, so one service's breach need not become a breach of everything
Each service runs on its own physical server in a separate building by design
explain: Microservices isolate components behind controlled interfaces, so a compromise can be contained at the service boundary. Isolation does not remove the need to authenticate service-to-service traffic, and services need not sit on separate physical servers.

q: A growing platform lets its busiest service scale up independently during sales peaks while the rarely used services stay small. Which architectural property makes this possible?
options: A monolith, because the whole application scales as one efficient single unit, following established practice rather than an exception made for this case
Proprietary software, because vendor code is optimized for peak traffic loads
Microservices, because each service can be scaled and deployed independently of the others
Private cloud hosting, because dedicated infrastructure always scales faster
explain: Independent services can be scaled and released on their own, which a monolith cannot do — scaling a monolith means scaling the entire application. Hosting model and licensing do not provide per-component scaling.

q: A three-person startup considers splitting its simple application into thirty separate services. What is the MOST realistic security concern with that plan?
options: Small applications are prohibited from using service-based designs at scale
Microservices cannot use encryption when services communicate with each other, with responsibilities written down and confirmed by the accountable manager
Each additional service legally requires its own separate security department
The operational overhead of securing, patching, and monitoring many services can exceed a tiny team's capacity
explain: Microservices trade a large blast radius for more moving parts to secure and observe. For a very small team that overhead is a genuine risk; encryption between services is entirely possible and no staffing law applies.

q: A firm chooses an open-source database partly so its own engineers can inspect exactly how the software handles sensitive records. Which advantage of open source is it using?
options: Guaranteed vendor support, because open-source projects staff help desks
Transparency, because anyone can review the code to see how it behaves
Accountability, because a vendor contract assigns liability for defects
Freedom from patching, because community software updates itself safely
explain: Open source brings transparency — the code is reviewable by anyone. The trade-off is that support and patching discipline fall on the adopter, not on a contracted vendor.

q: A hospital buys a proprietary records system largely because a named vendor is contractually accountable for support and fixes. Which trade-off has it accepted?
options: It gains vendor support and accountability at a price, while giving up the ability to review the source code itself
It gives up vendor support, because proprietary software is sold entirely as-is
It gains full code transparency, because proprietary vendors publish their source to customers, reviewed alongside the other controls that protect the same environment
It gains the right to modify and redistribute the vendor's code without restriction
explain: Proprietary software offers vendor support and accountability in exchange for cost and closed code. Reviewing and modifying the source are open-source characteristics, the reverse of this choice.

q: A defense contractor keeps all systems in its own building on hardware it owns, with its staff responsible for power, patching, physical security, and replacement. Which model is this?
options: Community cloud, because employees from several departments use the systems
On-premises, because the organization owns the facility and hardware and carries full responsibility for all of it
SaaS, because the staff use software that runs on the company's own servers
Private cloud, because any company-owned equipment automatically counts as cloud, as a standing arrangement rather than a one-time response to this incident
explain: On-premises means your building, your hardware, and your responsibility for everything. Calling owned equipment a cloud requires cloud characteristics such as on-demand self-service provisioning, which are absent here.

q: After moving to the cloud, a manager argues the provider now handles all security, so the company's configuration and access reviews can stop. Why is this wrong under the shared responsibility model?
options: The provider handles security only during the first year of a cloud contract
Cloud contracts transfer all legal accountability to the provider by default
Responsibility is shared: the provider secures the underlying cloud, but the customer still owns configuration, identities, and data
The customer is responsible for the provider's physical data center security
explain: Shared responsibility never reduces the customer's share to zero in any service model. Misconfiguration, identity, and data decisions stay with the customer even when the provider secures the facilities and platform.

q: A storage bucket containing customer records is left publicly readable because of a setting the customer's own team chose. The provider's platform worked as designed. Under shared responsibility, whose failure is this?
options: The provider's, because any data stored in a cloud is the provider's responsibility, under formal change control so the decision can be audited later if needed
Nobody's, because publicly readable storage is a normal default in cloud platforms
The customer's, because data classification and access configuration remain customer duties in every cloud model
The software vendor's, because the bucket was created through a management console
explain: The customer always owns its data and the access settings it chooses, in IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS alike. A platform working as designed while a customer setting exposes data is a customer-side failure.

q: A small clinic wants a simple internal scheduling tool built quickly, with almost no IT staff to run it. Which build approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Thirty microservices, because more services always produce stronger security
Serverless only, because monoliths are prohibited for health-related software, consistent with the handling standard already in force for this data class
A monolith, because one simple deployable unit matches a small application's needs and a small team
A multicloud design, because a single clinic needs several provider contracts
explain: Monoliths are simple to build, deploy, and secure for small applications, which suits a tiny team. Microservices and multicloud add operational burden that buys this clinic nothing at its scale.

q: A retailer keeps payment data in its private environment but bursts overflow web traffic to a public cloud during holiday peaks. Which model describes this deliberate design?
options: Public cloud only, because customers reach the store over the internet
Hybrid cloud, with sensitive workloads kept private and elastic workloads placed in the public cloud
Multicloud, because the retailer uses both a building and a cloud service
Community cloud, because retail traffic peaks are shared across the industry, applied uniformly so no team invents its own version of the procedure
explain: Keeping sensitive systems private while using public cloud elasticity is the classic hybrid pattern. Multicloud requires multiple cloud providers, not a mix of premises and one provider.

q: An architecture review notes that a company's cloud environment is dedicated to it alone and operated to meet its strict regulatory control requirements. Which benefit of a private cloud is driving this choice?
options: Automatic compliance, because private clouds are certified for every regulation
Single-tenant control over configuration and compliance, at higher cost than shared services
Shared operating costs with unrelated tenants who use the same equipment
Lower cost than public cloud, because dedicated infrastructure is cheaper to run, with periodic checks that the arrangement is still doing what was intended
explain: A private cloud trades the public cloud's economy for exclusive control, which regulated organizations may need. It is not cheaper, it confers no automatic certification, and by definition it has no unrelated tenants.

q: A new startup with unpredictable demand wants computing capacity it can grow or shrink within minutes without buying hardware. Which model BEST fits?
options: Public cloud, because shared rented capacity provides rapid elasticity without capital purchase
Community cloud, because startups share concerns with other new companies
On-premises, because owned hardware can be ordered and installed within minutes, following the documented escalation path when exceptions are requested
Private cloud only, because elasticity exists only on dedicated infrastructure
explain: Rapid elasticity on rented, shared infrastructure is the public cloud's defining strength. Owned hardware cannot be procured in minutes, and elasticity is not exclusive to private deployments.

q: A group of universities pools funding for a shared research computing environment shaped by their common grant and data rules. Which model is this?
options: Private cloud, because each university is a separate legal organization, as specified in the organization's own architecture standards for this tier
Hybrid cloud, because each university also owns campus computer labs
Community cloud, because organizations with shared concerns jointly sustain a common environment
Public cloud, because research results are eventually published openly
explain: Shared concerns and a jointly operated environment make a community cloud — the same pattern as hospitals under common health rules. Owning separate labs does not convert the shared environment into a hybrid design.

q: During a major outage at one cloud provider, a firm fails its customer portal over to a second provider where the portal also runs. Which strategy is being exercised?
options: Hybrid cloud bursting, because traffic grew beyond the first provider's capacity, with the outcome logged so a later review can verify what was decided
Monolith recovery, because the whole portal was restored from one backup
Serverless scaling, because the portal's functions multiplied automatically
Multicloud resilience, using a second provider so one vendor's failure cannot halt the service
explain: Running workloads across providers specifically so a single provider's outage cannot stop the business is multicloud. The trigger here is failure, not traffic growth, and the design spans vendors rather than deployment locations.

q: A firm adopts functions that run only in response to events, billed per execution. Auditors ask who patches the servers. What is the correct answer, and what must the firm still secure?
options: Nobody patches the servers; the firm secures only its office network
The provider patches the servers; the firm has no remaining security duties
The provider patches the servers and runtime; the firm must still secure function code, dependencies, permissions, and data
The firm patches the servers monthly; the provider secures the function code, applied consistently across the environment in question
explain: Serverless removes server administration from the customer entirely. It does not remove responsibility for code, third-party dependencies, overly broad permissions, or the data the functions handle.

q: A team uses a managed platform that includes the database engine. The vendor patches the engine, but a breach occurs through weak application-level access rules the team wrote. Who owns that failure?
options: The team's customers, because they chose weak passwords for their accounts
Nobody, because platform services transfer all application risk to the vendor
The vendor, because patching the database makes the vendor responsible for its contents, subject to periodic review by the responsible team
The team, because application access control stays with the customer even when the provider patches the platform
explain: PaaS shifts platform patching to the provider but leaves application logic, access rules, configuration, and data with the customer. A customer-written access flaw is a customer failure under shared responsibility.

q: A customer rents IaaS networking and leaves a management port open to the entire internet, leading to a compromise. The provider secured its physical network correctly. Whose responsibility was the exposed port?
options: The internet service provider's, because it routed the attacker's traffic
The customer's, because virtual network configuration in IaaS is controlled and owned by the customer
The hypervisor vendor's, because virtual ports are created by hypervisor code
The provider's, because all network security transfers to the provider in IaaS, in line with the organization's documented standards for comparable systems
explain: In IaaS the customer configures virtual networks, firewall rules, and security groups. The provider's duty is the physical plant and hypervisor, which performed correctly here.

q: A company wants the provider to run the application entirely but needs assurance it can retrieve and move its data if it changes vendors. Which customer duty is MOST important to plan before signing?
options: Designing the vendor's data center network, because tenants approve the layout
Hiring the vendor's support engineers, because SaaS includes no vendor support
Patching the vendor's application servers, because SaaS customers share that duty, following the same approval process used elsewhere in the organization
Data ownership, export, and backup arrangements, because the customer remains accountable for its data in SaaS
explain: Even in SaaS the data is the customer's, so export rights, retention, and backup arrangements must be settled up front. Application patching and data center design remain entirely the vendor's side of the line.

q: A plant's industrial control systems must keep running with millisecond timing and no dependence on an internet link, isolated from corporate IT. Which placement decision BEST fits these constraints?
options: Move the control systems to a public SaaS platform to gain vendor patching
Place the control systems in a community cloud shared with other manufacturers, with ownership assigned and the arrangement reviewed on a regular schedule
Keep the control systems on-premises in a segmented operational technology environment designed for local, isolated operation
Run the control systems as internet-facing serverless functions for elasticity
explain: Operational technology with strict timing and isolation needs belongs in a local, segmented on-premises environment. Internet-dependent models introduce latency and exposure that control systems cannot accept.

q: Services inside a microservices application must prove their identities to each other so a compromised service cannot freely call the payment API. Which design choice supports this?
options: Mutual authentication between services, enforced at the controlled interfaces between them
Removing authentication inside the application because the perimeter firewall exists, as part of the standard operating procedure for systems of this kind
Giving every service one shared administrator password for simplicity of rotation
Publishing all internal APIs to the internet so they can be monitored centrally
explain: Microservices talk through controlled interfaces, and authenticating those calls — for example with mutual TLS — stops one compromised service from impersonating others. A shared password and a perimeter-only model both defeat the isolation the design provides.

q: A single corrupted deployment crashes an entire monolithic application for all users at once. Leadership asks what redesign would have limited the outage. What is the BEST answer?
options: Adding more users gradually, which spreads the crash across smaller groups
Buying the monolith as proprietary software instead of building it in-house
Moving the same monolith to a public cloud, which prevents application crashes, under the same governance applied to similar decisions across the business
Splitting the application into microservices, so a fault in one service need not take down the whole system
explain: The monolith's total blast radius is an architectural property, not a hosting one — the same monolith crashes the same way in any cloud. Decomposing into isolated services is what contains a single fault.

q: A hybrid cloud design struggles because identities and policies must stay consistent across the premises environment and the cloud tenant. Which risk of hybrid architecture does this illustrate?
options: Total blast radius: one failure anywhere destroys both environments fully, documented in the runbook and checked again at the next scheduled review
Vendor lock-in: a single provider controls both halves of the environment
Integration complexity: two environments must be made to behave as one secure system
Patch transfer: the provider patches premises systems without permission
explain: Hybrid designs combine two environments, and keeping identity, policy, and monitoring consistent across both is their characteristic difficulty. Lock-in is the multicloud concern, and neither half automatically patches or destroys the other.

q: A multicloud firm discovers each provider expresses firewall rules, logging, and identity differently, so a control set correctly in one cloud is missing in the other. Which multicloud trade-off is this?
options: Shared responsibility failure, because providers promised identical tooling, consistent with how the organization already handles comparable cases today
Inconsistent controls across non-identical provider systems, the accepted cost of avoiding lock-in
Community cloud drift, because other tenants changed the shared settings
Monolithic coupling, because the two clouds were deployed as one unit
explain: Provider systems are never identical, so multicloud buys independence at the price of duplicated, differing control implementations. No provider promises identical tooling, and no other tenant is involved in this scenario.

q: In IaaS, which layer does the cloud provider secure and maintain for every customer?
options: The customer's user accounts, access policies, and data classifications, with the details recorded and revisited whenever roles or systems change
The physical facilities, hardware, and virtualization layer beneath the customer's systems
The customer's guest operating systems and installed applications
The customer's application code and its security testing program
explain: The provider's side of IaaS covers the physical plant, hardware, and hypervisor. Everything the customer builds on top — systems, identities, code, and data — remains the customer's side.

q: A firm with heavy legacy software needs full control of the operating system kernel and custom drivers in the cloud. Which service model fits this requirement?
options: Infrastructure as a service, because it gives the customer control of the guest operating system
Serverless functions, because functions run with full operating system access, applied the same way in every department that operates this kind of system
Software as a service, because SaaS tenants choose their own kernel versions
Platform as a service, because platforms expose kernel-level configuration
explain: Only IaaS hands the customer the guest OS, including kernel and driver control — with the patching duty that comes with it. Platform, serverless, and SaaS models deliberately hide that layer.

q: A department wants to eliminate its backlog of operating system patching for a standard business application without managing servers at all. Which change achieves this?
options: Staying with IaaS and patching faster, because IaaS includes OS patching
Moving the application on-premises, where patching becomes the vendor's duty, following established practice rather than an exception made for this case
Converting the application to a monolith, which removes operating systems
Moving the application to a platform or software service model, where the provider patches everything below the application
explain: Reducing the customer's patching burden means moving up the service models: PaaS and SaaS place the OS with the provider. IaaS and on-premises both leave OS patching with the customer, and application shape does not change who patches.

q: A public marketing website with no sensitive data needs cheap, scalable hosting. Which placement is MOST appropriate?
options: A community cloud, because website visitors form a community of users
An air-gapped on-premises room, because all websites require isolation
A private cloud, because marketing pages must never share infrastructure, with responsibilities written down and confirmed by the accountable manager
Public cloud, because the content is public and benefits from shared, elastic infrastructure
explain: Match protection to sensitivity: public content gains nothing from isolation and benefits from public cloud elasticity. Private and community models exist for exclusivity and shared regulated concerns, not for public pages.

q: An open-source component in a product is found vulnerable. The vendor that sold the product says patching community components is the adopter's job. Which open-source trade-off does this show?
options: Support and patching discipline rest on the adopter, because no vendor is accountable for community code
Automatic updating, because community components patch themselves in products
Proprietary accountability, because the seller must patch every component used, in accordance with the policy the organization applies to similar assets
Transparency fails, because open-source code cannot be inspected after release
explain: Open source's transparency is paired with self-reliance: the adopter must track and patch components. A selling vendor's contract covers its own product duties, but community code carries no vendor accountability of its own.

q: A procurement team cannot audit a proprietary product's code and must rely on the vendor's claims and certifications instead. Which limitation of proprietary software is this?
options: Open code is unavailable, so the team must write a replacement product itself, reviewed alongside the other controls that protect the same environment
Vendor support is absent, so the team must rely entirely on community forums
Proprietary software receives no patches, so assurance comes only from audits
Closed code cannot be independently reviewed, so assurance depends on the vendor's accountability and attestations
explain: Proprietary software trades reviewability for vendor support and accountability — buyers lean on certifications and the vendor's name because they cannot inspect the code. Proprietary products are patched and supported; that support is the other side of the trade.

q: A company runs its customer database in the cloud but keeps the physical servers' security, power, and cooling entirely out of its own duties. In which model does the provider ALWAYS carry those physical duties?
options: Only in private cloud, because public clouds share physical duties with tenants, as a standing arrangement rather than a one-time response to this incident
Only in SaaS, because other models rent physical space to the customer
In no cloud model, because tenants must verify physical security in person
Every cloud service model, because physical facilities are always on the provider's side of shared responsibility
explain: Physical security of the cloud itself is the provider's in IaaS, PaaS, serverless, and SaaS alike — it is the constant at the bottom of the shared responsibility stack. What changes by model is everything above it.

q: An architecture board compares two candidate designs for a payment platform: one deployable application versus separate services for authorization, ledger, and settlement. Which comparison point is MOST decisive for security?
options: Physical security: the split design requires fewer data center controls overall
Blast radius: a compromise of one service in the split design need not expose the ledger and settlement functions
Deployment speed: the split design always deploys faster than a single application, with the same rigor the organization applies to its other critical systems
Licensing cost: separate services are always cheaper to license than one product
explain: The decisive security difference between monolith and microservices is containment — what one compromise can reach. Deployment speed and licensing vary by case, and application shape does not reduce physical control needs.

q: A firm adopts a serverless design and an auditor asks how the firm's responsibilities changed compared with its old IaaS servers. Which answer is correct?
options: Operating system and runtime patching moved to the provider; code, configuration, identity, and data duties stayed with the firm
No duties changed, because serverless is simply IaaS with smaller servers
All duties moved to the provider, including the security of the firm's own code
Only data duties stayed; configuration and identity moved to the provider too
explain: Moving from IaaS to serverless removes the OS and runtime layer from the customer's list. Code, configuration, permissions, and data never transfer — they are the customer's in every model.

q: A university consortium, a hospital network, and a single law firm each need cloud environments. Which pairing is correct?
options: The law firm fits community cloud, because lawyers share professional rules
The hospital network fits private cloud only, because health data bans sharing, consistent with the handling standard already in force for this data class
All three fit public cloud, because each serves members of the public
The consortium and the hospital network fit community cloud; the single law firm alone fits private cloud
explain: Community cloud is defined by several organizations with shared concerns operating a common environment — a consortium or a hospital network under shared rules. A single organization acting alone is the private cloud pattern.

q: A CIO wants one sentence that captures how responsibility changes across IaaS, platform, and SaaS models. Which sentence is accurate?
options: As the model moves toward SaaS, the customer patches more of the stack to keep control, because buying more of the service means maintaining more of it directly
Responsibility is identical in every model; only the billing method changes, because the shared responsibility model assigns the same duties regardless of service type
As the model moves from IaaS toward SaaS, the provider patches more of the stack and the customer's duties shrink toward code, configuration, and data
In every model the customer is responsible for the provider's physical security, because physical facilities remain the customer's duty under all cloud service models
explain: The service models form a spectrum: the higher the model, the more the provider manages and patches, until the customer's share is essentially its configuration, identities, code where it writes any, and data. The spectrum never reaches zero customer responsibility.

q: In a Zero Trust architecture, which component weighs identity, device health, and context to decide whether a specific request should be allowed?
options: The secure web gateway, because it inspects web traffic at the cloud edge
The policy administrator, because it pushes configuration to enforcement points, with periodic checks that the arrangement is still doing what was intended
The policy enforcement point, because it sits in the path and forwards traffic
The policy engine, because it evaluates the signals and makes the access decision
explain: The policy engine decides, the policy administrator carries the decision into configuration, and the policy enforcement point enforces it in the path. The secure web gateway is an SSE service, not a Zero Trust decision component.

q: In a Zero Trust design, an access decision has been made and must now be turned into the actual configuration that gateways will apply. Which component performs that step?
options: The policy enforcement point, because it writes policy for the whole network, following the documented escalation path when exceptions are requested
The policy engine, because it re-evaluates every packet as it passes through
The policy administrator, because it translates decisions into configuration for enforcement points
The CASB, because it brokers access between users and cloud applications
explain: The division of labor is decide, configure, enforce: the engine decides, the administrator converts decisions into configuration, and the enforcement point applies it where traffic flows.

q: A Zero Trust gateway sits directly in the traffic path and allows through only the sessions that policy has approved, blocking everything else. Which component is this?
options: The policy enforcement point, because it sits in the path and lets through exactly what was decided
The policy engine, because it weighs identity and device health signals
The identity provider, because it issues the user's authentication tokens, as specified in the organization's own architecture standards for this tier
The policy administrator, because it distributes decisions to gateways
explain: The enforcement point is the in-path gatekeeper. The engine and administrator work behind it — one deciding, one configuring — while the identity provider only supplies authentication, not per-request enforcement.

q: A company verifies a user at login, then grants network access for the entire day without further checks. Which Zero Trust principle is it violating?
options: Least functionality, because the user was given more applications than needed, with the outcome logged so a later review can verify what was decided
Continuous verification, because trust must be re-evaluated per request rather than granted once for a session
Out-of-band management, because logins must use a separate management path
Micro-segmentation, because the user received access to more than one segment
explain: Zero Trust verifies every request with current identity, device, and context signals. A one-time login followed by blanket trust is the old perimeter model the architecture replaces.

q: After a workstation is compromised, investigators find the attacker could not reach the database servers because each application tier sits in its own tightly controlled segment. Which control limited the damage?
options: Security Service Edge, because cloud edge services inspect branch web traffic
Data masking, because database values were hidden from the attacker's queries
Micro-segmentation, because dividing the network into small controlled zones stops one foothold from becoming the whole network
Group Managed Service Accounts, because service passwords rotate automatically
explain: Micro-segmentation confines lateral movement: a foothold in one zone reaches only that zone. The other options protect credentials, web access, or displayed data, not network reachability.

q: A firm replaces its castle-and-moat network, where anything inside was trusted, with per-request decisions based on who and what is asking. Which statement BEST describes the new perimeter?
options: Location is the perimeter: requests from the office are trusted more than remote ones, subject to periodic review by the responsible team
The VPN is the perimeter: once the tunnel is up, traffic inside it is trusted
Identity is the perimeter: each request is authorized on identity, device health, and context wherever it originates
The firewall is the perimeter: rules at the edge decide what the network trusts
explain: Zero Trust moves the perimeter from network location to identity and context, verified continuously. Trusting office, VPN, or edge-passed traffic by location is exactly the model being replaced.

q: Remote staff reach the internet and SaaS applications through security services delivered from cloud points of presence near them, including a secure web gateway, a CASB, and zero-trust network access. What is this delivery model called in the current objectives?
options: Security Access Service Edge, the older combined WAN and security bundle the objectives replaced, in line with the organization's documented standards for comparable systems
Security Service Edge, the cloud-edge delivery of secure web gateway, CASB, and zero-trust network access
A virtual private network concentrator, because all access passes one appliance
Software-defined WAN, because traffic is routed intelligently between office sites
explain: The current objectives name Security Service Edge — secure web gateway, CASB, and ZTNA delivered from cloud points of presence. The older combined term and SD-WAN are no longer the named model, and a single concentrator is the backhaul design SSE replaces.

q: Which set of services is delivered as part of Security Service Edge?
options: A cloud access security broker, a site-to-site VPN mesh, and an on-premises proxy pair, following the same approval process used elsewhere in the organization
A secure web gateway, a cloud access security broker, and zero-trust network access delivered from cloud points of presence
Zero-trust network access, a load balancer pair, and an offline backup appliance set
A secure web gateway, a wide-area routing platform, and a data center firewall refresh
explain: SSE is exactly the security side delivered at the cloud edge: secure web gateway, CASB, and ZTNA. Routing platforms, VPN meshes, load balancers, and backup appliances are not SSE components.

q: A branch office's web traffic is currently hauled over a VPN to headquarters for inspection, adding latency. Leadership wants inspection near the branch instead. Which design change accomplishes this?
options: Require branch staff to use headquarters desktops through remote display only
Disable web inspection for the branch and rely on endpoint antivirus alone
Install a larger firewall at headquarters so backhauled traffic is inspected faster
Adopt Security Service Edge so the secure web gateway and related controls are delivered from cloud points of presence near the branch
explain: SSE exists precisely to end backhauling: security services are delivered at the edge near the user. A bigger headquarters firewall keeps the hairpin, and dropping inspection removes the control rather than relocating it.

q: A Windows service runs under an account whose password has not changed in six years because changing it breaks the application. Which solution removes this risk permanently?
options: A longer shared password, stored in a sealed envelope in the server room
A second identical service account, so one can be used while the other rests
A Group Managed Service Account, because Active Directory generates and rotates the password automatically and nobody needs to know it
A policy requiring administrators to change the password every five years
explain: gMSAs end the static service password problem: AD creates and rotates the credential automatically, one gMSA can serve several servers, and no human knows the password, so none can leak or reuse it.

q: One application runs on four servers that all need the same service identity. With conventional accounts, the shared password is known to six administrators. What does a Group Managed Service Account change here?
options: The four servers share one password that administrators rotate every 30 days
The service stops needing an identity, so authentication is removed entirely
Each server gets a gMSA, and administrators rotate all four passwords manually, under the same governance applied to similar decisions across the business
One gMSA can serve all four servers while Active Directory rotates its password automatically, so no administrator knows it
explain: A single gMSA serves multiple servers with an automatically managed password. Services still authenticate — the difference is the credential is machine-managed and unknown to staff.

q: An employee has changed roles three times in five years, gaining new access each time while keeping every previous entitlement. What is this condition called, and what cures it?
options: Privilege creep; regular access reviews and recertification, where managers confirm each entitlement is still needed
Standing privilege; issuing the employee a second account for the old duties
Access drift; moving the employee's accounts to a Group Managed Service Account, documented in the runbook and checked again at the next scheduled review
Privilege escalation; reimaging the employee's workstation to remove old tools
explain: Privilege creep is the slow accumulation of unneeded access across role changes. Its cure is periodic review and recertification — not reimaging, extra accounts, or service-account tooling, which address different problems.

q: During a quarterly review, a manager finds a former team member's replacement still holds database rights from a project that ended a year ago. Which practice, applied on schedule, is designed to catch exactly this?
options: End-to-end encryption, which protects the review messages from interception
Micro-segmentation, which limits which segments the account can reach from
Access recertification, in which managers periodically confirm that each person's entitlements are still required
Out-of-band management, which separates administrative paths from production, consistent with how the organization already handles comparable cases today
explain: Recertification exists to surface stale entitlements like these so they can be removed. Segmentation may limit reach, but only the review process identifies that the right itself is no longer justified.

q: Production networking has failed at a data center, yet administrators can still reach every device through a separate dedicated management network that users never touch. Which practice provides this?
options: Security Service Edge, because cloud points of presence route the commands
In-band management, because administrators share the production network path
Zero-trust network access, because each request is verified before connecting, with the details recorded and revisited whenever roles or systems change
Out-of-band management, because a separate path administers devices even when production is down
explain: Out-of-band management keeps a dedicated administrative channel independent of production — available during outages and never exposed to ordinary user traffic. In-band management is the opposite arrangement.

q: An attacker who compromises the production network finds no path to device administration because management traffic travels on an entirely separate network. Which benefit of out-of-band management is demonstrated?
options: Data protection, because management traffic is masked before it is transmitted
Isolation of the administrative path, so users and attackers on production never touch device management
Faster administration, because separate networks always carry traffic more quickly, applied the same way in every department that operates this kind of system
Automatic patching, because management networks update devices without staff
explain: The security value of out-of-band management is separation: the path attackers would need to administer devices is not reachable from the network they compromised. Speed and automatic patching are not its purpose.

q: Executives require that sensitive internal messages be unreadable to every intermediary service that carries them, with only sender and recipient able to read the content. Which control provides this?
options: End-to-end encrypted messaging, because content is protected from every intermediary between the participants
Data masking, because message previews show only the last few characters
Tokenization, because message bodies are replaced with random stand-in values
Transport encryption to the mail server, because the server can then read messages, following established practice rather than an exception made for this case
explain: End-to-end encryption means only the endpoints hold the keys, so carriers and servers cannot read content. Encryption that stops at the server leaves the server able to read, and masking or tokenization transform stored values, not message content.

q: A company opens a 12-person branch. Which option is the COMPLETE design that applies current architecture guidance to the branch?
options: A site-to-site VPN that trusts branch traffic once inside; SSE for web access only; the branch server managed out-of-band; its service using an administrator's personal account

Per-request Zero Trust verification for users and devices; SSE-delivered web and SaaS security near the branch; the branch server managed out-of-band; its service running under a Group Managed Service Account
Per-request Zero Trust verification; SSE near the branch; the branch server managed out-of-band; its service using a static password stored in a sealed envelope

Per-request Zero Trust verification for users and devices; all branch traffic backhauled to headquarters for inspection; the branch server managed in-band; its service using a shared static password, with responsibilities written down and confirmed by the accountable manager
explain: The complete design combines all four elements: Zero Trust verification, SSE instead of backhaul, out-of-band management, and a gMSA so no static service password exists. Each other option keeps at least one retired practice — backhaul, in-band management, or a known static credential.

q: A Zero Trust rollout is reviewed. Which option lists the COMPLETE set of working parts and practices the architecture requires?
options: A policy engine that decides, policy enforcement points in the path, and a strong perimeter firewall at the internet edge
A policy administrator that configures, policy enforcement points in the path, and trust granted for the full login session, in accordance with the policy the organization applies to similar assets
A policy engine that decides, a policy administrator that configures, policy enforcement points in the path, continuous verification, and micro-segmentation
Continuous verification, micro-segmentation, and a VPN concentrator that all remote users must pass through
explain: Zero Trust needs all three components — engine, administrator, enforcement point — plus continuous verification and micro-segmentation. The partial sets omit a component or reintroduce perimeter trust and session-long trust, which the model rejects.

q: A firm deploys Security Service Edge for its offices. Which option is the COMPLETE and correct SSE rollout?
options: Secure web gateway, CASB, and zero-trust network access all delivered from cloud points of presence near the users
Zero-trust network access at the cloud edge, with web inspection still backhauled to the headquarters data center
Secure web gateway, CASB, and zero-trust network access installed as appliances in the headquarters data center
Secure web gateway and CASB at the cloud edge, with application access still granted by broad network-level VPN tunnels
explain: SSE delivers all three services — SWG, CASB, and ZTNA — from the cloud edge near users. Keeping VPN network-level access, keeping backhaul, or centralizing the services in headquarters each abandons part of the model.

q: A hospital segments its network after an audit. Which option is the COMPLETE segmentation outcome the auditors should accept?
options: Medical devices isolated in their own segment, with workstations, servers, and guest access combined for simplicity
Guest access isolated in its own segment, with clinical systems and servers combined on one flat clinical network
Workstations, medical devices, servers, and guest access each in separate controlled segments, with only explicitly required flows allowed between them
Workstations and servers in separate segments, with medical devices and guest access sharing the workstation segment, as a standing arrangement rather than a one-time response to this incident
explain: Complete segmentation isolates every class of system and permits only required flows — the micro-segmentation principle. Each partial option leaves a high-risk class sharing a segment, such as guests with workstations or clinical devices with general systems.

q: An audit finds static service passwords, stale entitlements, and in-band-only device management. Which option is the COMPLETE remediation set?
options: Run access recertification for executives only and document the stale entitlements as accepted risks
Establish out-of-band management and require administrators to share one rotating break-glass account
