The RTO should be 30 minutes only if backups are taken every 30 minutes
Cold sites fail because their backups are stored on magnetic tape media
A cold site must be equipped and built out after the disaster, which cannot meet a 30-minute restoration target
explain: Recovery targets dictate site choice: minutes-level RTO demands a hot or warm standby already prepared. A cold site's build-out time is measured in days, so the plan cannot satisfy the objective as written.

q: Snapshots of a virtual machine are kept on the same storage array as the machine itself, and the team calls them its backups. Which weakness does this create?
options: Snapshots are illegal copies under software licensing for virtual machines, so keeping them on the same array exposes the team to licensing action rather than data loss
Snapshots cannot be restored, so the team has no recovery option at all, because a snapshot is only a pointer that disappears when the machine is powered down
Snapshots encrypt the machine, preventing administrators from restoring it, because the snapshot process locks the virtual disks until the array is replaced
Loss or compromise of that one array destroys the machine and its supposed backups together, and snapshots are not independent backup copies
explain: Snapshots share fate with their source when they live on the same storage — true backups are separate copies, ideally in separate placements. Snapshots do restore, but as convenience points, not as a backup strategy.

q: A generator starts automatically when utility power fails, and battery units carry the load during the seconds before it starts. Which pairing of power controls is this?
options: Load balancers distributing power, with autoscaling adding generators on demand
Air gaps isolating the power, with immutability preserving the charge
Surge protectors absorbing the outage, with redundant power supplies generating electricity, applied uniformly so no team invents its own version of the procedure
Uninterruptible power supplies bridging short gaps, with a generator providing sustained backup power
explain: Batteries bridge the instant gap and generators sustain long outages — the layered power redundancy the objective names, alongside dual supplies and surge protection against spikes rather than losses.

q: A spike from a lightning strike damages equipment despite the building having a generator and batteries. Which power control was missing?
options: Longer battery runtime, because spikes drain batteries before equipment
Redundant power supplies, because single supplies pass spikes to components, with periodic checks that the arrangement is still doing what was intended
A second generator, because one generator cannot absorb electrical spikes
Surge protection, because generators and batteries address power loss, not damaging voltage spikes
explain: Each power control addresses a different electrical event: loss (generator, battery), and excess (surge protection). Backup power sources do nothing against a spike, which is why the layers are distinct.

q: Backups complete successfully, but the recovery team has never timed a full rebuild, and the business assumes a 2-hour restoration. What risk does restoration testing address here?
options: Whether off-site tapes are labeled in the correct language for couriers, because mislabeled media is the most common reason full rebuilds miss their assumed times
Whether the backup media is formatted with a current file system version, because outdated formats are the main reason restoration times go untested for years
Whether the assumed recovery time is achievable at all — untested recovery times are guesses, and the RTO may be unmeetable with the current backups
Whether backup jobs are running under the correct service account identity, because rebuilds fail when the service account used for the original jobs has changed
explain: Restoration testing converts assumptions into measurements: rebuild, time it, and compare with the RTO. Account, format, and labeling details do not test the recovery claim the business is relying on.

q: A differential backup taken Thursday is corrupt. Backups available: Sunday full, Monday through Wednesday differentials, and Friday's backup has not yet run. What is the best recovery position?
options: Restore Sunday's full plus Monday's differential only, as differentials must be used in strict order
No recovery is possible, because the latest differential is required for any restore
Restore Wednesday's differential alone, because it contains the full dataset as of Wednesday
Restore Sunday's full plus Wednesday's differential, losing only Thursday's changes, because each differential independently holds all changes since the full
explain: Any single differential pairs with the full — that independence is the scheme's strength. Wednesday's differential restores everything through Wednesday; only Thursday's changes are lost, matching the failure's actual cost.

q: An incremental chain has a corrupt backup on Tuesday. Backups available: Sunday full and Monday through Thursday incrementals. What is the recovery consequence?
options: Only Sunday's full is usable, because one corrupt piece voids the entire week
The chain can be restored only through Monday's incremental, because each incremental depends on all previous ones in order
Thursday's incremental can still be applied after skipping the corrupt Tuesday piece, with the outcome logged so a later review can verify what was decided
The corrupt piece is ignored automatically, because incrementals are self-contained
explain: Incremental restores stitch pieces in sequence, so a break in the chain caps recovery at the last good link — Monday here. This fragility is the accepted cost of incremental's small, fast backups.

q: Which statement about full backups is correct within the backup-type comparison?
options: A full backup is required daily because incremental backups cannot start a chain
A full backup copies all data every time — the largest and slowest to take, but the simplest single-piece starting point for any restore
A full backup copies only data changed since the previous full backup
A full backup stores no data itself and only indexes the other backup types
explain: Full means everything, every time — 100 GB for the reference server — which is why schemes anchor a weekly full and fill the week with incremental or differential backups rather than repeating fulls nightly.

q: Which single image correctly anchors the difference between the two recovery objectives?
options: RPO looks to the past — how far back your data goes; RTO looks to the future — how long until you are running again
Both look to the past, but RPO is measured in hours and RTO in transactions
Both look to the future, but RTO is measured in data and RPO in downtime
RPO looks to the future — how long until running; RTO looks to the past — how far back data goes, subject to periodic review by the responsible team
explain: The anchor: data equals RPO, downtime equals RTO. RPO reaches backward to the last good copy; RTO reaches forward to restored service. Every swapped pairing reverses the pair the exam most loves to test.

q: A retailer can tolerate being down for one full business day but can lose at most one hour of sales records. Which pair expresses this?
options: MTTR of one day and MTBF of one hour, because targets use the mean metrics
A single combined objective of one day, because the two cannot differ
RTO of one hour and RPO of one day, because the tighter limit always comes first, in line with the organization's documented standards for comparable systems
RTO of one day and RPO of one hour — downtime tolerance and data-loss tolerance are set independently
explain: The objectives are independent business decisions: a leisurely restoration can pair with strict data protection, which is why this retailer needs hourly backups but only a day-scale recovery capability. MTTR and MTBF are measured outcomes, not set targets.

q: An incident review shows failures at hours 100, 300, and 600 of operation, each repaired in 3 hours. Which metrics can be computed from this record?
options: Only the RTO, because objectives are computed from incident timestamps, and the intervals and repair times in the record are not inputs to either reliability metric
MTBF from the operating intervals between failures and MTTR as the 3-hour average repair time, because both need only the incident record
Only the RPO, because data loss is recorded at each failure time, and neither operating intervals nor repair durations can be derived from an incident record
Neither metric, because a full calendar quarter of data is required before any reliability metric may be computed from a system's operating history
explain: Incident history is exactly what the mean metrics summarize: intervals between failures give MTBF and repair durations average to MTTR. RTO and RPO are business-set targets, not values computed from incident records.

q: A cloud region failure takes a service offline, but its twin deployment in a distant region assumes the load within the hour. Which two resilience elements combined here?
options: Immutability with surge protection, so backups and power survive the region, with ownership assigned and the arrangement reviewed on a regular schedule
Autoscaling with air gapping, so capacity grows while copies stay isolated
Restoration testing with masking, so rebuilt systems hide sensitive data
Geographic separation with load balancing, so a regional event stays regional and work shifts to surviving capacity
explain: A second region provides the separation; balancing shifts work onto it. The other pairings mix power, backup, and display controls that play no role in surviving a regional outage.

q: A data center's servers each have two power supplies fed from separate circuits. One circuit fails during maintenance. What happens and why?
options: The load balancer moves the workloads, because power faults trigger failover
The servers keep running on the surviving circuit, because redundant power supplies remove power as a single point of failure
The servers shut down safely, because dual supplies require both circuits live, as part of the standard operating procedure for systems of this kind
The generator starts, because any circuit failure triggers generator power
explain: Redundant supplies mean one feed's loss is a non-event for the server — the same containment logic as other redundancy, applied to power. Generators address total utility loss, and workload failover is unnecessary when nothing stopped.

q: A recovery plan is audited. Which option is the COMPLETE plan that satisfies resilience guidance?
options: Load-balanced autoscaling instances with geographic separation, nightly snapshots on the same array counted as the backup strategy, and a documented contact tree for declaring a disaster
Immutable off-site backups with scheduled restoration testing, single-instance deployment, and power redundancy at one site only, with recovery dependent on that site's hardware
Backups in full-plus-incremental rotation stored on the production array, annual restoration discussion in a meeting, redundant power supplies in each server, and no off-site copies of any backup

Backups in full-plus-incremental rotation with immutable and off-site copies, scheduled restoration testing against the RTO, load-balanced instances with autoscaling, and redundant power with geographic separation
explain: The complete plan covers every mechanism family: sound backup types and placements with immutability, actual restoration testing, capacity resilience, power redundancy, and geographic separation. Each partial plan drops a family — testing, placement independence, or capacity — that the objective requires.

q: A business defines its recovery requirements. Which option states the COMPLETE and correct requirement set?
options: An RTO capping tolerated downtime, an RPO capping tolerated data loss with backup frequency set to meet it, and MTTR and MTBF tracked to show the targets are being met
An RTO capping tolerated data loss, an RPO capping tolerated downtime, and backup frequency set by the RTO value
Backup frequency set by vendor default, an RTO for downtime, and MTBF used in place of an RPO
An RPO capping tolerated data loss and MTTR tracked as the target, with no downtime objective defined
explain: Requirements pair each objective with its quantity — RTO with downtime, RPO with data — and use the mean metrics as evidence against them. Swapping the pairings, substituting a mean for a target, or defaulting the backup frequency each breaks the framework the objective teaches.

q: A regulator requires a firm to independently examine the code of a critical cryptographic library before approving its use. Which software model can satisfy this requirement, and what duty comes with it?
options: Open source, because community libraries require no patching once approved
Proprietary, because vendors routinely publish full source code for regulated customers, consistent with how the organization already handles comparable cases today
Open source, because the code can be reviewed by anyone — with support and patching discipline resting on the firm itself
Proprietary, because a vendor's marketing claims substitute for code review
explain: Only open code can be independently examined — the transparency side of the trade. The same choice puts patching discipline on the adopter, and proprietary assurance rests on vendor accountability rather than published source.

q: Visitors to an office connect to a guest wireless network that can reach the internet but has no route to any internal system. Which architecture practice is this?
options: Out-of-band management, because guests administer their own devices on it, with the details recorded and revisited whenever roles or systems change
Segmentation of untrusted guest access away from internal resources, allowing only internet-bound traffic
Privilege recertification, because guest access is reviewed every quarter
Security Service Edge, because the guest traffic is inspected at the edge
explain: Isolating guests into their own segment with no internal reach is basic segmentation: untrusted devices get connectivity without footholds. It is not a management path, an edge service bundle, or an entitlement review.

q: Administrators must use a hardened, dedicated workstation — used for nothing else — whenever they perform privileged tasks. What risk does this design reduce?
options: Privilege creep, because dedicated workstations expire unused entitlements automatically whenever administrators stop signing in from their everyday machines
Data loss, because privileged workstations encrypt all data they display, so nothing shown during an administrative session can ever be copied or captured
A compromised everyday workstation cannot be used to hijack privileged sessions, because administration happens only from the dedicated, hardened device
Phishing, because administrators stop receiving email on their main accounts once a dedicated workstation exists for performing privileged tasks
explain: Separating the administrative device from the daily-driver device means malware or compromise on the everyday machine does not inherit administrative reach. It does not expire entitlements, encrypt displayed data, or change email exposure.

q: Servers in a protected segment accept administrative connections only from a single hardened intermediary host that administrators connect to first. What is this intermediary pattern called and why is it used?
options: A policy engine, used so access decisions are made on the intermediary host
A jump server, used so administrative access funnels through one controlled, monitored entry point into the segment
A load balancer, used so administrative sessions spread across many servers
A secure web gateway, used so administrative traffic is filtered as web traffic, following established practice rather than an exception made for this case
explain: A jump server concentrates administrative entry into a protected segment at one auditable point. It does not distribute load, make policy decisions, or filter web content.

q: A cloud workload's network rules currently allow inbound connections from any address. The team restricts them to the two application servers that actually call the workload. Which principle is being applied?
options: Least-privilege network exposure: a workload should be reachable only from the sources its function actually requires
Micro-segmentation is unnecessary in cloud environments with default rules
Autoscaling, because fewer sources means the workload scales more efficiently, with responsibilities written down and confirmed by the accountable manager
Out-of-band management, because the workload now has a separate admin path
explain: Tightening reachability to actual required sources is least-privilege applied to network rules — the cloud expression of segmentation. It creates no management path and has nothing to do with scaling behavior.

q: Before a server goes live, engineers disable every service and port the application does not use. Which hardening principle is this?
options: Least functionality, because removing unused services and ports shrinks the attack surface the server exposes
Continuous verification, because each remaining port is verified per request, in accordance with the policy the organization applies to similar assets
Privilege creep prevention, because unused services accumulate entitlements
End-to-end encryption, because closed ports cannot carry readable traffic
explain: Least functionality removes what is not needed so there is less to attack. The other options concern entitlements, message content, and request verification — none describes stripping a system to its required functions.

q: A wired office network requires every device to authenticate before its port activates, so an unauthorized laptop plugged into a wall jack gets no access. Which control provides this?
options: A secure web gateway, because the laptop's web traffic would be filtered
A Group Managed Service Account, because the jack's identity rotates automatically, reviewed alongside the other controls that protect the same environment
Data masking, because the laptop cannot see full values on the network
Port-based network access control such as 802.1X, because devices are authenticated before network access is granted
explain: 802.1X-style admission control makes the network itself demand authentication before granting a port — the wired counterpart of verified access. Web filtering happens after access exists, and service accounts and masking address other layers entirely.

q: A registration form collects only the fields the service genuinely needs, after a review removed dates of birth and national ID numbers it never used. Which data-protection strategy is this?
options: Transposition, because the form's layout was restructured for privacy, as a standing arrangement rather than a one-time response to this incident
Deidentification, because the removed fields identified the customers
Data minimization within the lifecycle: collecting and retaining less data reduces what a breach can expose
Tokenization, because unnecessary fields were replaced with stand-ins
explain: Collecting less in the first place shrinks exposure across the whole lifecycle — data never held cannot be breached. The fields were removed rather than transformed, so none of the transformation techniques describes it.

q: Encrypted archives are found worthless after an incident because the only copy of the keys was stored in the same compromised system as the data. Which key-management principle was violated?
options: Keys must be held separately from the data they protect, under their own strict, Restricted-level controls
Keys must be rotated only when the data itself is reclassified downward
Keys should be printed and stored with the archives for reliable recovery, with the same rigor the organization applies to its other critical systems
Keys belong to the processor, so the data owner need not manage them
explain: Encryption's protection collapses when the key shares the data's fate; separation of keys, with strict need-to-know control, is what makes at-rest encryption real. Keys are themselves Restricted-tier assets in the classification scheme.

q: An employee tries to email a document labeled Confidential to a personal address, and the system blocks the send based on the label. Which concept is operating?
options: Deidentification, because the document was stripped of identifiers at send
Data transposition, because the document's shape triggered the block
Classification-driven protection: the label the data carries determines which controls apply to it, including blocking improper sharing
Tokenization, because the recipient address was replaced with a token
explain: This is the classification model working as designed — label the data and let the label drive the controls, here at the sharing stage of the lifecycle. No transformation of the document's values or shape occurred.

q: A company cannot protect data it does not know it has, so it inventories where personal data lives across systems before setting controls. Which lifecycle need does the inventory serve?
options: You cannot classify, protect, or schedule destruction for data you have not located; discovery underpins every later lifecycle stage
It replaces classification, because located data no longer needs labels
It transfers ownership, because the inventory team becomes the data owner
It satisfies the destruction stage, because inventoried data counts as retired
explain: Classification, retention, and protection all presuppose knowing what data exists and where. An inventory changes none of the data's status by itself — it makes the rest of the lifecycle governable.

q: A marketing team wants to reuse support-ticket personal data, collected to resolve customer problems, for an unrelated advertising study. Which data-role and lifecycle principle is challenged?
options: The custodian's duty, because custodians approve new uses of stored data, and any reuse must be cleared by the team that physically maintains the storage systems
The controller set the purpose for which the data is processed; using it for an unrelated purpose breaks the purpose the data was collected under
The processor's role, because processors may repurpose data they handle whenever the new use stays inside the same company that collected the data originally
No principle, because data inside one company may be used for any purpose, and the purpose recorded at collection only matters when data is sold to outsiders
explain: Purposes are the controller's decision and they bind later use — data gathered to resolve tickets was not gathered for advertising studies. Custodians handle data, processors act on instructions, and internal possession does not erase purpose limits.

q: A standby site has equipment installed and data replicated periodically, but systems are not running; after a disaster it can be brought online within several hours. Which site type is this?
options: A cold site, because the systems are not running at the moment of failure, with periodic checks that the arrangement is still doing what was intended
A warm site, because it is partially prepared — equipped and supplied with data, but not live like a hot site
A hot site, because any site with equipment installed counts as hot
An air-gapped site, because its data arrives by periodic replication
explain: Warm sites sit between hot and cold: real equipment and recent data, but activation still takes hours. Hot sites are already running and current; cold sites are essentially empty space awaiting build-out.

q: A payment service sets an RPO of one hour. Its current backups run at midnight and noon. What change does the objective require?
options: Backup or replication at least every hour, because the 12-hour interval permits losing up to 12 hours of transactions — twelve times the tolerated loss
No change, because two backups a day average out to one hour of loss when the failures are spread evenly across the full twenty-four-hour period
A longer RTO, because backup frequency and recovery time are the same control, so extending one automatically repairs the other in the plan
Hourly restoration testing, because testing frequency sets the recovery point, and more frequent tests move the recovery point closer to the failure
explain: Backup frequency sets the achievable RPO, full stop: a 12-hour gap is a 12-hour worst-case loss. Meeting a one-hour RPO requires captures at least hourly, regardless of testing cadence or the RTO value.

q: A new application server is scanned after installation and is found listening on eight services, but its approved role requires only the application, SSH, and its database connection. What is the BEST hardening action?
options: Rename the unneeded services so automated scanners are less likely to find them across all affected systems in the environment
Remove or firewall the five unneeded services so only the three approved services remain reachable
Leave all eight services running but monitor them closely for unusual activity
Disable SSH and require administrators to use the application console instead
explain: Removing the five unneeded services reduces the attack surface to the approved baseline; each removed service eliminates an entire exploitation path. Monitoring alone leaves the exposure in place, and renaming services is obscurity, not hardening.

q: An administrator discovers that several production servers no longer match the approved secure configuration because local changes were made over several months. Which practice BEST addresses this problem going forward?
options: Enforce the secure baseline with automated drift detection and correction
Restrict all administrative access until a full manual audit is completed
Require administrators to document changes in a shared spreadsheet each month
Reimage every server from scratch at the end of each calendar year
explain: Baseline enforcement with drift detection finds and corrects deviations from the approved build continuously. A spreadsheet records drift without fixing it, and annual reimaging leaves long windows of exposure.

q: During an investigation, analysts find that a planted service account that no employee should ever use was successfully authenticated from an internal workstation at 2 a.m. What does this MOST likely indicate?
options: An intruder is using a compromised or planted credential and the workstation should be investigated immediately
A legitimate administrator forgot the account password policy and needs retraining
An automated backup job is misconfigured and is testing old credentials nightly
The account was created incorrectly and should simply be deleted without investigation and document the outcome in the team's tracking system
explain: Canary accounts are never used legitimately, so any use is a high-confidence signal of compromise rather than user error. Deleting the account or blaming a backup job would discard a near-zero-false-positive detection.

q: Developers keep accidentally committing cloud access keys to the company code repository, and two keys have already been exposed. Which control BEST prevents this from recurring?
options: Rotating all cloud keys once per quarter on a fixed calendar schedule
Moving the repository to a private server with restricted network access using the tools and processes already in place for this purpose
Secrets scanning that checks code and commits and blocks keys before they are pushed
A policy memo reminding developers that committing keys is prohibited
explain: Secrets scanning inspects commits and blocks leaked keys before they spread, addressing the cause at the point of commit. Reminders and quarterly rotation do not stop the next leak, and a private server does not prevent keys from being committed.

q: A public login page is being hit by thousands of credential-stuffing attempts per hour from rotating addresses. Which technique MOST directly blunts this attack?
options: Requiring users to choose longer passwords at their next scheduled reset
Publishing the list of attacking addresses on the company status page
Encrypting the login page traffic with a newer TLS version and cipher suite on a recurring basis as part of normal operations
Rate limiting the number of authentication attempts a client can make in a time window
explain: Rate limiting caps how fast a client can submit attempts, which directly slows guessing and stuffing. TLS protects data in transit but does not limit attempt volume, and longer passwords do not stop automated reuse of breached pairs.

q: A hotel wants guests to accept terms and identify themselves before getting internet access, holding new devices on a landing page until they do. Which control provides this?
options: An 802.1X deployment that requires certificates on every guest device
A captive portal that holds clients until they accept terms or authenticate
A wireless intrusion prevention system that contains unauthorized clients before any other remediation or response steps are attempted
A network access control policy that assigns guests to a quarantine VLAN
explain: A captive portal holds new clients on a landing page until they accept terms or authenticate, which is exactly the guest Wi-Fi gate described. WIPS contains rogue devices rather than onboarding guests, and certificate-based 802.1X is impractical for transient guests.

q: A company wants its verified brand logo to appear beside its messages in customer inboxes to make impersonation harder. Its SPF and DKIM are configured, but DMARC is set to monitoring only. What must happen before the logo can be displayed?
options: SPF must be replaced with a stricter sender list published in the company portal
A second DKIM selector must be published so messages carry two signatures
DMARC must be moved to an enforced policy, since the logo program requires SPF, DKIM, and enforced DMARC
The company must register its logo with each receiving mailbox provider individually with the results reviewed by the security team afterward
explain: BIMI displays a verified brand logo only when SPF, DKIM, and an enforced DMARC policy are already in place. Monitoring-only DMARC does not qualify, and extra selectors or provider-by-provider registration are not the requirement.

q: An endpoint shows a suspicious process injecting into other processes and beginning to encrypt files. Which tool can watch this behavior and isolate the machine mid-attack?
options: Data loss prevention, which inspects content leaving the organization
Endpoint detection and response, which monitors process behavior and can isolate the host
Traditional signature-based antivirus, which compares files against known hashes applied consistently rather than on a case-by-case basis
A web content filter, which blocks categories of websites for all users
explain: EDR watches process behavior and can isolate a machine during an attack, which matches the in-progress encryption. Signature antivirus is a first layer that often misses novel behavior, and DLP and web filtering address different data flows.

q: Policy forbids sending customer records to personal email or copying them to removable media. Which control inspects content leaving through email, web, and USB and blocks what policy forbids?
options: Data loss prevention deployed across email, web, and removable-media channels
Full-disk encryption applied to every workstation and laptop in the fleet as a standing part of the organization's security operations
Network segmentation separating the records database from other servers
A password manager rolled out to all staff with generated credentials
explain: DLP inspects content in motion through email, web, and removable media and blocks or flags policy violations. Encryption protects data at rest on a lost device but does not stop an authorized user from sending records out.

q: Staff keep reaching gambling and known malware sites from office workstations. Which control BEST keeps users away from known-bad and policy-barred destinations?
options: Secrets scanning that checks browser bookmarks and saved pages
Rate limiting that caps the number of web requests per user per hour and verify the result through the normal review process
A captive portal that requires users to accept terms at each sign-in
Web and content filtering that blocks barred categories and malicious sites
explain: Web and content filtering blocks known-bad and policy-barred destinations, which is the stated goal. A captive portal gates initial access only, and rate limiting controls volume rather than destination.

q: A security team wants the same hardened configuration applied consistently across 800 laptops without visiting each machine. Which approach BEST achieves this?
options: A detailed hardening checklist emailed to each laptop user to apply themselves across all affected systems in the environment
A one-time imaging project with no ongoing configuration management afterward
Group policy and configuration enforcement that push the baseline to the whole fleet
Manual spot checks of a small sample of laptops at each office location
explain: Group policy and configuration enforcement push the baseline to fleets of machines, making hardening consistent and repeatable. Checklists and spot checks depend on individual effort and cannot hold 800 machines to one standard.

q: Employees are plugging personal devices into wall ports in conference rooms and joining the internal network without any check. Which control decides who may join the network at the port level?
options: 802.1X port authentication that requires authentication before network access is granted
A captive portal page that asks visitors to enter their names
Port mirroring that copies switch traffic to a monitoring sensor
A wireless intrusion prevention system that scans for rogue access points as the primary response to the problem described
explain: 802.1X port authentication decides who may join the network at all by requiring authentication on the port before access. A captive portal is a lighter guest gate, and port mirroring only observes traffic without controlling admission.

q: A facilities team reports an unknown access point broadcasting the company network name from a parking area. Which system watches the air for rogue access points and can contain them?
options: A wireless intrusion prevention system monitoring for rogue APs and unauthorized clients
A network management system tracking switch and router device health and document the outcome in the team's tracking system
A firewall rule set filtering traffic at the network boundary
A packet analyzer used by an analyst to inspect a captured exchange
explain: WIPS watches the airwaves for rogue access points and unauthorized clients and can contain them. The other tools observe wired traffic or device health but do not police the wireless perimeter.

q: A file server must be hardened to its approved baseline. Which option is the COMPLETE correct set of actions for that baseline?
options: Close unneeded ports and apply the secure configuration, but skip removing default accounts this cycle
Disable unneeded services and close unneeded ports, but keep default accounts for vendor support access
Apply the approved secure configuration and remove default accounts, but leave unneeded services running using the tools and processes already in place for this purpose
Disable unneeded services, remove default accounts, close unneeded ports, and apply the approved secure configuration
explain: A secure baseline combines all four elements: unneeded services off, default accounts gone, unneeded ports closed, and the secure configuration applied. Each partial set leaves a known opening — default accounts and extra services are classic entry points.

q: A branch office shares one flat network for servers, workstations, and guest devices, and a compromised guest laptop reached a file server. Which control BEST limits this kind of spread?
options: Network segmentation that separates guests, workstations, and servers into distinct zones
Installing antivirus software on the file server and keeping signatures updated on a recurring basis as part of normal operations
Enabling detailed logging on the file server for later investigation
Requiring stronger passwords for all accounts that access the file server
explain: Segmentation limits which zones can reach each other, so a compromised guest device cannot reach servers directly. Antivirus, passwords, and logging help other problems but do not remove the flat-network path.

q: Attackers are sending convincing invoices that appear to come from the company's finance department. The company already has SPF and DKIM and an enforced DMARC policy. Which additional control raises the cost of this impersonation in customer and partner inboxes?
options: Rate limiting outbound mail to a fixed number of messages per hour
A captive portal requiring recipients to sign in before reading invoices
Secrets scanning of the finance department's outbound message attachments before any other remediation or response steps are attempted
BIMI, so the verified brand logo appears only beside genuinely authenticated company mail
explain: With SPF, DKIM, and enforced DMARC in place, BIMI lets the verified logo ride beside legitimate mail, making unauthenticated imitations stand out. Rate limiting and portals do not authenticate brand identity to recipients.

q: A security analyst plants a fake document containing an embedded token in a shared folder. Two days later the token fires an alert from an external address. What is the BEST interpretation?
options: Someone accessed the planted file, which no legitimate user should touch, indicating possible compromise
The token expired early and generated a false alert that can be safely closed
A backup service copied the folder and triggered the token during routine processing
The document management system is indexing shared folders more aggressively than expected with the results reviewed by the security team afterward
explain: Canary tokens are planted in files no legitimate user touches, so a trigger means someone took the bait — a low-false-positive sign of intrusion. Routine indexing explanations should be ruled out during investigation, not assumed to close the alert.

q: A web application is being scraped by a single client making thousands of requests per minute, degrading service for real users. Which technique MOST directly addresses this?
options: Rate limiting that caps how fast a client can make requests to the application
Requiring all users to reset their passwords before their next session
Migrating the application database to a server with more storage capacity applied consistently rather than on a case-by-case basis
Adding a second firewall at the perimeter with the same rule set
explain: Rate limiting caps request speed per client, blunting scraping and brute force alike. Capacity and password changes do not slow the abusive client, and a duplicate firewall adds no per-client request control.

q: A server baseline requires its database port to be reachable only from the application tier, but a scan shows it open to the whole internal network. What is the BEST action?
options: Move the database to a new address and keep the change undocumented
Restrict the database port with firewall rules so only the application tier can reach it
Disable database logging so probing attempts are not recorded
Accept the exposure because the server is on the internal network only as a standing part of the organization's security operations
explain: The baseline counts a service as properly placed only when its reachability is limited — here, to the application tier. Internal-only exposure still leaves every workstation as a potential launch point, and hiding the address is not a control.

q: A company still relies only on signature-based antivirus, and a new fileless attack using built-in system tools went undetected. Which addition BEST closes this gap?
options: A second antivirus product from a different vendor running alongside the first and verify the result through the normal review process
EDR that monitors process behavior rather than only matching known file signatures
A web filter blocking downloads of executable files from the internet
More frequent signature updates scheduled every hour instead of daily
explain: Fileless attacks abuse legitimate tools and leave few files to sign, so behavioral EDR is the control that sees them. Stacked signature products and faster updates still depend on known signatures the attack avoids.

q: A public web login is under credential-stuffing attack. Which option is the COMPLETE set of mitigating actions for this problem?
options: Apply rate limiting, enforce multifactor authentication, and block or challenge automated traffic
Apply rate limiting only, and review the results at the next monthly meeting across all affected systems in the environment
Block the single loudest source address and consider the incident closed
Enforce multifactor authentication only, with no limit on attempt volume
explain: Stuffing is blunted by combining attempt-rate limits, MFA so stolen pairs alone fail, and automation challenges. Any single measure leaves a working path: unlimited attempts defeat weak factors, and blocking one address ignores rotating sources.

q: Default vendor accounts with published passwords are found enabled on several newly deployed network devices. What is the BEST immediate hardening step?
options: Restrict the devices to business-hours access through a time-based rule
Rename the default accounts to less obvious names and keep the passwords
Document the default accounts in the asset register and review them quarterly as the primary response to the problem described
Remove or disable the default accounts and set unique credentials before production use
explain: Default accounts must be gone under a secure baseline because their passwords are publicly known. Renaming keeps a known-password account alive, and documentation or time limits do not remove the exposure.

q: An auditor finds that a hardened server's configuration was changed by an administrator to fix an outage and never changed back. Which practice would have caught this earliest?
options: A change freeze prohibiting all configuration changes during business hours and document the outcome in the team's tracking system
An annual configuration review performed by the internal audit team
Continuous drift detection comparing the server against its approved baseline
A requirement that administrators narrate changes on a recorded phone line
explain: Drift detection compares systems to the approved baseline continuously, so an un-reverted change surfaces quickly. An annual review finds it months late, and process narration does not measure the actual configuration.

q: A coffee-shop-style guest network is being added to headquarters. Management wants guests identified and terms accepted, but no software installed on guest devices. Which control fits?
options: 802.1X with device certificates issued to every guest device
Endpoint detection and response agents installed on guest laptops using the tools and processes already in place for this purpose
A captive portal presenting terms and a sign-in before granting access
Group policy objects pushed to guest devices at connection time
explain: A captive portal is the friendly gate for guests: a landing page for terms or authentication with nothing installed. Certificates, agents, and group policy all assume managed devices, which guests are not.

q: Sensitive design files were found on a public code-hosting site after an engineer pasted an internal snippet containing an API key. Which control would MOST likely have blocked the key from spreading?
options: Secrets scanning that detects keys in code and blocks them before publication
An annual security awareness refresher covering the handling policy
Full-disk encryption on the engineer's workstation and backup drives
A data classification label applied to the design files in the document system
explain: Secrets scanning examines code and commits for leaked keys and blocks them before they spread — the exact failure here. Classification and encryption do not inspect what is pasted into a repository.

q: A retailer wants to stop card-testing bots that submit hundreds of small authorization attempts against its checkout API. Which technique is MOST targeted?
options: Enforcing the secure baseline on the payment application servers
Rate limiting on the checkout API endpoints the bots are abusing
Segmenting the payment database onto its own isolated network zone
Deploying a wireless intrusion prevention system in retail stores
explain: Card testing is a request-volume abuse, and rate limiting caps how fast a client can submit attempts. Segmentation and baselines are sound hygiene but do not slow the bot's attempt rate.

q: Which statement BEST describes a secure baseline?
options: A backup image kept in case a server needs to be rebuilt quickly
A one-time scan report listing every vulnerability found on a server with the results reviewed by the security team afterward
A list of every software package installed across the organization
An approved standard build with unneeded services off, default accounts removed, and secure settings applied
explain: A baseline is the approved build standard — services, accounts, ports, and configuration set securely — against which drift is measured. A scan report or inventory describes a moment; the baseline defines what correct looks like.

q: A university wants to prevent students in dorms from reaching the administrative systems network while still allowing internet access. Which control BEST enforces this separation?
options: Content filtering that blocks administrative websites by category applied consistently rather than on a case-by-case basis
Network segmentation with firewall filtering between the student and administrative zones
A captive portal that students pass through once each semester
Rate limiting student connections to a lower bandwidth allocation
explain: Segmentation with boundary filtering controls which networks can reach which, directly enforcing the separation. Content filtering governs destinations on the web, not internal zone-to-zone reachability.

q: An alert shows a workstation attempting to send a large archive to a personal cloud storage account, which policy forbids. Which control is designed to block or flag exactly this?
options: A firewall rule blocking all outbound traffic after business hours
Endpoint detection and response isolating hosts showing ransomware behavior
Data loss prevention inspecting outbound content against policy
An email gateway that strips attachments larger than a set size
explain: DLP inspects content leaving through web, email, and removable media and blocks or flags what policy forbids — here, records moving to personal storage. Size limits and schedules are blunt substitutes that miss the content-based policy.

q: A penetration tester reports that from one compromised workstation she could reach every other workstation because the user network is flat and unrestricted. Which mitigation MOST directly removes this lateral-movement path?
options: Segment the user network and filter traffic between segments and server zones
Enable host firewalls but leave their default allow-all rules in place
Require users to change passwords every thirty days instead of ninety
Deploy additional antivirus licenses to every workstation in the network and verify the result through the normal review process
explain: Segmentation with filtering removes the unrestricted workstation-to-workstation path the tester used. Host firewalls left at allow-all change nothing, and password cadence does not affect network reachability.

q: A SaaS provider's API keys were found in a public repository within an hour of a commit. The team wants detection at the moment of commit. Which control provides this?
options: Secrets scanning integrated into the commit and push workflow
Branch protection rules requiring two reviewers on every merge
A policy requiring keys to be stored in a shared team password vault
A quarterly review of all repositories by the security team
explain: Secrets scanning at commit time examines code as it is pushed and blocks leaked keys before they spread. Quarterly reviews find exposures months late, and vault policy does not inspect commits.

q: A company is deploying deception controls on its internal network. Which option is the COMPLETE correct deployment for early, low-noise intrusion detection?
options: Publish a list of decoy servers and announce them to staff as test systems
Plant canary accounts and canary tokens that no legitimate user touches, and alert on any use
Create extra shared folders with realistic names and monitor their storage growth as the primary response to the problem described
Plant canary accounts for administrators only and review their logs each quarter
explain: Deception works because canary accounts and tokens are never touched legitimately, so any use is a flare with almost no false positives. Announcing decoys or limiting them to quarterly review destroys the quiet, immediate signal.

q: A firewall at the network boundary is upgraded to an intrusion prevention system. What does the prevention system add beyond the firewall's filtering?
options: It can actively block malicious traffic patterns it detects, not just filter by rules
It encrypts all traffic passing through the boundary for confidentiality and document the outcome in the team's tracking system
It replaces the need for any host-based security controls on servers
It authenticates every user before allowing any packet to pass through
explain: Firewalls filter and block at boundaries by rule; an IPS also detects malicious patterns and blocks them in line. It does not encrypt traffic or authenticate users, and host controls remain necessary.

q: A clinic's workstations keep losing their hardened settings after vendor maintenance visits. Which approach keeps the fleet at the approved build between visits?
options: Photographing each workstation's settings before and after each visit
Asking the vendor to sign a statement that settings were left unchanged using the tools and processes already in place for this purpose
Locking the clinic's network closet so vendor staff need an escort
Configuration enforcement that reapplies the baseline and reports drift automatically
explain: Configuration enforcement through group policy pushes the baseline to fleets and corrects drift without per-machine effort. Signed statements and photographs document drift after the fact rather than preventing or repairing it.

q: An attacker is trying password after password against a VPN gateway, thousands per hour. Which control MOST directly slows this guessing?
options: Moving the VPN gateway behind the internal firewall segment
Rate limiting authentication attempts at the VPN gateway
Increasing the gateway's log retention from thirty to ninety days
Requiring users to acknowledge a warning banner at sign-in
explain: Rate limiting caps attempts per client per time window, directly slowing brute force. Banners and log retention do not change attempt speed, and placement alone does not limit guessing volume.

q: Which scenario is the BEST use case for a canary token?
options: A token in an email header proves the sender's domain is authenticated
A token printed on asset tags identifies hardware during inventory counts before any other remediation or response steps are attempted
A token issued to each employee replaces their password for daily sign-in
A token embedded in a decoy file alerts the team the moment an intruder opens it
explain: A canary token is a planted artifact no legitimate user touches; its use signals an intruder holding something they should not have. It is a deception tripwire, not an authentication factor, inventory tag, or email control.

q: A mail administrator has SPF and DKIM passing but phishing emails spoofing the company still reach customers, who cannot tell real mail from fake. DMARC is at enforcement. Which control helps recipients visually distinguish genuine mail?
options: A stricter SPF record listing fewer authorized sending servers with the results reviewed by the security team afterward
A warning banner inserted into all inbound customer replies
Longer DKIM keys rotated on a more frequent schedule
BIMI displaying the verified brand logo beside authenticated messages
explain: With SPF, DKIM, and enforced DMARC in place, BIMI adds the verified logo beside genuine mail in the inbox, raising the cost of impersonation. Tightening SPF or DKIM further does not give recipients a visual trust signal.

q: A warehouse deploys unmanaged IoT cameras on the same network as its inventory servers. Which mitigation BEST protects the servers if a camera is compromised?
options: Require warehouse staff to use stronger passwords on their workstations
Install antivirus software on the inventory servers and update it weekly applied consistently rather than on a case-by-case basis
Give the cameras static addresses so they are easier to identify later
Place the cameras on a separate network segment with filtered access to servers
explain: Segmentation contains a compromised camera so it cannot freely reach inventory servers. Addressing and passwords do not remove the network path, and antivirus is a layer, not isolation.

q: What is the primary purpose of hardening a server before it enters production?
options: To test its backup and recovery procedures under a simulated failure
To increase its processing speed by disabling background maintenance tasks as a standing part of the organization's security operations
To document its hardware specifications for the asset inventory register
To reduce its attack surface by removing unneeded services, accounts, and ports and applying secure settings
explain: Hardening applies the approved baseline: unnecessary services off, default accounts gone, unneeded ports closed, secure configuration applied. The goal is a smaller attack surface, not performance, inventory, or recovery testing.

q: A help desk reports that a user's machine is beaconing to a known malicious domain every few minutes. Which endpoint capability helps an analyst investigate and stop it remotely?
options: A DLP rule scanning the user's outbound email attachments
A content filter update adding the domain to the block list
EDR telemetry and remote isolation of the affected endpoint
A group policy change forcing a password reset at next sign-in
explain: EDR watches endpoint behavior and can isolate a machine mid-incident while preserving telemetry for investigation. A block list helps the fleet, but the compromised host itself needs detection-and-response tooling.

q: A new server role is being added and the security team must define its hardening package. Which option is the COMPLETE package consistent with a secure baseline?
options: Unneeded services disabled and default accounts removed, with drift monitoring deferred to next year
Approved secure configuration, unneeded services disabled, unneeded ports closed, default accounts removed, and drift monitoring enabled
Approved secure configuration and unneeded ports closed, with default accounts kept for break-glass use across all affected systems in the environment
Secure configuration applied at build time only, with no ongoing drift monitoring afterward
explain: The baseline is the full set: configuration, services, ports, and accounts set securely at build, plus drift detection so the state is maintained. Keeping default accounts or skipping drift monitoring leaves the baseline unenforced.

q: Two departments share a printer VLAN. A scan shows a legacy file-sharing service still running on a print server, unused for years. What is the BEST action under baseline hardening?
options: Rename the service account and note the exception in the risk register
Leave the service but restrict it to daytime hours with a schedule rule as the primary response to the problem described
Remove the legacy service, since every running service is attack surface the baseline does not approve
Monitor the service for a full quarter before deciding whether to act
explain: Hardening arithmetic counts every unneeded listening service as an attack story waiting to happen; an unused legacy protocol should be removed, not scheduled or renamed. Monitoring an unneeded service preserves risk the baseline already decided against.

q: A company wants one consistent screen-lock, encryption, and update policy across all Windows laptops, including remote staff. Which mechanism enforces this centrally?
options: Group policy and configuration enforcement applied to the laptop fleet
A yearly laptop refresh that reapplies settings at replacement time and document the outcome in the team's tracking system
Individual configuration guides sent to each remote employee
Spot audits of laptops that happen to visit the headquarters office
explain: Group policy pushes and enforces the baseline across fleets, including remote machines, so hardening is not a per-laptop craft project. Guides and spot audits cannot hold a distributed fleet to one standard.

q: An employee reports a realistic-looking email that appears to be from the CEO asking for gift cards. The company's mail passes SPF, DKIM, and enforced DMARC checks. Which control helps staff recognize that genuine executive mail carries a mark this message lacks?
options: BIMI, which shows the verified brand logo only beside authenticated company mail
Rate limiting, which slows the rate of fraudulent requests per sender
A captive portal, which requires sign-in before the message can be read using the tools and processes already in place for this purpose
Data loss prevention, which scans the message content for payment terms
explain: BIMI's verified logo appears only when SPF, DKIM, and enforced DMARC are in place, so its absence beside a spoof is a visible cue. DLP, rate limiting, and portals do not authenticate brand identity in the inbox.

q: A database server must accept connections from the application tier and from administrators using SSH, but a scan finds a debugging interface also listening. Under the approved baseline, what should happen to the debugging interface?
options: It should be removed or firewalled off, because the baseline approves only the services the role requires
It should be left running but moved to a nonstandard port number
It should be documented as an accepted exception with no further action on a recurring basis as part of normal operations
It should be restricted to the vendor's support hours each weekday
explain: The baseline for the role approves the application, SSH, and database paths — a leftover debugging interface is exactly the kind of service hardening removes. Moving or documenting it keeps an unapproved entry point alive.

q: Which control BEST prevents an attacker who steals one user's password from simply signing in from an unmanaged device on the internal network?
options: Secrets scanning of the network configuration files each night
Web content filtering blocking sign-in pages from unmanaged locations
802.1X port authentication combined with device checks before network admission
A wireless intrusion prevention system scanning the air for rogue clients before any other remediation or response steps are attempted
explain: 802.1X decides who and what may join the network at the port, so a password alone does not grant admission from an unmanaged device. The other controls watch traffic or content but do not gate network admission.

q: A retail chain finds rogue access points plugged into store networks by employees wanting better Wi-Fi. Which control detects and can shut down these unauthorized wireless devices?
options: A captive portal redirecting the rogue clients to a terms page
Port mirroring feeding store traffic to a central monitoring sensor with the results reviewed by the security team afterward
Wireless intrusion prevention monitoring the air and containing rogue access points
Network segmentation applied to the stores' point-of-sale systems
explain: WIPS watches for rogue access points and unauthorized clients and can contain them — the wireless perimeter problem described. Segmentation protects payment systems but does not detect or contain rogue radios.

q: A developer argues that a leaked API key in a repo is low risk because the repo is internal. Which response reflects the correct control strategy?
options: The key is safe as long as the repository requires a company login
The key can stay if the repository is excluded from internet indexing applied consistently rather than on a case-by-case basis
The key only needs rotation if an external party reports finding it
Secrets scanning should still block the key at commit, because internal repos leak and keys spread beyond them
explain: Secrets scanning exists because keys in repos spread — through forks, logs, and breaches — regardless of the repo's intended audience. Waiting for an external report or trusting the login gate leaves a live credential exposed.

q: An organization wants to stop employees from uploading source code to unapproved file-sharing sites. Which control inspects this outbound content and enforces the rule?
options: A firewall rule blocking the file-sharing category at the perimeter only
Full-disk encryption on developer workstations and build servers
Data loss prevention monitoring web uploads and other egress channels
An acceptable use policy acknowledged by employees each year
explain: DLP inspects content leaving through web, email, and removable media and blocks what policy forbids — here, source code to unapproved sites. A category block helps but misses other channels, and policy alone does not inspect content.

q: After a ransomware incident, leadership asks why the infected workstation could encrypt a department file share within minutes. Which missing control MOST allowed the spread?
options: The file share required only a password rather than a smart card and verify the result through the normal review process
Network segmentation between workstation and server zones was absent
The workstation's antivirus signatures were one day out of date
Users had not completed the annual phishing awareness module
explain: On a flat network, one compromised workstation reaches shares directly; segmentation would have filtered workstation-to-server traffic and slowed or stopped the spread. Signature freshness and training are layers, but reachability was the enabling condition.

q: During an incident, responders find an unmanaged device plugged into the network that no one can identify. Which underlying failure does this MOST directly reveal?
options: An asset inventory failure, because the organization did not know what it had on its network
A password policy failure, because the device used a weak credential
A vulnerability scanning failure, because the scanner missed one device across all affected systems in the environment
A logging failure, because the device generated no security alerts
explain: You cannot secure what you do not know you have; an unmanaged device on the network is an inventory failure first. Scanners scan the inventory's world, so the gap begins with asset management, not the scan itself.

q: A company is formalizing its asset life cycle. Which stage comes FIRST, before anything is purchased?
options: Maintenance, including patching and ongoing support tracking
Assignment and deployment, issuing the asset to its first owner as the primary response to the problem described
Planning and scoping, deciding what is needed and what good looks like
Disposal and decommissioning, including data sanitization
explain: The life cycle begins with planning and scoping — deciding what is needed before acquisition. Deployment, maintenance, and disposal all happen later, in that order.

q: Retired laptops containing customer data will be donated to a charity outside the organization. Which sanitization grade is MOST appropriate?
options: Clearing, because a simple reset defeats the recovery methods that matter here and document the outcome in the team's tracking system
No sanitization, because the charity signs a confidentiality agreement
Formatting the drives and reinstalling the operating system image
Destruction or purging, because the media is leaving organizational control with sensitive data
explain: Media leaving control with sensitive data calls for purging or destruction; clearing defeats only simple recovery and suits media staying inside the organization. A format and reinstall leaves recoverable data behind.

q: An SSD holding regulated data must be sanitized, and the drive is fully encrypted. Which purging method makes the data unrecoverable by destroying the key?
options: Cryptographic erasure, where destroying the encryption key makes the data unreadable
Deleting the partition table and creating a fresh file system
Overwriting the drive once with a pattern of zeros and ones
Degaussing the drive with a strong magnetic field until it demagnetizes using the tools and processes already in place for this purpose
explain: Cryptographic erasure purges by abandonment: the data stays encrypted and the destroyed key makes it unrecoverable, defeating laboratory recovery. Degaussing works on magnetic media, not SSDs, and overwriting or repartitioning is clearing-level at best.

q: An auditor asks for proof that 200 decommissioned drives were actually destroyed last quarter. Which artifact IS the disposal evidence in an audit?
options: The purchase order showing replacement drives were ordered on schedule
The help desk ticket showing the drives were collected from the offices
The certificate of destruction recording what was destroyed, by which method, and when
The inventory export listing the drives as retired in the asset register on a recurring basis as part of normal operations
explain: A certificate of destruction records what was destroyed, by which method, and when — in an audit, that certificate is the disposal. Collection tickets and register entries show handling, not verified destruction.

q: Magnetic backup tapes holding financial records need sanitization that defeats laboratory recovery before reuse outside the department. Which method fits magnetic media at the purging grade?
options: Degaussing, which destroys the magnetic patterns holding the data
Overwriting, which passes new data over the tapes a single time
Cryptographic erasure, which destroys the tapes' encryption keys
Incineration, which physically ends the tapes' existence entirely
explain: Degaussing is the classic purge for magnetic media, defeating laboratory recovery. Incineration is destruction rather than purging for reuse, and a single overwrite is clearing, which defeats only simple recovery.

q: A department buys laptops and records them in the inventory only when they are first repaired, months later. Which life cycle stage is being skipped at purchase time?
options: Planning and scoping, where the need for the laptops was evaluated
Maintenance, where patching and support are tracked over time
Disposal, where the laptops will eventually be sanitized and retired with the results reviewed by the security team afterward
Acquisition, where assets should be bought and recorded as they enter the organization
explain: Acquisition is when assets are bought and recorded; recording months later leaves a window where owned devices are invisible to every control that depends on the inventory. The other stages occur before or after this gap.

q: Each issued laptop should have a named person accountable for it. At which life cycle stage is the owner assigned?
options: Acquisition, when the purchase is approved and recorded
Assignment and deployment, when the asset is issued to its owner
Planning and scoping, when requirements are first defined
Disposal and decommissioning, when the asset leaves service applied consistently rather than on a case-by-case basis
explain: Assignment and deployment is when the asset is issued with an owner, creating accountability for its use and return. Planning defines needs and acquisition records the purchase, but neither issues the device.

q: A hospital's inventory covers laptops and servers but not its growing list of SaaS subscriptions and cloud accounts, where patient data now also lives. What is the risk of this gap?
options: The hospital will overspend on licenses because renewal dates are untracked
Auditors will object only to the inventory's formatting and completeness notes as a standing part of the organization's security operations
Assets outside the inventory escape the controls that depend on it, including scanning, access review, and disposal
Cloud accounts cannot hold regulated data, so the gap carries no real risk
explain: The modern inventory includes cloud accounts and SaaS subscriptions alongside hardware, software, and data. Anything outside it is invisible to vulnerability scanning, access review, and end-of-life handling — a control gap, not a paperwork issue.

q: A drive that held internal-only documents will be reused by another team inside the same company. Which sanitization grade is generally sufficient?
options: Purging by degaussing, because internal transfers require laboratory-grade erasure and verify the result through the normal review process
Destruction, because any reuse of storage media is prohibited
No sanitization, because both teams work for the same company
Clearing, because the media stays inside the organization and simple recovery is the concern
explain: Clearing — overwriting or resetting — defeats simple recovery and suits media staying inside the organization. Destruction wastes a reusable asset, and skipping sanitization leaves the prior team's data readable by the next.

q: Which inventory is described as the control underneath every other control in security operations?
options: The asset inventory covering hardware, software, data, cloud accounts, and SaaS subscriptions
The vulnerability scan schedule covering all production server subnets across all affected systems in the environment
The firewall rule base covering all permitted network communications
The incident response contact list covering all on-call team members
explain: Vulnerability scanners, access reviews, and incident response all work from the inventory's world. If an asset is not in the inventory, no downstream control reliably covers it.

q: A company shreds drives from its most sensitive systems and keeps certificates, but a regulator asks why one batch was only cleared before leaving for a recycler. What principle was violated?
options: The sanitization grade must match the data's sensitivity and who controls the media next
Clearing is acceptable whenever a recycler signs a handling agreement
Certificates are required only for media destroyed on company premises as the primary response to the problem described
All retired media must be retained for seven years before any disposal
explain: Sanitization is matched to sensitivity and next control: clearing suits media staying inside, while sensitive data leaving control requires purging or destruction. A recycler's agreement does not lower the grade the data demands.

q: An employee leaves the company, and her laptop is reassigned the same day without any processing. Which life cycle steps were MOST likely skipped?
options: Planning and scoping for the replacement employee's equipment needs
Maintenance and disposal processing — retrieving, sanitizing, and recording the asset before reassignment
Acquisition recording for the laptop when it was originally purchased and document the outcome in the team's tracking system
Decommissioning documentation for the building the employee worked in
explain: Reassignment without retrieval, sanitization, and recording skips the maintenance and end-of-assignment handling that keeps data from following the device to its next user. The laptop's original purchase record is not the issue.

q: What is the main purpose of an asset inventory?
options: To schedule conference rooms and shared equipment for employees
To know what hardware, software, data, and cloud assets the organization has so they can be secured
To record which employees have completed security awareness training
To calculate the resale value of equipment for the finance department using the tools and processes already in place for this purpose
explain: The inventory is the foundation of security operations: you cannot secure what you do not know you have. Finance valuation and training records serve other purposes and do not drive security controls.

q: A software audit finds dozens of unauthorized applications installed on workstations, some with known vulnerabilities. Which asset management practice BEST addresses this?
options: Quarterly password audits across all local workstation accounts
Network monitoring of workstation traffic during business hours
Hardware tagging of every workstation with a tamper-evident asset label on a recurring basis as part of normal operations
Software inventory and approved-application control tied to the asset register
explain: Software is an asset class in the inventory; tracking what is installed and enforcing an approved list addresses unauthorized applications directly. Hardware tags and traffic monitoring do not govern what software runs.

q: Data itself is an asset. A team discovers an old database export containing customer records on a file share nobody owns. Which asset management action comes FIRST?
options: Move the export to an encrypted folder and consider the matter closed
Assign the data an owner and record it in the inventory so it can be classified, protected, and eventually disposed of
Delete the export immediately without checking whether it is still needed before any other remediation or response steps are attempted
Copy the export to backup storage in case the original is corrupted
explain: Unowned data cannot be protected or disposed of properly; ownership and inventory recording come first so classification, protection, and retention decisions can follow. Deleting without review risks destroying a needed record, and moving it hides rather than manages it.

q: Which sequence correctly orders the asset life cycle?
options: Assignment and deployment, acquisition, planning and scoping, maintenance, disposal with the results reviewed by the security team afterward
Planning and scoping, acquisition, assignment and deployment, maintenance, disposal and decommissioning
Maintenance, acquisition, assignment and deployment, disposal, planning and scoping
Acquisition, planning and scoping, disposal, assignment and deployment, maintenance
explain: The life cycle runs planning and scoping first, then acquisition, assignment and deployment, maintenance, and finally disposal and decommissioning. Every other sequence places a stage where its inputs do not yet exist.

q: A decommissioned server's drives will be physically destroyed. Which methods are examples of destruction?
options: Degaussing the drives and returning them to the spare-parts shelf
Resetting the drives to factory defaults through the vendor utility applied consistently rather than on a case-by-case basis
Overwriting the drives with multiple passes of random data patterns
Shredding, incinerating, or disintegrating the media so it no longer exists as storage
explain: Destruction ends the question physically — shredding, incinerating, disintegrating. Overwriting is clearing, degaussing is purging for media that will not be reused as the same asset, and a factory reset is a form of clearing.

q: An organization keeps excellent hardware records but cannot say which business data resides on which systems. Why does this matter for disposal decisions?
options: Disposal law requires a data map before any hardware can be retired
Hardware cannot be decommissioned until its purchase price is recovered as a standing part of the organization's security operations
Sanitization grade is chosen from the data's sensitivity, so unknown data means the grade cannot be chosen correctly
Data location only matters for backup scheduling, not for disposal
explain: Clearing, purging, and destruction are selected by the sensitivity of the data and who controls the media next. Without knowing what data a device holds, the organization cannot match the grade — it will over-destroy cheap media or under-sanitize sensitive media.

q: Patch compliance is poor because many servers are missing from the patching tool's target list. Which asset practice fixes the root cause?
options: Reconciling the asset inventory with the patching tool so every known server is targeted
Patching the servers that are already in the tool more frequently
Excluding unpatched servers from the next compliance report
Extending patch deadlines so compliance percentages improve on paper and verify the result through the normal review process
explain: Maintenance depends on the inventory: scanners and patch tools work from the inventory's world. Reconciling the lists fixes coverage; deadline and reporting changes only disguise the gap.

q: A cloud storage account created for a finished project still holds client files two years later, unknown to the security team. Which practice would have prevented this?
options: Including cloud accounts in the asset inventory with owners and end-of-life review
Restricting cloud account creation to the finance department only
Encrypting the project files before uploading them to the account
Requiring stronger passwords on all cloud storage accounts at creation across all affected systems in the environment
explain: Cloud accounts and SaaS subscriptions belong in the inventory with owners, so finished projects get reviewed and decommissioned. Encryption and passwords protect the data but do not surface an forgotten account for disposal.

q: Two drives are retired the same week: one held public marketing files and stays in-house; the other held merger documents and goes to a recycler. Which pairing is correct?
options: Clear both drives, because a recycler agreement covers the merger documents
Clear the in-house marketing drive; purge or destroy the merger drive leaving organizational control
Destroy both drives, because all retired media must receive the same treatment as the primary response to the problem described
Purge the marketing drive and clear the merger drive to balance total cost
explain: Grade follows sensitivity and next control: clearing suffices for low-sensitivity media staying inside, while highly sensitive media leaving control requires purging or destruction. Uniform treatment either wastes assets or under-protects the merger data.

q: What does cryptographic erasure rely on to make data unrecoverable?
options: Physical shredding of the media into particles below a set size and document the outcome in the team's tracking system
The data being encrypted, with the encryption key destroyed so the data can never be read
Repeated overwriting of every sector with verified patterns
A magnetic field strong enough to randomize the storage media
