Search logs, EDR telemetry, and images across the environment for that hash to map every occurrence
explain: Hash-based hunting turns one indicator into an environment-wide scope map across telemetry sources. Recollection and footage cannot enumerate file occurrences.

q: Two copies of the same disk image produce different SHA-256 values during verification. What does this mean?
options: At least one copy no longer matches the acquired evidence, so it must not be relied on until the discrepancy is resolved against the custody record
The hashing tool needs recalibration, since hashes vary slightly between runs, and documented in the central system of record for audit purposes, under the direction of the accountable system owner
The image was compressed during copying, which normally changes the hash, using only the tools already approved for this environment, with findings reported to management at the next scheduled review

The original drive must be re-imaged immediately to create a matching pair, in line with the organization's stated retention requirements, whenever the associated account or system is used, from any location
explain: Hash verification is binary: a mismatch means the bits changed, and that copy's evidentiary value is broken. Hashes do not drift, and silent recompression of evidence is itself a handling failure.

q: A new security document states, at a high level, what must be true across the company and why it matters, and it is approved by senior management. Which type of governance artifact is this?
options: A formal policy that expresses management's intent for the organization
A technical standard that lists exact mandatory configuration settings
A step-by-step runbook written for the analyst performing a task
An external benchmark that collects consensus expert configuration advice
explain: A policy sits at the top of the document pyramid and states management's intent — what must be true and why. Standards carry the specific mandatory settings, runbooks carry task steps, and benchmarks come from outside bodies.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: An engineer needs the exact, mandatory TLS versions and cipher settings every web server must use. Which artifact should she consult?
options: A policy, because it lists the precise algorithms approved for production use
A standard, because it defines the specific mandatory settings that implement policy
A runbook, because it records the approved cipher list for each server build
A benchmark, because it is the internal document that mandates cipher settings across the whole server estate
explain: Standards are the specific, mandatory 'how' that implements a policy's intent, including configurations and algorithms. Policies stay at the level of intent, runbooks describe task steps, and benchmarks are external reference guides rather than internal mandates.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A desktop team is told that no workstation may be configured below a defined minimum security level, no matter who requests an exception. Which artifact establishes that floor?
options: A benchmark, because it sets the lowest configuration the company will tolerate in every department
A guideline, because it fixes the mandatory floor for every workstation build
A baseline, because it sets the minimum acceptable security level for the system
An advisory, because it warns administrators about minimum configuration levels
explain: A baseline is the minimum acceptable security level — the floor nobody configures below. Benchmarks are external consensus guides, guidelines are recommendations rather than mandates, and advisories warn about threats rather than set configuration floors.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company adopts the CIS Benchmarks to harden its servers. Why are these documents classified as benchmarks rather than standards?
options: They are mandatory internal documents written by the company's own security leadership team
They are step-by-step procedures written for the administrator performing a specific server task
They are management statements of intent that explain what must be true and the reasons behind it in its sector
They are consensus guides produced by an outside body that the organization chooses to adopt as a reference
explain: Benchmarks are consensus expert guides from outside bodies, such as CIS, that an organization adopts as its reference. Internal mandatory settings are standards, task steps are runbooks, and statements of management intent are policies.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: During an incident at 3 a.m., a junior analyst must rebuild a compromised mail relay in the correct order without improvising. Which artifact serves her best?
options: A runbook containing the step-by-step operational instructions for that specific rebuild task
A policy explaining why the mail relay must meet the organization's security requirements as written
A benchmark describing how peer organizations typically configure their mail relays
A standard listing the mandatory encryption settings that apply to all company servers
explain: A runbook gives step-by-step operational instructions for a specific task, written for the person doing it under pressure. Policies explain intent, benchmarks describe external consensus practice, and standards list settings without sequencing a task.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A network engineer wants the authoritative open document that defines how a protocol actually works so two vendors' products interoperate. Which artifact is that?
options: An implementation guide published by one vendor for its own product line
An RFC, the open document series that defines how internet technologies work
An internal standard that mandates which protocol versions the company allows
A bulletin issued to warn customers about an actively exploited protocol flaw
explain: RFCs are the open documents that define how internet technologies actually work. Vendor implementation guides cover one product line, internal standards mandate what a company allows, and bulletins warn about current threats.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A vendor issues an urgent notice warning customers about a newly exploited vulnerability and urging an immediate workaround. What is this document?
options: A baseline that resets the minimum security level for the affected product line
A policy that states management's long-term intent for vulnerability management
An advisory or bulletin that warns about a current threat and how to respond to it
A runbook that walks an analyst through the complete rebuild of the affected system
explain: Advisories and bulletins are authority or vendor guidance that warns about current threats and how to apply requirements. Baselines set configuration floors, policies state long-term intent, and runbooks sequence a specific operational task.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A firewall rule set follows the corporate policy but conflicts with the mandatory standard for administrative access. Which document governs the engineer's decision, and why?
options: The policy, because a broad statement of intent always overrides any specific technical requirement
The benchmark, because external consensus guidance outranks every internal document in a conflict
The runbook, because operational instructions written for a task supersede both policy and standards in a conflict
The standard, because standards carry the specific mandatory requirements that put policy into practice
explain: Standards contain the specific, mandatory how that implements policy, so a compliant build must satisfy the standard's concrete requirements. A policy's broad intent does not override its own implementing standard, and benchmarks and runbooks do not outrank either document.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A document recommends, but does not require, that administrators review firewall logs weekly, and it allows local judgment. This is best described as which artifact?
options: A guideline, because it offers recommended practice that staff may adapt to their situation
A standard, because any written security expectation is automatically mandatory for staff for all staff
A baseline, because it describes the minimum review activity the company will accept
A policy, because management intent documents always use flexible, advisory wording
explain: Guidelines recommend practice without mandating it, leaving room for judgment. Standards are mandatory, baselines set a minimum acceptable level rather than a suggestion, and policies state binding management intent.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Which statement best distinguishes a standard from a policy?
options: A standard is written by an outside body; a policy is written by the company's own auditors under company rules
A standard gives the specific mandatory requirements; a policy states management's intent and direction
A standard applies only to cloud systems; a policy applies only to on-premises systems
A standard is optional guidance; a policy contains the exact settings engineers must apply
explain: Policies state what must be true and why — management's intent — while standards supply the specific, mandatory how. Standards are internal documents, they are binding rather than optional, and neither is limited to one environment.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A security team wants a vendor's detailed explanation of how to apply a regulatory requirement inside that vendor's platform. Which artifact should they request?
options: A request for comments that defines the underlying protocol the platform is built on
A corporate policy that states the company's intent for meeting the regulation
An implementation guide that explains how to apply the requirements in that platform
A risk register entry that records the compliance gap as an organizational risk
explain: Implementation guides explain how to apply requirements in practice, often for a specific platform. RFCs define protocols, policies state internal intent, and a register entry records a risk rather than explaining how to meet a requirement.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company writes a policy requiring encrypted storage, then discovers teams interpret 'encrypted' four different ways. Which artifact most directly removes the ambiguity?
options: A second policy restating management's commitment to protecting stored information once again
An advisory warning teams that weak encryption is being exploited by attackers
A benchmark subscription so teams can compare themselves with peer organizations
A standard naming the approved algorithms, key lengths, and settings teams must use
explain: Ambiguity about the mandatory 'how' is resolved by a standard that names approved algorithms, key lengths, and settings. Restating intent in another policy keeps the ambiguity, an advisory warns rather than specifies, and a benchmark is a reference, not the internal mandate.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: An auditor asks who is accountable for approving security policies and accepting the risk when a policy cannot be met. Which concept answers her?
options: Management oversight, because only management can set direction and accept risk on the business's behalf
The security operations team, because it monitors the environment around the clock every day on every shift
The internal audit function, because it authorizes the policies it will later test against
The vendor management office, because it tracks every third party the company depends on
explain: Governance rests on management oversight: leadership approves policy and alone can accept risk for the business. Operations executes controls, audit must stay independent of what it tests, and vendor management covers third parties, not enterprise policy approval.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A policy has not been reviewed in five years, and the business has moved to cloud services the policy never mentions. What is the governance concern?
options: The policy is too old to be legally binding, so staff may ignore it until it is replaced
The policy lifecycle has failed — artifacts must be reviewed and updated as the organization and its risks change
The policy should be converted into a runbook so cloud teams can follow its steps directly, step by step for each team
The policy's age is irrelevant as long as the original approval signature is still on file
explain: Governance artifacts live in a lifecycle of creation, review, and update; a policy that no longer matches the environment stops guiding behavior. Age alone does not void a policy, converting it to a runbook changes its purpose, and a signature does not cure stale content.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A business unit cannot meet a mandatory standard for a legacy application and asks to operate out of compliance for six months. What is the correct governance path?
options: Quietly note the deviation in the team's wiki so the next engineer understands the situation
Ask the standard's author to delete the requirement so the application becomes compliant again to speed things up
Request a documented exception with a compensating control, an owner, and an expiry date approved by management
Treat the benchmark for the platform as permission to ignore the internal mandatory standard
explain: Exceptions are governance decisions: documented, time-bound, owned, paired with compensating controls, and approved by management, who owns the risk. An informal note hides the risk, deleting requirements defeats the standard, and an external benchmark cannot waive an internal mandate.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: New hires must confirm they have read and understood the acceptable use rules before receiving accounts. What does this acknowledgment accomplish for the program?
options: It transfers legal responsibility for any misuse from the organization entirely onto the employee in all future cases
It replaces the need for technical controls that monitor how systems are actually used
It guarantees that employees will never misuse the systems they have been given access to
It creates evidence that expectations were communicated, which supports enforcement and later investigations
explain: A signed acknowledgment proves the rules were communicated, which underpins fair enforcement and investigations. It does not transfer all responsibility, replace monitoring controls, or guarantee future behavior.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A team is choosing between writing its own server-hardening reference from scratch and adopting an established external one. What is the main advantage of adopting the external reference?
options: It reflects broad expert consensus, so the organization starts from vetted practice instead of reinventing it
It becomes legally binding on the organization the moment any employee downloads a copy from the publisher's website
It removes the need to write any internal standards for the systems it happens to cover
It guarantees the hardened servers will pass every future audit without further changes
explain: Benchmarks such as the CIS Benchmarks package consensus expert practice an organization can adopt as its reference point. Adoption does not make them law, internal standards are still needed to mandate settings, and no reference guarantees future audit results.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A CISO wants one document that tells a database administrator exactly which steps to follow, in order, when rotating encryption keys on a production system. Policies and standards already exist. What is missing?
options: A benchmark, because the administrator needs consensus guidance from an outside expert body for routine work
A runbook, because the ordered operational steps for that specific task have not been written down
A second standard, because the existing standard failed to include a narrative procedure
An advisory, because key rotation is usually announced through vendor threat bulletins
explain: Runbooks hold the ordered, step-by-step instructions for a specific operational task. Benchmarks give external consensus settings, standards state mandatory requirements rather than task sequences, and advisories warn about threats.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Which artifact would a change advisory board most likely consult to confirm a proposed server build meets the company's mandatory configuration requirements?
options: The policy, which explains the reasoning behind the company's configuration philosophy
The runbook library, which describes how previous builds were performed step by step
The standard for that platform, which lists the mandatory settings every build must satisfy
The vendor registry, which lists the suppliers involved in delivering the server hardware for the build
explain: Mandatory configuration requirements live in standards. Policies explain intent and reasoning, runbooks describe how a task was performed rather than what is required, and the vendor registry tracks suppliers, not build requirements.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Which of the following is the BEST example of a baseline in a security program?
options: The executive statement explaining why protecting customer data matters to the company overall
The consensus hardening guide published by an external center for internet security
The ordered checklist an analyst follows when wiping and reissuing a returned laptop
The minimum security configuration that every laptop must meet before it joins the network
explain: A baseline is the minimum acceptable security level — here, the floor every laptop must meet. The executive statement is a policy, the external consensus guide is a benchmark, and the ordered checklist is a runbook.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A regulator asks how the company knows its written security rules reflect current threats rather than the threats of a decade ago. Which practice best answers the question?
options: Regularly reviewing policies and standards against current advisories, bulletins, and the evolving risk picture
Pointing to the original approval date, which proves the documents were valid when they were written by the board
Converting every policy into a benchmark so external bodies become responsible for its accuracy
Deleting any policy older than two years, regardless of whether its content is still accurate
explain: Ongoing review against current advisories, bulletins, and risk keeps artifacts aligned with today's threats. An old approval date proves nothing about currency, external bodies do not own internal documents, and age-based deletion discards still-valid rules.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A hospital's policy says patient data must be protected; its standard requires AES-256 at rest; its baseline forbids unencrypted portable media. A nurse asks which document tells her the encryption algorithm. The answer is:
options: The policy, because it is the highest document and therefore holds every technical detail in full detail
The standard, because it specifies the mandatory technical requirements that implement the policy
The baseline, because minimum levels always include the approved algorithm list
The runbook, because algorithm choices are recorded as steps in operational procedures
explain: Standards carry the specific mandatory requirements — algorithms, key lengths, settings — that implement policy intent. Policies stay general, baselines state minimum levels, and runbooks sequence tasks rather than define approved cryptography.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: An organization publishes a single internal page that collects current threat warnings from its vendors and government sources for administrators. What are these collected documents?
options: Baselines that reset the minimum acceptable configuration for each affected platform on each affected platform
Standards that mandate the exact response steps for every newly announced threat
Advisories and bulletins that warn about current threats and explain how to apply requirements
Policies that restate management's intent in response to each emerging threat
explain: Advisories and bulletins are the warning channel from vendors and authorities about current threats and applying requirements. They do not reset baselines, mandate response standards, or restate policy intent for each threat.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Two departments disagree: one follows the corporate standard, the other follows a well-known external benchmark that is slightly stricter. The corporate standard is met either way. What is the governance-correct view?
options: The benchmark automatically replaces the internal standard whenever the two documents differ at all
The department following the benchmark is noncompliant because it deviated from the internal document
Both departments must stop work until management rewrites the standard to match the benchmark exactly, halting all deployments in the meantime
Meeting the internal standard is the compliance requirement; the stricter benchmark is an adopted reference, not a competing mandate
explain: Internal standards define what compliance means inside the organization; benchmarks are adopted references that inform them. A benchmark does not silently replace a standard, exceeding a standard is not noncompliance, and no rewrite is required when the mandate is already met.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A security program is being built from nothing. In which order do the core artifacts normally come into existence?
options: Policy first, then the standards that implement it, then baselines and procedures built on those standards
Runbooks first, then benchmarks, and only then the policies that describe what the runbooks do
Baselines first, then policies, because a configuration floor must exist before intent is stated
Benchmarks first, because external guidance must be approved before any internal document is written and formally signed
explain: The document pyramid flows downward: policy states intent, standards make it mandatory and specific, and baselines and procedures build on the standards. Runbooks and benchmarks support the structure but do not precede the policy that authorizes the program.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A risk team identifies a new threat, analyzes its likelihood and impact, chooses a treatment, and schedules a review next quarter. Which statement best describes what they are doing?
options: Completing a one-time project, because a risk only needs to be assessed when it is first discovered
Working the risk management loop — identify, analyze, treat, and keep monitoring, under management oversight
Performing a compliance audit, because any structured review of risk is classified as an audit activity in the program
Transferring the risk, because documenting a threat in a register shifts its impact to another party
explain: Risk management is a continuous loop of identification, analysis, treatment, and monitoring, with management owning the decisions. It is not one-time, it is distinct from audit, and recording a risk does not transfer it.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A web store's ordering system is valued at $200,000. An outage-and-corruption event would destroy 25% of that value. What is the single loss expectancy (SLE)?
options: $25,000, because SLE equals the asset value divided by the exposure factor of 0.25
$80,000, because SLE equals the asset value multiplied by an exposure factor of 0.40 when worked out in full
$50,000, because SLE equals the asset value multiplied by the exposure factor of 0.25
$125,000, because SLE equals the asset value minus a loss estimate of $75,000
explain: SLE = asset value × exposure factor = $200,000 × 0.25 = $50,000, the cost of the event happening once. The other figures come from dividing, using the wrong factor, or subtracting an unrelated amount.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A system has an SLE of $40,000 and the event is expected once every four years, giving an ARO of 0.25. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE)?
options: $40,000, because the ALE always equals the SLE whenever the event is rare in any given year
$160,000, because ALE equals the SLE divided by the ARO of 0.25
$2,500, because ALE equals the SLE multiplied by an ARO of 0.0625
$10,000, because ALE equals the SLE of $40,000 multiplied by the ARO of 0.25
explain: ALE = SLE × ARO = $40,000 × 0.25 = $10,000 per year on average. Equating ALE with SLE ignores frequency, dividing inflates the figure, and 0.0625 is not the stated rate of occurrence.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: An asset is worth $1,000,000 with an exposure factor of 10%, and the event is expected twice a year. What is the ALE?
options: $200,000, because the SLE is $100,000 and multiplying by an ARO of 2 gives $200,000
$100,000, because the ALE equals the SLE regardless of how often the event occurs in a typical year
$20,000, because the SLE is $10,000 and multiplying by an ARO of 2 gives $20,000
$50,000, because the SLE is $100,000 and the ARO should be treated as 0.5 here
explain: SLE = $1,000,000 × 0.10 = $100,000; ALE = $100,000 × 2 = $200,000. Ignoring the ARO understates the annual figure, a $10,000 SLE uses the wrong exposure factor, and twice a year means an ARO of 2, not 0.5.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A flood is expected to strike a warehouse roughly once every four years. What is the annualized rate of occurrence (ARO)?
options: 4.0, because the number of years between events is used directly as the rate
0.25, because the event occurs on average one-quarter of a time per year
0.40, because the rate is calculated as the event's impact percentage per year
1.25, because a small allowance is added for the uncertainty in the estimate
explain: ARO expresses events per year: once every four years is 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25. Using 4.0 inverts the relationship, 0.40 confuses rate with impact, and uncertainty padding is not part of the ARO definition.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A database is valued at $800,000. A corruption incident is estimated to cause $200,000 in losses. What is the exposure factor (EF)?
options: 20%, because EF equals the loss divided by an assumed asset value of $1,000,000
40%, because EF is estimated from the likelihood of the incident occurring each year
25%, because EF equals the loss of $200,000 divided by the asset value of $800,000
75%, because EF equals the portion of the asset expected to survive the incident
explain: EF = loss ÷ asset value = $200,000 ÷ $800,000 = 0.25, or 25%. The other answers use a wrong asset value, confuse EF with likelihood, or describe the surviving portion rather than the portion lost.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A risk has an ALE of $90,000. The only available safeguard costs $120,000 per year and would eliminate the loss entirely. Based on the quantitative analysis alone, what is the sound conclusion?
options: The safeguard should be bought immediately, because any control that eliminates a risk is worth its price regardless of its cost
The safeguard is justified, because an SLE above $90,000 always requires a control regardless of cost
The ALE must be recalculated, because a control's cost is added to the ALE before comparing them
The safeguard is not justified on ALE grounds alone, because it costs more per year than the expected annual loss
explain: Controls are priced against ALE: paying $120,000 a year to remove a $90,000-a-year expected loss fails the quantitative test by itself, whatever other justifications might exist. Elimination alone does not justify any price, and control cost is compared with ALE, not added to it.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A risk carries an ALE of $60,000. A control costing $20,000 per year would reduce the ALE to $15,000. What is the annual value of implementing the control?
options: $25,000, because the $45,000 reduction in ALE minus the $20,000 control cost leaves $25,000
$45,000, because the full reduction in ALE is counted without subtracting the control's cost
$5,000, because the reduced ALE of $15,000 minus the control cost gives the final figure
$60,000, because the value of a control always equals the original ALE of the risk it treats
explain: Value = (ALE before − ALE after) − control cost = ($60,000 − $15,000) − $20,000 = $25,000 per year. Counting the full $45,000 ignores cost, the $5,000 figure subtracts the wrong pair, and original ALE alone is not the control's value.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A laptop fleet is valued at $50,000, and theft of a single batch would expose 40% of that value. What is the SLE for the theft event?
options: $40,000, because SLE equals the exposure factor expressed directly as a dollar amount
$20,000, because SLE equals the asset value of $50,000 multiplied by the exposure factor of 0.40
$12,500, because SLE equals the asset value multiplied by an exposure factor of 0.25
$30,000, because SLE equals the asset value minus the $20,000 portion expected to remain once the loss has occurred
explain: SLE = $50,000 × 0.40 = $20,000. The exposure factor is a proportion, not a dollar figure; 0.25 is not the stated factor; and SLE measures the loss, not what remains afterward.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company buys cyber insurance so that a breach's financial impact falls largely on the insurer. Which risk response is this?
options: Avoidance, because the company no longer has to think about the risk at all
Mitigation, because purchasing insurance directly reduces the chance of a breach
Transfer, because the financial impact of the risk is shifted to another party
Acceptance, because the company is proceeding with the risky activity unchanged
explain: Transfer shifts the financial impact — insurance is the classic example. The risky activity continues, so it is not avoidance; insurance does not itself lower breach likelihood, so it is not mitigation; and acceptance means proceeding without such a shift.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A retailer decides to stop storing card numbers entirely and let a payment processor handle all transactions, removing the risk from its own systems. Which response is this?
options: Transfer, because a third party is now involved somewhere in the payment process
Mitigation, because a control was applied to reduce the risk to an acceptable level
Acceptance, because the retailer has decided the risk is within its stated appetite
Avoidance, because the organization stops the activity that carries the risk
explain: Avoidance means ending the activity that carries the risk — here, no longer storing card numbers at all. A processor's involvement alone is not transfer of this risk, no control reduced a retained activity, and acceptance would mean keeping the storage and proceeding.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: After adding controls, a team finds the remaining risk is small, documented, and formally signed off by the business owner. What is this remaining risk called?
options: Residual risk — the risk that survives treatment and is accepted by leadership
Inherent risk — the risk measured before any controls were applied to it
Transferred risk — the risk whose impact now sits with an outside party
Zero risk — the state every treatment plan is expected to reach eventually in the end
explain: Residual risk is what survives treatment; it never reaches zero, and leadership's sign-off on it is the point. Inherent risk is the pre-control measure, transferred risk has been shifted to another party, and zero risk is not an achievable state.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A risk register entry shows a high inherent risk score, the controls applied, and a much lower current score with a named owner and review date. Which pair of concepts does the entry demonstrate?
options: Single loss expectancy before controls and annualized loss expectancy after the controls in the analysis
Inherent risk before controls and residual risk after controls, tracked as a living record
Risk appetite before controls and risk transfer after the controls were applied
Exposure factor before controls and annualized rate of occurrence after the controls
explain: The register contrasts inherent risk (before treatment) with residual risk (after treatment) and keeps both under review with an owner. SLE/ALE are loss calculations, appetite is a leadership threshold rather than a before/after score, and EF/ARO are inputs to the math, not register states.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Who has the authority to accept a residual risk that exceeds the security team's recommended threshold?
options: The security analyst who discovered the risk, because she understands it best
The internal auditor, because audit independence includes approving exceptions
Management, because only management can accept risk on behalf of the business
The insurance provider, because it prices the risk the organization carries
explain: Risk acceptance is a business decision, and only management can accept risk on the business's behalf. Analysts assess and recommend, auditors must remain independent of decisions they later review, and insurers price transferred risk rather than accept an organization's internal risk.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A leadership team states it will accept minor operational risks but has no tolerance for risks that expose customer records. What have they defined?
options: The organization's risk register — the living record of its identified risks and owners and treatments
The organization's residual risk — the exposure that remains after controls are applied
The organization's exposure factor — the proportion of asset value a threat can destroy
The organization's risk appetite — how much and what kinds of risk it is willing to accept
explain: Risk appetite is leadership's stated willingness to accept risk, and it frames every treatment decision. The register records individual risks, residual risk is what remains after treatment, and exposure factor is a number used in loss calculations.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Two risks are plotted on a heat map: one is likely but low-impact, the other is rare but catastrophic. What does the heat map help decision-makers do?
options: Compare likelihood against impact visually so treatment priority reflects both dimensions together
Calculate the exact dollar loss each risk will cause over the next twelve months precisely to the nearest dollar
Eliminate the need for a risk register by replacing it with a single color-coded chart
Prove to auditors that both risks have already been treated to an acceptable level
explain: A risk matrix or heat map plots likelihood against impact so priorities weigh both dimensions — a rare catastrophe may outrank a frequent nuisance. It does not produce dollar figures (that is quantitative analysis), replace the register, or prove treatment has happened.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A team scores risks using expert judgment and categories like high, medium, and low instead of dollar figures. Which analysis type are they using?
options: Quantitative analysis, which expresses every risk as a calculated dollar amount for each risk
Qualitative analysis, which ranks risk by judgment and category rather than by money
Actuarial analysis, which prices risk using an insurer's historical loss tables
Deterministic analysis, which guarantees the outcome of each identified risk
explain: Qualitative analysis uses expert judgment and descriptive scales such as high/medium/low. Quantitative analysis assigns monetary values like SLE and ALE; the other two options are not the standard contrast the exam draws.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: When is quantitative analysis MOST appropriate for a risk decision?
options: When the team has no historical data and must rely entirely on expert opinion instead
When the risk involves reputation only and no financial estimate can be attached to it in any form at all
When reliable asset values, loss estimates, and occurrence data exist to support the calculation
When a decision is needed within the hour and no numbers of any kind are available
explain: Quantitative analysis needs credible numbers — asset value, exposure factor, and occurrence rate — to produce a meaningful ALE. Where data is absent or the impact is purely reputational, qualitative judgment is the honest method, and a rushed decision cannot manufacture the missing inputs.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A risk owner reviews the register monthly and notices a vendor-related risk's likelihood has doubled since the last review. What does this illustrate?
options: Risk avoidance, because noticing a change in likelihood means the activity must now stop
A gap analysis, because comparing two register entries is the definition of that activity the security team performs
Risk transference, because the risk involves a vendor and therefore belongs to the vendor
Continuous monitoring — risks change after treatment, so the register is revisited rather than filed away
explain: Risk management keeps watching after treatment; a changed likelihood updates the analysis and possibly the treatment. Nothing has been avoided or transferred by the observation itself, and comparing register entries over time is monitoring, not a framework gap analysis.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A project proposes a feature that would create a risk clearly outside the stated risk appetite, with no available control. What is the correct outcome?
options: The activity should not proceed in that form — appetite is the boundary management set for exactly this decision
The security team should accept the risk itself so the project is not delayed by escalation
The risk should be recorded in the register and the project allowed to proceed without changes without any changes at all
The feature should be insured, which automatically brings any risk inside the stated appetite
explain: Risk appetite is management's boundary: activity that cannot be brought inside it should not proceed as designed. Analysts cannot accept business risk, recording a risk is not permission to exceed appetite, and insurance does not redefine what leadership said it would tolerate.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A safeguard costing $15,000 per year would prevent most of a loss whose ALE is $50,000. A second proposal costs $80,000 per year for the same risk. Which analysis is correct?
options: Both safeguards are justified, because any control costing less than the asset value is worthwhile in every such case
The $15,000 safeguard is justified on its face; the $80,000 one needs other justifications beyond the ALE comparison
Neither safeguard is justified, because controls must cost less than the single loss expectancy
The $80,000 safeguard is better, because spending more on a control always reduces risk further
explain: ALE is the number controls are priced against: $15,000 against a $50,000 annual expected loss makes sense on its face, while $80,000 exceeds the expected loss and needs other justification. Asset value and SLE are not the comparison figure, and higher spend does not automatically mean proportionally lower risk.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Which item belongs in a well-maintained risk register?
options: The personal contact details of every employee who might be affected by it
The complete packet capture proving the risk was observed on the network
The risk description, its owner, its score, and the treatment chosen for it
The vendor's full contract, attached so the register doubles as a contract file
explain: The register is the living record of risks, owners, scores, and treatments. Personal contact lists, raw packet captures, and full contracts live in their own systems; the register references the risk and its handling, not every underlying artifact.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company decides a low-impact risk is acceptable and proceeds with the activity, documenting the decision. Which risk response is this?
options: Mitigation — applying a control that lowers the likelihood of the risk occurring
Avoidance — ending the activity that gives rise to the risk in the first place
Transfer — shifting the financial consequences of the risk to an insurance company at the outset
Acceptance — proceeding with the activity, eyes open, within the stated risk appetite
explain: Acceptance means proceeding deliberately, with the decision documented and inside appetite. Mitigation applies controls, avoidance ends the activity, and transfer shifts the financial impact to another party.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A risk was accepted last year when it was low-impact. The business has since built its flagship product on the affected system. What should happen to that acceptance?
options: It should be revisited, because the impact side of the risk has materially changed since acceptance
It stands permanently, because an acceptance decision can never be reopened once it is signed
It converts automatically into a transfer, because the system is now important to the business over time
It should be deleted from the register, because accepted risks no longer require any tracking
explain: Acceptance is conditional on the facts at the time; a material change in impact reopens the analysis through the monitoring loop. Signatures do not freeze risk forever, importance does not transfer anything, and accepted risks stay tracked precisely so changes like this are caught.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A team applies encryption, access reviews, and monitoring to reduce the chance and impact of a database breach, and keeps operating the database. Which response is this?
options: Avoidance, because strong controls mean the risky activity has effectively been stopped
Mitigation, because controls were applied to lower a risk the organization still carries
Acceptance, because operating the database means the team agreed to carry the full risk
Transfer, because several different controls were combined to treat the same single risk
explain: Mitigation applies controls to lower likelihood or impact while the activity continues. The database still operates, so nothing was avoided; controls were added, so the full untreated risk was not simply accepted; and combining controls is not transfer, which requires shifting impact to another party.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: What is the primary purpose of assigning a named owner to each risk in the register?
options: To make that person personally liable for any loss the risk eventually causes the company
To allow the risk to be removed from the register once ownership has been assigned
To make one accountable person responsible for monitoring the risk and driving its treatment
To transfer the risk to that employee in the same way insurance transfers financial impact in full
explain: Ownership creates accountability for watching the risk and executing its treatment. It does not create personal financial liability, remove the risk from tracking, or transfer the risk — transfer shifts impact to an outside party such as an insurer.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A firm's quantitative analysis shows a control saves $30,000 in ALE for $10,000 a year, but the risk also involves potential regulatory sanctions the model cannot price. What is the best decision process?
options: Follow the numbers alone, because a positive ALE comparison settles every aspect of the decision of the decision being made
Discard the analysis entirely, because one unpriced factor makes all of the numbers meaningless
Delay the decision indefinitely until the regulatory impact can be expressed as an exact figure
Use the quantitative result as one input and weigh the unpriced regulatory impact qualitatively before deciding
explain: Good risk decisions combine methods: the ALE math informs the choice, and impacts the model cannot price — sanctions, reputation — are weighed qualitatively. Numbers alone ignore real exposure, one gap does not void the whole analysis, and indefinite delay is itself an unmanaged risk decision.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Which sequence correctly orders the risk management process?
options: Identify risks, analyze them, treat them, then monitor and review on an ongoing basis
Treat risks, identify them, monitor them, and analyze them only if an incident occurs
Accept all risks first, then identify which ones should have been treated differently
Analyze risks, insure them, delete the register, and repeat the cycle every five years
explain: The loop runs identify → analyze → treat → monitor, continuously, under management oversight. Treating before identifying is impossible, blanket acceptance skips analysis, and deleting the register destroys the record the loop depends on.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A hospital keeps a risky legacy imaging system running because replacing it would interrupt patient care, and it adds network isolation and monitoring instead. How should this be characterized?
options: A pure avoidance, because isolation means the legacy system is no longer really in use
A mitigation paired with management's acceptance of the residual risk that remains after isolation
A transfer, because the monitoring tools were purchased from an outside security vendor
A policy violation, because legacy systems may never be operated under any circumstances that is still running
explain: The organization mitigated with isolation and monitoring, and management accepts the residual risk that remains — the common real-world combination. The system is still in use, buying tools is not transfer, and legacy operation is a governed risk decision, not an automatic violation.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company's risk analysis shows a supplier outage risk with an SLE of $75,000 and an ARO of 0.4. Leadership asks what annual figure should be used when pricing a backup supplier. What is the ALE?
options: $75,000, because the ALE always equals the SLE whenever a supplier contract is involved in the analysis
$18,750, because ALE equals the SLE multiplied by an ARO of 0.25 instead of the stated rate of 0.4
$150,000, because ALE equals the SLE divided by the ARO of 0.4 and then adjusted for the contract term
$30,000, because ALE equals the SLE of $75,000 multiplied by the ARO of 0.4
explain: ALE = SLE x ARO = $75,000 x 0.4 = $30,000 per year, the figure a backup supplier's cost should be priced against. The $75,000 figure ignores how often the event occurs, $18,750 uses the wrong rate, and dividing by the ARO inflates the number instead of annualizing it.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company exploring a new market first wants to learn what solutions and capabilities exist before committing to any purchase. Which procurement document should it issue?
options: A request for quote, which asks vendors to name a price for an exact specification
An expression of interest, which asks which vendors are interested in doing the work
A request for information, which asks vendors what exists and what they are able to do
A request for proposal, which asks vendors to propose a solution to a defined problem for the company
explain: An RFI gathers information about what exists and what vendors can do, early in the process. An RFQ prices an exact specification, an EOI gauges interest, and an RFP solicits proposed solutions to a stated problem.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Before shortlisting suppliers, a government agency wants to know simply which firms are interested in performing a large facilities contract. Which document fits?
options: A request for information, which asks vendors to describe the solutions that exist
A request for proposal, which asks vendors to design a solution to the problem
A request for quote, which asks vendors to price a precisely defined specification
An expression of interest, which asks who is interested in taking on the work
explain: An EOI asks the threshold question — who is interested in this work? An RFI explores what exists, an RFP solicits solutions, and an RFQ prices an exact specification.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A hospital describes its patient-scheduling problem and invites vendors to design and propose how they would solve it. Which document is this?
options: A request for proposal, which asks vendors to propose a solution to the stated problem
A request for quote, which asks vendors to price a solution the hospital already designed
A request for information, which asks vendors only what products exist in the market
An expression of interest, which asks vendors only whether the work interests them
explain: An RFP presents a problem and asks vendors to propose a solution. An RFQ assumes the specification is already fixed and asks only for price, an RFI explores the market, and an EOI only gauges interest.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company knows the exact laptop model, quantity, and configuration it wants and only needs competing prices. Which document should it issue?
options: A request for proposal, which asks vendors to invent a solution to a business problem from scratch
A request for quote, which asks vendors to name their price for the exact specification
An expression of interest, which asks vendors whether they want to participate at all
A request for information, which asks vendors to explain what products are available
explain: An RFQ is used when the specification is exact and only the price is in question. An RFP seeks designed solutions, an EOI gauges interest, and an RFI explores what exists — all earlier or broader steps than pricing a fixed spec.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A procurement team receives four documents: one explores the market, one gauges interest, one solicits designed solutions, and one prices a fixed spec. In the typical sequence, which comes last?
options: The request for information, because market exploration is always the final procurement step
The expression of interest, because confirming interest happens after contracts are negotiated are signed
The request for quote, because pricing an exact specification happens once the solution is settled
The request for proposal, because proposed solutions are evaluated after prices are finalized
explain: The usual flow narrows over time: RFI explores, EOI gauges interest, RFP solicits solutions, and RFQ prices the settled specification last. Exploration and interest checks belong at the front of the process, and proposals precede final pricing.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A cloud contract promises 99.9% uptime and one-hour response to critical incidents, with monthly reports against those targets. What are these targets called?
options: Service-level exceptions — the conditions under which the vendor may set the contract's terms aside entirely
Vendor registry entries — the internal records of what the vendor is allowed to access
Risk appetite statements — leadership's tolerance for the vendor failing to perform
Service-level objectives — measurable targets that vendor performance is reported against
explain: SLOs are the measurable targets — uptime, response time — that make vendor performance checkable rather than impressionistic, and they are reported against regularly. The other options name records or tolerances, not performance targets.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A vendor meets its contract's overall service-level agreement but consistently misses the specific one-hour critical-response target inside it. Why does the distinction matter?
options: The specific target is an SLO; missing it is a measurable performance failure even if the broader agreement looks satisfied
It does not matter, because an agreement cannot contain targets more specific than its own headline terms that a contract can possibly contain
The vendor is in breach of the vendor registry, which is the document that sets response-time targets
The target was only an RFI response, so it stopped being binding when the contract was signed
explain: Contracts turn promises into measurable SLOs; a missed SLO is a concrete, reportable failure regardless of the agreement's overall appearance. Specific targets inside an agreement are exactly how performance is enforced — they are not registry entries or pre-contract conversation.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A security team needs a single internal record of every vendor the company uses, what each one touches, and who owns each relationship. What should they maintain?
options: A risk register, which records organizational risks rather than the vendor inventory
A vendor registry that tracks who the vendors are and what they have access to
A runbook library, which stores the procedures used when a vendor system fails
A benchmark collection, which stores the external guides each vendor follows
explain: The vendor registry tracks who the vendors are and what they touch — the inventory the third-party program runs on. The risk register records risks, runbooks hold procedures, and benchmarks are external guidance documents.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A SaaS product stores all customer data in a proprietary format with no export function, and leaving would mean abandoning years of records. What is this trap called?
options: Vendor consolidation — the deliberate strategy of reducing the number of suppliers used
Service-level drift — the gradual decline of a vendor's performance against its targets
Vendor lock-in — leaving has become so expensive that renewal is effectively compulsory
Supply chain diversity — dependence on several vendors for the same critical function
explain: Vendor lock-in arises from proprietary formats and missing export paths that make exit prohibitively costly, shifting pricing power to the vendor. It is assessed before signing, when avoiding it is still cheap — the other terms describe different vendor-management concepts.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: When is vendor lock-in cheapest to address, according to sound third-party risk practice?
options: At renewal time, when the vendor is most eager to keep the contract and will concede anything to keep the business
After migration begins, when the true cost of leaving can finally be measured with precision
During an incident, when the vendor's support team is fully engaged with the account
Before signing, by requiring export paths and standard formats while the organization still has leverage
explain: Lock-in must be assessed before signing, when avoiding it is still free — export clauses and standard formats are negotiated with pre-contract leverage. At renewal the lock-in itself has already moved pricing power to the vendor, and later stages only confirm the cost.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Before signing with a payroll provider that will hold employee banking data, a company reviews the provider's security certifications, financial health, and incident history. What is this activity?
options: Due diligence — assessing the vendor's risk before the relationship and its trust begin
Offboarding — the controlled process of ending a vendor relationship and revoking access
Benchmarking — comparing the vendor's configuration guides against external consensus
Attestation — the vendor's customers confirming the provider met its obligations last year
explain: Third parties are assessed before signing; due diligence examines the vendor's security posture, stability, and history before trust is extended. Offboarding happens at exit, benchmarking compares guidance documents, and attestation confirms past performance rather than vetting a new partner.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A contract with a data-processing vendor includes the company's right to inspect the vendor's controls and evidence on request. Why does this clause matter?
options: It transfers all legal liability for a vendor breach from the customer to the vendor permanently in all circumstances
It preserves the customer's ability to verify the vendor's security rather than relying on trust alone
It exempts the customer from ever assessing the vendor again during the contract's lifetime
It allows the customer to set the vendor's internal security policies and staffing decisions
explain: A right-to-audit clause keeps verification possible throughout the relationship. It does not erase the customer's own accountability, remove the need for ongoing assessment, or hand the customer control of the vendor's internal management.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A vendor relationship ends, but the vendor's support accounts and API keys remain active in the customer's environment months later. Which phase of third-party risk management failed?
options: Procurement — the original request for proposal should have prevented the accounts existing
Due diligence — the initial assessment should have predicted the exact date access would linger afterward
Exit and offboarding — access must be revoked and data returned or destroyed when the relationship ends
Benchmarking — the vendor's configuration guides were never compared with external consensus
explain: Vendors are exited carefully: accounts disabled, keys revoked, and data returned or verifiably destroyed. Procurement and due diligence happen at the front of the relationship, and benchmarking is unrelated to closing out access.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A critical vendor suffers a breach that exposes the data of all its customers, including your company, even though your own systems were never touched. What does this illustrate?
options: Insider risk, because the vendor's employees are treated as members of your own workforce in the partner organization
Residual risk, because any risk remaining after an incident is classified by that name
Zero-day risk, because the vendor's vulnerability was unknown to the security community
Third-party risk — vendors inherit your trust and extend your attack surface beyond your own perimeter
explain: Vendor compromise is third-party risk in action: the trust and data you extend to a partner become part of your exposure. The vendor's staff are not your insiders, residual risk is what remains after your own treatment, and nothing here establishes an unknown vulnerability.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company sends prospective vendors a detailed set of questions about encryption, access control, incident response, and compliance certifications. What is this tool?
options: A security questionnaire used to assess a vendor's controls during evaluation and review
A request for quote, because any document sent to several vendors is a pricing instrument
A service-level objective, because the questions define the vendor's performance targets
A gap analysis, because the answers will be compared against a target framework later
explain: Security questionnaires are a standard vendor-assessment tool for collecting control evidence. An RFQ asks for price on a fixed spec, SLOs are measurable performance targets, and a gap analysis compares an organization's own controls against a framework.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A vendor scores well on its questionnaire but refuses to provide any supporting evidence and has suffered two undisclosed breaches. What is the sound conclusion?
options: The questionnaire result settles the assessment, because vendors are required to answer every question honestly throughout the assessment process
Self-reported answers without evidence are weak assurance; the undisclosed breaches deepen the concern and warrant escalation before signing
The breaches are irrelevant, because they happened before the current contract discussions began
The vendor should be signed quickly, because a high questionnaire score indicates a mature security program
explain: Questionnaire responses are claims, not proof; assessors corroborate them with evidence, and concealed incidents undermine the trust the whole relationship depends on. Scores alone do not settle an assessment, and past breaches are directly relevant to the risk being accepted.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A business line wants to adopt a free file-sharing tool immediately, with no contract, no assessment, and employee data uploaded by Friday. What is the third-party risk concern?
options: There is no concern, because free tools fall outside the scope of third-party risk management entirely in the program
The only concern is cost, because procurement rules exist mainly to negotiate better pricing
An unassessed vendor would hold company data outside every control the program applies to approved suppliers
The concern is lock-in, because a free tool can never be replaced once employees begin using it
explain: Data given to any outside provider creates third-party risk whether or not money changes hands; unassessed tools bypass due diligence, registry tracking, and contractual protections. Cost is not the issue here, and a free tool is replaceable — the exposure is the unvetted data flow.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Which clause in a vendor contract MOST directly protects a company if the vendor's service is discontinued?
options: A marketing clause allowing the vendor to use the company's logo in its customer materials for the duration of the agreement
A confidentiality clause covering information the two parties exchange during the contract
An indemnity clause describing how certain legal costs will be shared between the parties
An exit clause guaranteeing data return in a usable format and transition assistance at the end of the contract
explain: Exit protections — data returned in a usable format plus transition help — are the direct counterweight to discontinuation and lock-in. Logo rights, confidentiality, and indemnity are legitimate clauses but none of them gets the company's data and operations out intact.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company depends on a single vendor for a critical function, and that vendor announces it is exiting the market in six months. Which earlier practice would have reduced this exposure the most?
options: Assessing concentration and lock-in risk before signing, including exit terms and alternative suppliers
Negotiating a lower price at the last renewal, which would have funded an emergency migration in time to help
Requiring the vendor to complete a longer questionnaire at the start of the relationship
Adding the vendor to the vendor registry, which documents the dependency after the fact
explain: Concentration and lock-in are strategic risks evaluated before signing, when exit terms and alternatives can still be arranged. Price savings do not create an exit path, a longer questionnaire does not reduce dependence, and registering a dependency only documents it.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Midway through a three-year contract, a vendor quietly disables several security features and its response times slip for two consecutive quarters. Which process should catch and address this?
options: The original RFI process, which can be rerun to ask the vendor what it is able to do now
Ongoing vendor monitoring — performance and security posture are watched during the relationship, not only at signing
The expression of interest, which confirms whether the vendor still wants the company's business over the coming contract term
The gap analysis, which compares the company's internal controls against a target framework
explain: Third-party risk is managed during the relationship through monitoring against SLOs and security requirements, with contractual remedies when performance slips. The procurement documents belong to selection, and a gap analysis examines the company's own controls.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A master services agreement is in place, and a specific project needs its scope, deliverables, and timeline defined. Which document provides that?
options: A request for proposal that invites the vendor to suggest what the project should include and deliver under the master agreement once selected
A service-level objective that sets the uptime target for the project's production system
A statement of work that defines the specific project's scope, deliverables, and schedule under the broader agreement
A vendor registry entry that records the project's existence for tracking purposes only
explain: A statement of work defines a specific engagement's scope and deliverables beneath a master agreement. An RFP solicits proposals before selection, an SLO sets a measurable performance target, and a registry entry merely records the relationship.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Two finalists remain for a sensitive contract. One is cheaper; the other provides independent audit reports, clear exit terms, and standard data formats. What does third-party risk practice counsel?
options: Select the cheaper vendor, because procurement's role is to minimize the contract's purchase price in this procurement
Select neither vendor, because any third party that handles sensitive data is an unacceptable risk
Require both vendors to merge their offerings, which eliminates the need to choose between them
Weigh the full risk picture — assurance evidence, exit cost, and lock-in — rather than selecting on price alone
explain: Vendor selection balances cost against assurance, exit terms, and lock-in exposure; the cheapest bid can carry the most expensive risk. Outsourcing sensitive work is routine when it is assessed and governed, and combining vendors is not a real option.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A vendor will store regulated customer data in its cloud. Which requirement should the contract address explicitly?
options: Security and compliance obligations for the data, including breach notification duties and evidence of controls
The vendor's office locations, so employees know where their support calls will be answered
The vendor's product roadmap, so the company can plan around features that do not exist yet
The vendor's hiring plans, so the company can approve the staff who will join the account team over the next several years
explain: When a vendor holds regulated data, the contract must carry the security and compliance obligations — protection duties, breach notification, and evidence of controls. Office locations, roadmaps, and hiring plans may interest the business but they do not govern the data risk.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A firm discovers an approved vendor has begun subcontracting data processing to a fourth party the firm never assessed. What is the core issue?
options: There is no issue, because subcontracting automatically extends the original vendor's assessment to every subcontractor at any point
The firm's data now flows to an unassessed party outside the due diligence and contract controls it applied to the vendor
The issue is purely pricing, because subcontractors usually charge less than the original vendor does
The issue is that the vendor registry must be reformatted to include the subcontractor's logo and address
explain: Subcontracting extends the trust chain to a party that was never assessed — a classic fourth-party risk that contracts should govern with notice and approval rights. Assessment does not transfer automatically, and the concern is unvetted data access, not price or registry formatting.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A vendor's monthly reports show every SLO met, yet users experience repeated outages the reports never mention. What is the management lesson?
options: The SLOs should be deleted, because performance targets clearly cannot describe a real service
The vendor should be replaced immediately, because any reporting gap proves deliberate fraud
Reported metrics must be verified against reality — SLO reporting is checkable evidence, not a substitute for monitoring
Users should be trained to trust the reports, because perception is not a valid security metric in security reporting generally
explain: SLOs exist so performance is checkable rather than based on impression — and checking includes validating that the reported numbers reflect actual service. Deleting targets removes the leverage, a gap does not by itself prove fraud, and dismissing user experience ignores the verification the metric was built for.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A regulation requires a firm to file quarterly reports demonstrating that its controls over customer funds are operating. What is this activity?
options: Compliance training — the instruction that teaches employees which obligations they personally carry they personally carry at work
A legal hold — the suspension of normal deletion for material relevant to anticipated litigation
A gap analysis — the comparison of current controls against a target framework's requirements
Compliance reporting — the internal and external reporting that proves obligations are being met on the required schedule
explain: Compliance reporting proves obligations are being met, on the schedule the obligation itself sets. Training teaches people their duties, a legal hold preserves evidence, and a gap analysis compares controls to a framework rather than reporting to an authority.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Litigation is anticipated, and the legal team orders that all emails and documents related to a contract dispute be preserved, overriding the normal 90-day deletion schedule. What is this?
options: A legal hold — retention schedules are overridden and disposal of relevant material is suspended
A compliance report — a scheduled filing that demonstrates obligations are being met are being met this quarter
An opt-out request — an individual's instruction to stop certain uses of their data
A data correction — a request to fix an inaccurate record about an individual
explain: A legal hold stops normal deletion for anything relevant once litigation is anticipated; destroying held material becomes an offense of its own. It is not a report, a privacy preference, or a record correction.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: An employee, following the standard retention schedule, deletes a mailbox that was under legal hold, believing he was helping with storage cleanup. What is the consequence profile?
options: There is no consequence, because following a written retention schedule is always a complete defense in cases of this kind
The destruction of held material can itself become a serious legal offense, separate from the underlying dispute
The only consequence is that the legal team must reconstruct the mailbox from employee memory
The hold is automatically extended to all remaining mailboxes as the standard penalty
explain: Under a legal hold, disposal is suspended and destroying held material is an offense of its own — good intentions and the old schedule do not protect the deleter. Reconstruction cannot restore destroyed evidence, and no automatic extension penalty exists.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A customer exercises her right to stop receiving marketing messages while keeping her service account. The company must honor this promptly. Which privacy concept is this?
options: An opt-in choice — the individual's affirmative consent given before a use of data begins in any company system
A data correction — the individual's request to fix information that is recorded wrongly
An opt-out choice — the individual's decision to end a specific use of their information, which the company must respect
A legal hold — the preservation of the customer's records for anticipated litigation
explain: Opt-out is the choice to stop a use of one's data, and honoring it is a day-to-day compliance duty. Opt-in is consent given before a use starts, correction fixes inaccurate records, and a legal hold concerns litigation preservation.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A company may not enroll customers in a new data-sharing program unless each customer affirmatively agrees first. What is this requirement?
options: Opt-out consent — the use begins automatically unless the person objects to it later
Implied consent — long-standing customers are assumed to agree based on the relationship
Grandfathering — existing customers are permanently exempt from the consent requirement
Opt-in consent — the use of the data begins only after the person actively agrees to it
explain: Opt-in means affirmative agreement before the use begins. Opt-out starts the use and waits for objection, implied consent assumes agreement from circumstances, and grandfathering exempts a group — none of which matches a requirement for active agreement first.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A customer notifies a bank that his address and date of birth on file are wrong and asks for them to be fixed. How should the bank treat the request?
options: As a compliance task with a deadline — correcting a person's inaccurate record is a privacy duty, not a favor
As a courtesy request that can be handled whenever the branch happens to have free time
As a security incident, because incorrect records always indicate an account takeover attempt in the account records
As an opt-out, because the customer is objecting to how his information is being used
explain: Data correction is a privacy right in daily operation: when a person says their record is wrong, fixing it is a compliance obligation with a deadline. It is not discretionary courtesy, not automatically an incident, and not an opt-out from a data use.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Which set of duties belongs to anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing compliance?
options: Setting password complexity rules, reviewing firewall logs, and patching internet-facing servers
Knowing your customer, monitoring for laundering patterns, and reporting suspicious activity as required
Negotiating vendor contracts, tracking service-level objectives, and maintaining the vendor registry for the business
Running phishing simulations, scoring employee behavior, and delivering remedial security training
explain: AML/CTF compliance centers on knowing the customer, watching for laundering patterns, and reporting suspicion. The other sets describe technical security operations, vendor management, and awareness programs — different compliance territory entirely.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A salesperson offers a procurement official an expensive gift shortly before a contract decision, expecting favorable treatment. Which compliance area does this implicate?
options: Anti-money-laundering rules, because any valuable item offered to an official is laundered money
Data correction duties, because the gift must be recorded accurately in the official's file
Anti-bribery rules — gifts must never become purchases of influence over a decision
Opt-in requirements, because the official must affirmatively consent before receiving anything
explain: Anti-bribery duties draw the line at gifts becoming influence over decisions. No funds are being disguised here, so it is not laundering; the issue is the influence attempt, not record accuracy or consent mechanics.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: A new regulation takes effect in six months. Which action best prepares the compliance program?
options: Wait for the first external audit under the new rule, which will list everything that must change before anything else is done
Announce the regulation in a newsletter and consider the workforce's obligations fully handled
Ask each department to interpret the rule independently so local practices can develop naturally
Map the new obligations to affected processes, assign owners, and build the reporting that will prove compliance
explain: Effective compliance is proactive: obligations are mapped, owned, and given reporting before the deadline arrives. Waiting for an audit discovers gaps too late, a newsletter is not implementation, and uncoordinated local interpretation produces inconsistent compliance.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: Call-center staff handle payment cards, warehouse staff never do. The compliance lead gives deep payment-card training to the call center and a short general module to the warehouse. What principle is she applying?
options: Compliance training should be role-specific, so the people carrying an obligation know that they are carrying it
Compliance training must be identical for everyone, and her approach violates that requirement regardless of the roles involved
Training depth should follow seniority, because senior staff carry every compliance obligation
Only staff who request training need it, because obligations apply only to the willing
explain: Compliance training is role-specific instruction matched to the obligations each role actually carries. Identical training wastes depth where it matters, seniority does not determine who handles regulated data, and obligations bind staff regardless of whether they volunteer.
domain: Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight

q: An internal compliance review finds a control failing, and the same failure appears in the report filed with the regulator because the reviewer assumed the internal report could be copied directly. What is the underlying lesson?
options: External reports should always be softer than internal ones so regulators see fewer problems
Internal and external compliance reporting serve different audiences and must each be prepared accurately for their purpose
